title:
Photobiocatalytic Diastereo-
and Enantioselective
Synthesis of Noncanonical Amino Acids Bearing Challenging Stereochemical
Dyads and Triads
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Catalyst-controlled stereodivergent synthesis of acyclic molecules bearing multiple stereogenic centers remains a longstanding challenge in asymmetric catalysis, particularly through intermolecular radical C–C coupling. Here, we report the directed evolution of pyridoxal 5′-phosphate (PLP)-dependent biocatalysts for the stereodivergent synthesis of noncanonical amino acids bearing either skipped α,γ-stereochemical dyads or contiguous α,β,γ-stereochemical triads. Starting from a thermophilic tryptophan synthase β-subunit, protein engineering generated complementary enzyme variants that selectively construct three of the four possible α,γ-stereoisomers through biocatalyst-controlled reversal of both remote γ-stereochemistry and proximal α-stereochemistry. These engineered enzymes catalyzed intermolecular radical C–C bond formation with a broad range of secondary alkyltrifluoroborates, affording α,γ-disubstituted amino acids in excellent yields and stereoselectivities. Furthermore, directed evolution enabled efficient β-dehydroxylative radical coupling of the non-native threonine-derived aminoacrylate intermediate, providing amino acids bearing contiguous α,β,γ-stereochemical triads with up to 96:4:&lt;0.1:&lt;0.1 d.r. and &gt;99:1 e.r. To further demonstrate the synthetic utility of this platform, the stereochemically enriched amino acids were transformed into valuable γ-chiral amines through engineered PLP-dependent tryptophan decarboxylases, establishing a dual PLP enzyme-based biocatalytic cascade for the enantiodivergent synthesis of privileged amine scaffolds. Molecular dynamics simulations reveal that enzyme-controlled γ-stereoselectivity originates from active-site remodeling that modulates π–π interactions and steric contacts governing the facial selectivity of the radical addition step. This work expands the synthetic capabilities of radical biocatalysis by enabling catalyst-controlled stereodivergent assembly of complex acyclic stereochemical arrays and establishes engineered PLP enzymes as versatile catalysts for the synthesis of stereochemically complex amino acids and chiral amines.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Radical–Electrochemical
Coupling Enables Amination
of Methane
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The selective functionalization of methane under ambient conditions is widely regarded as a holy grail in chemistry, yet remains fundamentally limited not only by the inertness of the C–H bond but also by the transient nature of highly reactive intermediates. Short-lived species are often difficult to preserve and utilize prior to productive coupling, constraining accessible reaction pathways and product selectivity. Here, we establish a reaction framework based on in situ interfacial interception of reactive radicals, enabling the temporal coordination between radical lifetime and subsequent reaction processes. Plasma generates short-lived methyl radicals in immediate proximity to a gas–electrode interface, allowing their direct delivery and capture at the catalytic surface, while the electrochemical interface independently converts ammonia into surface-bound amino intermediates. Their coupling enables selective C–N bond formation. This spatially and temporally coordinated process allows highly reactive radical species to be synchronized with interfacial reaction steps, facilitating their productive utilization. Guided by density functional theory, we identify a nickel–cobalt layered double hydroxide catalyst that promotes interfacial coupling between *CH3 and *NH2 intermediates. The optimized system achieves a Faradaic efficiency of 54% for methylamine at 10 mA cm–2, with a productivity of 201 μmol cm–2 h–1 under ambient conditions. Beyond methane amination, this work demonstrates that coordinating the lifetime and transformation of reactive intermediates provides a generalizable strategy for catalytic control, offering new opportunities for the activation and selective transformation of inert molecules.</jats:p>

title:
Uncovering Microbial
Nitrogenous Chemical Diversity
through Isotope-Guided Molecular Networking
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Nitrogen-containing natural products are pivotal sources of bioactive molecules. However, their comprehensive investigation by metabolomics remains challenging due to background interference from primary metabolites and their high structural diversity including peptides, alkaloids, nucleosides, and others. Here, we present NitroVISION, an integrated pipeline that combines stable isotope labeling with targeted molecular networking to selectively detect nitrogen-containing metabolites from a complex mixture. Applied to five well-characterized Streptomyces strains, NitroVISION identified 42 nitrogen-containing natural products across 23 distinct compound classes, from which we characterized menaxinnamide, a new subclass of nonribosomal peptides incorporating a methylnaphthoquinone unit, and octapiperamide, a novel ribosomal peptide featuring a unique piperazine ring. Our work reveals the hidden chemical space of nitrogenous natural products and paves the way for the systematic exploration of microbial metabolic dark matter.</jats:p>

title:
Unraveling Water Balances
behind Salt Formation in
CO2 Reduction Electrolyzers
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Salt precipitation in CO2 electrolyzers remains a critical barrier to long-term stability, yet the underlying water-salt transport and balance are poorly understood. Here, we established a quantitative mass balance framework to account for water entering and leaving the cathode chamber from all possible sources and across different phases, thereby elucidating the origin of bicarbonate salt formation. We revealed that although the inlet CO2 stream typically flows through a water bubbler, it is often not fully saturated with water vapor and thus results in significant liquid water evaporation inside the cathode chamber. Although water crossover from the anolyte to the cathode is, in principle, sufficient to dissolve the cotransported K+ as carbonate species (or even bicarbonate in some cases), evaporation reduces the effective local liquid water-to-K+ ratio, leading to salt precipitation. Conversely, excessive humidification suppresses salt formation but induces electrode wetting and flooding, highlighting a fundamental trade-off between dehydration-induced crystallization and overhumidification-driven mass transport limitations. Together, these findings establish water management as a governing principle for stabilizing CO2 electrolyzers and provide engineering guidelines for controlling salt formation in electrochemical reactor systems.</jats:p>

title:
Operando Time-Resolved
Spectroelectrochemical Microscopy
Reveals Distinct Electron Depletion Pathways in Electrocatalysis
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Understanding electrocatalysis requires direct knowledge of how charge carriers are distributed and consumed at active sites under the operating conditions. However, the spatiotemporal dynamics of injected electrons in working catalysts remain largely inaccessible, hindering a mechanistic understanding of catalytic heterogeneity. Here, we develop an operando time-resolved spectroelectrochemical microscopy that enables direct and quantitative mapping of electron density with microsecond temporal resolution and micrometer spatial resolution. Using monolayer MoS2 as a model system, we directly visualize the spatial redistribution and depletion of electrochemically injected electrons during the hydrogen evolution reaction. We observe pronounced site-specific electron depletion that correlates with catalytic activity and further identify two distinct mechanisms governing charge loss: reaction-limited depletion at highly active sites, including edges and Pt-functionalized sites, and injection-limited depletion in bilayer regions. These results establish a quantitative link between local charge carrier dynamics and catalytic activity and provide a general framework for probing nanoscale carrier dynamics in electrocatalysts.</jats:p>

title:
Photoinduced Ge(II)-Catalyzed
Divergent Functionalization
of Pyridyl Halides via Electron Donor–Acceptor Complexes
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We report a photoinduced Ge(II)-catalyzed strategy for divergent functionalization of pyridyl halides that leverages in situ electron donor–acceptor (EDA) complex formation to catalytically generate pyridyl radicals, enabling aryl, alkynyl, and alkenyl couplings under mild, protic conditions without an external photocatalyst. Notably, the protocol exhibits excellent chemoselectivity for pyridyl C–X bonds, leaving other aryl halides, including those bearing electron-withdrawing substituents, intact. The protocol further enables unique transformations, including complete C8-selective coupling with 7-aminoquinoline and the modular assembly of benzo[f]isoquinolines from alkenyl boron reagents. Mechanistic studies support an EDA-mediated radical pathway. This work provides a sustainable platform for the divergent functionalization of pyridyl halides and expands the application of main-group elements in catalytic EDA chemistry.</jats:p>

title:
A DNA Origami Nanodevice
Programs CD20 Spatial Organization
for Selective Apoptosis of Malignant B Cells in Lymphoma Therapy
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Triggering CD20 clustering to induce B cell apoptosis is considered a promising therapeutic strategy for dysregulated, B cell-driven diseases, yet current methods lack the spatial precision to organize CD20 into defined clusters and fail to discriminate malignant from normal B cells. Here, we describe an intelligent DNA origami nanodevice that integrates an optimized anti-CD20 antibody array with a conformational switch to selectively induce CD20 clustering and apoptosis in B-cell lymphoma. Benefiting from the nanometric precision of DNA origami, we found that arranging anti-CD20 antibodies into a pentavalent array with approximately 10 nm spacing most effectively drives CD20 clustering and downstream apoptosis. Under resting conditions, the nanodevice stays in a closed, tubular shape that conceals the antibody array inside and therefore remains harmless to normal B cells. Upon encountering c-Met expressed on lymphoma B cells, the device unrolls into a planar sheet and exposes the antibody array, triggering potent apoptotic signaling specifically in these malignant cells. In a Raji xenograft mouse model, intravenously injected nanodevices specifically unrolled at the tumor site, inhibited tumor growth by more than 70%, and produced no significant systemic toxicity. By coupling programmable ligand nanopatterning with a shape-changing switch, this DNA origami platform offers a generalizable strategy for receptor-mediated disease therapy.</jats:p>

title:
Mechanistic Insights
of Jahn–Teller Effect
Suppression in High-Entropy Prussian Blue Analogue Cathodes
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The Jahn–Teller (J-T) effect, as discovered by Hermann Jahn and Edward Teller in 1937, often causes lattice distortion and structural instability in Mn-based battery materials. Recent studies suggest that high-entropy design may help suppress J-T distortion, yet the underlying mechanism remains largely elusive due to their compositional complexity and structural disorder. Herein, using a Mn-based Prussian blue analogue as a case study, we employed a machine learning interatomic potential combined with synchrotron extended X-ray absorption fine structure spectroscopy (EXAFS) to elucidate the fundamental mechanism of the J-T suppression in high-entropy materials. Unexpectedly, EXAFS spectra reveal the absence of the typical J-T Mn–N bond-length splitting in our high-entropy Prussian blue analogue sample, but instead a broader Mn–N bond-length distribution. Machine learning-assisted calculations demonstrate the [MnN6] octahedra exhibit randomly oriented distortions along x-, y-, and z-axes in high-entropy lattices, resulting in the local distortion averaging out at the macroscopic scale. Further analysis of the local Mn coordination environment reveals that the high-entropy configuration enhances d-electron delocalization and reduces the energy splitting between Mn dx2–y2 and dz2 orbitals. This allows two structurally and electronically distinct distortion modes to coexist within the lattice, which disrupts long-range cooperative J-T order. Strikingly, the ultralong cycling stability of high-entropy K0.46[Mn0.21Co0.19Ni0.21Cu0.20Zn0.19][Fe(CN)6]0.98·1.69H2O is experimentally demonstrated, achieving 91.0% capacity retention over 50,000 cycles for aqueous ammonium-ion storage, which surpasses all of the Mn-based rechargeable batteries to date. Our study uncovers the microscopic mechanism of J-T suppression in high-entropy materials and provides an effective strategy for designing durable high-entropy battery electrodes.</jats:p>

Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Low-Temperature
Aqueous Upgrading of Waste PET Plastics
into Metal–Organic Frameworks with Confined PdNi Clusters for
High-Performance Semihydrogenation of Alkynes
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The selective semihydrogenation of alkynes to alkenes is an important industrial process for the production of bulk and fine chemicals. However, the activity and selectivity trade-off of alkyne hydrogenation has been a long-standing challenge, due to undesirable overhydrogenation or insufficient activity of the designed catalysts. Here, we report a sustainable route for high-performance alkyne hydrogenation using a metal–organic framework (MOF) confined PdNi cluster (PdcNi) catalyst, synthesized directly from waste polyethylene terephthalate (PET) plastics under low-temperature aqueous conditions. The PdcNi@UiO-66 catalyst with dispersed Pd clusters anchored on Ni clusters not only maximizes Pd utilization but also establishes a new pathway for the recycling of plastics. Importantly, when employed as a catalyst for phenylacetylene semihydrogenation, PdcNi@UiO-66 exhibited outstanding activity and selectivity, achieving a turnover frequency (TOF) of up to 67,470 h–1 at 65 °C. This performance significantly surpasses that of previously reported catalysts and is nearly 20 times higher than that of the commercial Lindlar catalyst. DFT calculations combined with experimental results reveal that the PdcNi cluster exhibits a moderate adsorption strength toward both reactants and target products, compared with its nanoparticle and single-atom counterparts. This balanced adsorption leads to a more favorable thermodynamic tendency for styrene desorption rather than overhydrogenation, ultimately contributing to the high activity and selectivity. This study demonstrates a direct route to transforming PET waste into high-performance MOF-based catalysts for selective hydrogenation, offering a cost-effective and sustainable solution for plastic recycling and the development of high-performance catalysts.</jats:p>

title:
Finding the Sweet Spot:
Isomerization Strategy Enables
Balanced Energy Dissipation of NIR-II AIEgens for “One-for-All”
Tumor Phototheranostics
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>“One-for-all” phototheranostics with the second near-infrared window (NIR-II) emission have garnered great enthusiasm for seamlessly integrating superb imaging and high-efficiency therapy into a single formula. However, it is still a nontrivial conundrum to achieve balanced excited-state energy dissipation to guarantee high NIR-II brightness, photothermal conversion, and reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation. As a powerful tool for balancing radiative and nonradiative decays, aggregation-induced emission luminogens (AIEgens) are emerging as a promising frontier in developing “one-for-all” phototheranostic agents, while their phototheranostic performance needs to be further improved. In this contribution, we designed and synthesized two positional isomers, 5BT-PBPT and 6BT-PBPT, by attaching donors at the 5- and 6-positions of the benzo[b]thiophene (BT) segment, respectively, to investigate the effect of positional isomerism on the phototheranostic performance of NIR-II AIEgens. Interestingly, both experimental and computational results demonstrate that the isomerization affords great strength in tuning energy levels, structural conformations, aggregation behaviors, and excited-state energy dissipation. Consequently, a sweet spot for fully utilizing excitation energy was achieved in 5BT-PBPT nanoparticles (NPs), which exhibited not only strong NIR absorption but also high NIR-II fluorescence brightness, strong ROS production, and excellent photothermal conversion efficiency (η). Benefiting from this, 5BT-PBPT NPs afforded superior performance in the “one-for-all” phototheranostics for orthotopic breast tumor treatment. This study fully demonstrates the effectiveness of the isomeric engineering strategy in comprehensively improving the phototheranostic capabilities of NIR-II AIEgens and thereby provides an effective approach for the construction of high-performance NIR-II “one-for-all” phototheranostic agents.</jats:p>

                  <jats:p>Electrocatalytic conversion of CO2 into chemicals and fuels offers a promising route toward a circular carbon economy. High-temperature CO2 electroreduction in solid oxide electrolysis cells (SOECs) delivers high selectivity and energy efficiency, but balancing mechanical robustness and electrochemical performance remains challenging. Here, we address this challenge by introducing a hybrid ionic-conductor architecture that spatially decouples electrocatalysis, ionic transport, and mechanical support into function-specific layers. The resulting cell combines high mechanical robustness (fracture load &gt; 7 N) with 1.5–3.0-fold higher CO2-to-CO activity than state-of-the-art SOECs over 600–800 °C. Stable operation is maintained for over 1000 h at 1.0 A cm–2. Furthermore, we demonstrate scalability with a single-cell area of 100 cm2, achieving total currents up to 120 A and powers up to 200 W. This work establishes an effective strategy for developing mechanically resilient, efficient, and scalable energy conversion devices.</jats:p>

title:
MetaTag: A Biochemical
Reaction-Guided Design Strategy
for New Metabolite Discovery
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Most small-molecule features detected in untargeted metabolomics remain unannotated, representing the dark matter of the metabolome. Here, we introduce MetaTag, a biochemical-reaction-guided framework that generates high-probability novel metabolites by combining abundant endogenous metabolites with common enzymatic transformations derived from KEGG pathways. In this proof-of-concept implementation, we focused on N-acylation and N-alkylation reactions. We synthesized and characterized a physical library of 1068 compounds, creating a public MS/MS database (https://mtdb-website.vercel.app). Screening against 27 rat tissues matched 180 previously unreported metabolites with 6 at level 1 (confirmed by RT, formula, MS/MS) and 174 at level 2 (confirmed by RT, formula). These metabolites exhibited tissue-specific distributions and participated in the interorgan exchange during fasting. Functional interrogation of one such metabolite, N-propionyltaurine, demonstrated its role as a redox-sensitive regulator in brown adipocytes. This biochemistry-guided strategy provides a scalable platform for the discovery of previously uncharacterized bioactive metabolites.</jats:p>

title:
Breaking Symmetry Cancellation:
Heterovalent Substitution
Unlocks Ultrastrong, Phase-Matchable Nonlinearity in Deep-Ultraviolet
Tetrahedral Crystals
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Deep-ultraviolet (deep-UV) nonlinear optical (NLO) crystals demand a challenging integration of strong second-harmonic generation (SHG), sufficient birefringence for phase matching (PM), and a wide bandgap (λ &lt; 200 nm). In tetrahedron-based materials, the hyperpolarizabilities of constituent tetrahedra usually nearly cancel due to structural symmetry, resulting in weak SHG and small birefringence─a classic example being α-SiO2. Breaking this symmetry-driven cancellation while retaining deep-UV transparency thus represents a key chemical design challenge. Here, we report a deep-UV transparent NLO crystal BeSO4 derived from α-SiO2 via stepwise heterovalent tetrahedral substitution. This crystal crystallizes in the noncentrosymmetric tetragonal space group, with alternating BeO4 and SO4 tetrahedra forming [Be3S3O18] six-membered rings. By effectively breaking the symmetry cancellation via alternating low-valence (Be2+) and high-valence (S6+) tetrahedra, BeSO4 achieves a deep-UV cutoff at 176 nm, an exceptional SHG response of 5.1 × KDP at 1064 nm─the strongest among all deep-UV sulfates and Be-containing deep-UV crystals, and a birefringence of 0.038 at 590 nm, almost seven times that of the isostructural BPO4. Unlike BPO4 and α-SiO2, BeSO4 exhibits SHG behavior consistent with phase-matchability, and under 532 nm excitation, it produces a detectable second-harmonic signal at 266 nm. First-principles calculations reveal that the enhanced performance originates from shorter S–O bonds, stronger orbital hybridization, a narrower bandgap, and highly anisotropic electron density, all stemming from the successful cancellation-breaking strategy. It should be noted that the main novelty of this work lies in single-crystal growth, linear/nonlinear optical properties, and mechanistic analysis, since the crystal structure of BeSO4 has been previously reported.</jats:p>

title:
C–C
Bond Formation via the Addition or Redistribution
of Hydrogen: Chemical Synthesis Beyond Premetalated Reagents or Metallic
Reductants
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Stoichiometric organometallic reagents are used in countless C–C bond-forming processes but are often hazardous, display poor functional group compatibility, and require multistep preparation from the parent platform chemicals. Zerovalent metals are also used to mediate reductive C–C bond formation, but their use at scale poses similar safety and engineering concerns. The formation of C-nucleophiles as transient catalytic intermediates via hydrogen transfer from abundant low-molecular-weight reductants (H2, Me2CHOH, HCO2H) offers a more ideal alternative to preformed carbanions or zerovalent metals in reductive C–C bond formation. Related hydrogen autotransfer processes where reactants serve as redox pairs en route to products of C–C coupling also are desirable, as they avoid both sacrificial reductants and premetalated reagents. In this Review, hydrogen-mediated variants of classical reactions that exploit carbanions or zerovalent metals are described.</jats:p>

title:
Solid-State NMR Reveals
a Bifunctional Disordered
Linker That Couples Katanin Microtubule Anchoring to Condensate-Activated
Severing
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Microtubule severing by katanin drives rapid cytoskeletal remodeling for cell fate decision, yet how the catalytic subunit p60 (Kp60) recognizes the microtubule lattice to achieve efficient severing remains unresolved. Here, we report that the N-terminal intrinsically disordered region (IDR) of Kp60 is an essential bifunctional module for severing activity. Using solid-state NMR (ssNMR), we identified a microtubule-binding domain (MTBD) within the IDR which directly engages the lattice to guide substrate anchoring. Surprisingly, the same IDR also enables Kp60 phase separation. Our ssNMR analyses of the condensed phase pinpointed three discrete interaction regions within the IDR which cooperatively orchestrate this multivalent assembly. Importantly, Kp60 phase separation was associated with markedly increased ATPase activity, supporting a functional link between condensation and enzymatic activation. Using function-separation-mutation analyses, our studies show both microtubule binding and condensation are essential for severing: microtubule targeting provides spatial specificity, while condensation provides the catalytic threshold through local enrichment. Thus, the Kp60 IDR constitutes a bifunctional interface that integrates substrate recognition with enzymatic robustness, thereby establishing phase separation as a fundamental and efficient regulator of microtubule dynamics and cytoskeletal remodeling.</jats:p>

title:
Solid–Liquid
Transitions in 1D Metal–Organic
Chalcogenolates
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>A lack of melt processability is noted for emerging hybrid material systems like metal–organic frameworks, lead-halide perovskites, and metal–organic chalcogenolates (MOChas). Here, we report reversible solid-to-liquid phase transitions ranging from 67 to 184 °C in silver secondary-alkanethiolate 1-dimensional (1D) MOChas. These MOChas were synthesized using five different secondary alkanethiols: 2-propanethiol, 2-butanethiol, 2-pentanethiol, 3-hexanethiol, and 4-heptanethiol. Structural characterization using small-molecule serial femtosecond crystallography (smSFX) reveals a 1D wire crystal motif. These 1D wire lattices exhibit green-yellow photoluminescence that disappears upon melting. The low melting temperature is attributed to the conformational flexibility of the secondary alkanethiol ligands, providing entropic benefits for the amorphous state. Furthermore, the transition from a nonmolecular, infinite covalent (Ag-SR)∞ network in the solid state to oligomolecular species (Ag-SR)x in the molten state contributes to a higher enthalpy of fusion. Large crystallites are observed to evolve from the liquid near the phase transition temperature. Notably, unmixing of chiral domains occurs in the racemic crystals while the inorganic network remains unchanged.</jats:p>

title:
Biphasic Polyarylisocyanide
Liquid Crystals with Enhanced
Enantiodiscrimination for Residual Chemical Shift Anisotropy Measurements
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Anisotropic NMR spectroscopy has emerged as a powerful tool for the structural elucidation of complex small molecules. Compared with residual dipolar couplings (RDCs), however, the application of residual chemical shift anisotropies (RCSAs) has remained relatively limited, largely owing to the lack of simple and efficient methods for their acquisition. Here, we report a biphasic polyarylisocyanide lyotropic liquid-crystalline (LLC) system based on single-handed helical polyisocyanides prepared by alkyne-Pd(II)-catalyzed controlled polymerization. The biphasic nature of this medium enables straightforward extraction of ΔRCSAs from a single one-dimensional 13C NMR experiment on a single sample, without requiring specialized instrumentation, devices, or postcorrection. We demonstrate the broad applicability of this approach by measuring ΔRCSAs for eight structurally diverse natural products and organic molecules. The resulting 13C ΔRCSAs are sufficiently large to enable reliable structural verification and stereochemical elucidation. Notably, the method allowed us to unambiguously resolve previously questionable 13C NMR assignments in cryptotanshinone. In addition, the chiral LLC medium exhibits pronounced enantiodiscrimination, as demonstrated for indanol enantiomers as well as significant enantiodifferentiating capabilities for several natural alkaloids. Furthermore, 19F RCSA measurements enable direct differentiation of two enantiomers even within a racemic mixture. Together, these results establish biphasic polyarylisocyanide LLCs as a simple, robust, and broadly applicable alignment platform for ΔRCSA measurements, thereby expanding the utility of anisotropic NMR for structural elucidation and chiral molecular characterization.</jats:p>

title:
Noncovalent Metal–Water
Polarization Governs
Helmholtz Capacitance
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Electrified metal–water interfaces govern charge storage and electrochemical reactivity, yet the microscopic origin of their metal-dependent Helmholtz capacitance has remained unresolved. Here, we use extensive density functional theory-based ab initio molecular dynamics simulations to reproduce and explain the long-established experimental capacitance trend at fcc(111) metal–water interfaces. We show that this trend is governed primarily by the electrode-side electronic response of the explicit metal–water interface, which controls the effective electron spillover length and, hence, the bias capacitance. This relation remains predictive for cross-geometry Pt/Au systems. Our findings clarify the microscopic origin of metal-dependent Helmholtz capacitance and suggest a physically grounded design principle for electrode materials in sustainable-energy technologies.</jats:p>

title:
Understanding the Instability
Origin for Design of
Robust Pure RuO2 Anode Catalyst in PEM Water Electrolysis
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Ruthenium dioxide (RuO2) shows great promise as an acidic oxygen evolution reaction (OER) catalyst in proton exchange membrane water electrolysis (PEMWE), yet its insufficient stability─often attributed to Ru overoxidation─actually has a hidden cause. Herein, we show that the true culprit is instead residual chloride impurities inherited from the most commonly used RuCl3 precursor. Owing to strong Ru–Cl coordination, substantial chlorine residues are trapped in the RuO2 lattice during conventional synthesis; during electrolysis, they gradually leach out, dramatically accelerating Ru dissolution and lattice oxygen loss and triggering structural collapse. Guided by this insight, we developed a small-molecule-assisted synthesis that yields Cl-free RuO2. The resulting catalyst preserves exceptional structural integrity, sustains its initial activity through 80,000 accelerated degradation cycles, and delivers stable PEMWE operation at 500 mA cm–2 for 500 h, outperforming all reported single RuO2 catalysts and rivaling even the best doped or composite Ru-based catalysts. Our findings resolve a long-standing paradox in RuO2 catalysis and establish chloride elimination as a critical design principle for durable oxide electrocatalysts.</jats:p>

title:
Highly Enantioselective
Synthesis of 1,2,3-Trisubstituted
Cyclopropanes through DNA-Catalyzed Johnson–Corey–Chaykovsky
Cyclopropanation
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Developing enzymatic strategies for diverse reaction manifolds is a major objective in modern biocatalysis. Here, we report the first biocatalytic asymmetric Johnson–Corey–Chaykovsky (JCC) cyclopropanation via DNA catalysis. Unlike conventional small-molecule catalysis, which largely favors trans-cyclopropane formation, DNA catalysis enables diastereoselective access to both cis- and trans-cyclopropanes with excellent enantiocontrol from a single catalytic system. The platform accommodates sulfur ylides as well as amide- and ester-derived sulfoxonium ylides. In particular, phenolic ester-derived sulfoxonium ylides exhibit exceptional cis-selectivity while maintaining excellent stereocontrol, overcoming a longstanding limitation of small-molecule-catalyzed asymmetric JCC reactions. Preliminary mechanistic studies are consistent with a DNA scaffold-mediated pathway that promotes cis-diastereomer formation. Together with its scalability under low catalyst loading, this work establishes a previously inaccessible biocatalytic variant of the JCC reaction and expands the scope of DNA catalysis for diastereoselective synthesis.</jats:p>

title:
Vacancy-Induced
Ligand-Hole Character Redirects Oxygen
Redox in Li-Rich Layered Oxides
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Li-rich layered oxides access high capacities through the combined participation of transition-metal and oxygen redox, but oxygen oxidation is often coupled with irreversible structural rearrangement and voltage decay. Here, we show that oxygen-vacancy-preconditioning modifies the local Ni–O electronic structure and promotes oxygen-derived ligand-hole character in a Li-rich layered oxide. High-temperature quasi-single-crystal (QSC) formation generates oxygen-deficient local environments while preserving the overall layered framework. Synchrotron spectroscopy combined with density functional theory (DFT) calculations reveals enhanced Ni–O hybridization and redistribution of charge compensation toward oxygen-derived states. Mapping resonant inelastic X-ray scattering further shows earlier oxygen participation during charging, followed by increased delocalization of oxygen-derived holes within hybridized transition-metal–oxygen states. This modified redox pathway suppresses Mn reduction and is coupled to a distinct structural response in which transient lattice environments formed during the initial cycle progressively relax during prolonged cycling, while the layered framework is largely retained. The resulting cathode exhibits reduced voltage hysteresis and voltage decay, together with improved electrochemical reversibility. These results establish a direct connection between vacancy-modified ligand-hole character and oxygen-redox-driven structural relaxation, demonstrating how local electronic structure governs the structural pathway of oxygen-redox-active layered oxides.</jats:p>

title:
Smallest
Endohedral Water Cage Featuring a Nonclassic
Polyhedron: Experimental Observation of (H2O)17
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The structural transition from clustered water molecules to the hydrogen-bonding networks of bulk liquid defines one of the most fundamental problems in physical chemistry, yet the precise size at which the endohedral cages emerge remains experimentally elusive. While theory has long predicted that a fully encapsulated water molecule requires a minimum of 16–23 surrounding molecules, direct experimental identification has been hindered by the difficulty of size selection of neutral clusters. Using infrared spectroscopy coupled to vacuum-ultraviolet threshold photoionization, we provide the first experimental evidence that (H2O)17 forms the smallest water endohedral cage, achieving a decades-standing goal of establishing the molecular limit of a solvation shell. Surprisingly, the oxygen framework of this (H2O)17 cage defines an unprecedented, nonclassic polyhedron with four tetragonal, four pentagonal, and two hexagonal faces that breaks the symmetry constraints of all classical Platonic, Archimedean, and Johnson solids. This work establishes a critical structural precursor to the hydrogen-bonding network topology observed in condensed-phase water and offers new perspectives at the multidisciplinary sciences of mathematics, materials, physics, and chemistry.</jats:p>

title:
Highly Selective Artificial
Lithium Channels
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Sustainable mining and recycling of lithium (Li) have the potential to offer a secure and reliable global supply of lithium to meet rapidly growing energy-storage demands. Bioinspired technologies have the potential to increase sustainability and reduce the environmental impacts of lithium purification. In this study, we report the design of a class of bioinspired supramolecular membrane channels that, to the best of our knowledge, achieve one of the highest overall Li+ selectivities reported to date for artificial transmembrane ion channels, with conservative lower-limit selectivity estimates of Li+/Na+ ≥ 94, Li+/K+ ≥ 136, Li+/Mg2+ ≥ 286, and Li+/Ca2+ ≥ 228 under electrochemically driven transport conditions, thereby establishing a new benchmark for Li+-selective membrane channels. The single-channel conductance of this channel for Li+ ions was determined to be 13.35 pS, equating to Li+ ion transport rates of approximately 1.34 × 107 ions/s per channel at −160 mV. These channels were constructed using a central-ring pillar[5]arene appended with alkyl chains ending in diphenylphosphine oxide (DPP) ligands. Molecular dynamics simulations suggest that Li+ selectivity arises from coupled hydration-shell retention, ion-ligand coordination at the DPP-functionalized entrance, and confinement effects within the LAP5n10-DPP channel. At the DPP-functionalized entrance, Li+ retains much of its compact hydration shell while engaging the phosphoryl oxygen through a favorable ligand-exchange interaction, whereas Na+ interacts with the DPP region primarily through a water-separated outer-shell geometry, and K+ interacts more strongly with the adjacent hydrophobic/phenyl-rich region. At the central constriction, all ions experience hydration-shell disruption, but divalent Ca2+ and Mg2+ face the largest dehydration penalties because pore passage would require near-complete dehydration of their strongly bound hydration shells.</jats:p>

title:
Bridging Spectroscopy
and Reactivity: Identifying
the True Reactive CO Species in Electrocatalytic CO Oxidation
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In situ electrochemical vibrational spectroscopy has revolutionized our understanding of electrocatalysis. However, establishing a rigorous correlation between spectroscopic signatures and reaction kinetics is still very challenging because high-coverage surface species may dominate the signal, whereas the truly reactive participants may be short-lived or spectroscopically silent. To disentangle spectators from true reaction participants, we developed a high-sensitivity spectroelectrochemical platform that integrates the rotating disk electrode with surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (RDE-SERS). This approach enables the simultaneous acquisition of reaction kinetics and interfacial molecular information under well-defined mass transport conditions. Using this versatile approach, we investigated the benchmark carbon monoxide oxidation reaction (COOR) on the Pt surface, which enabled decoupling between the spectroscopically observable species and the catalytically active species. Despite persistent and intense Raman signatures of adsorbed CO (COad) in the diffusion-limited region, COad predominantly acts as a spectator that blocks surface sites without effectively participating in the reaction, as confirmed by the isotope substitution experiments. Conversely, the oxidation current is sustained by the continuous flux of solution-phase CO (COsol), which is identified as the kinetically relevant reactant. These findings offer a new perspective on the roles of adsorbed species versus solution-phase species during dynamic electrochemical reactions. Collectively, the RDE-SERS methodology is established as a reliable strategy for identifying true reaction pathways, bridging molecular-level spectroscopic identification with macroscopic reactivity in complex electrocatalytic systems.</jats:p>

title:
Macrocycle Size-Controlled
Dynamic and Static Chirality
in Donor–Acceptor [2]Catenanes
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Chiral [2]catenanes, a prominent class of mechanically interlocked molecules (MIMs), can exhibit either static or dynamic mechanostereochemistry. Controlling these mechanostereochemical states without altering the covalent connectivity, however, remains challenging. Herein, we report a series of chiral [2]catenanes derived from ExBox and cycloparaphenyleneperylene (CPPP), whose dynamic behavior is altered by the size of the CPPP macrocycle. We identified a sharp, size-dependent threshold: The conformational stereogenic unit of [7]CPPP is kinetically locked, whereas those of [8]CPPP and [9]CPPP are dynamic at room temperature. This conformational stereochemistry strongly biases the co-conformational stereochemistry in the catenane, effectively resulting in a single dominant diastereomer. This effective coupling of the two stereogenic units allows the conformational stereochemistry to be biased by the ion pairing of the interlocked cationic ring with a chiral anion. This research highlights the potential of mechanically interlocked architectures for controlling the dynamic mechanostereochemistry.</jats:p>

title:
Harnessing Surface
Wrinkling Instability for Visualizing
Dynamic Chemistry in Polymer Networks
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Studying dynamic chemical behaviors is fundamental to understanding and regulating the dynamic responses and functions of polymer materials. However, real-time, intuitive, and selective visualization of these molecular processes─particularly when multiple dynamic motifs coexist─remains a major challenge. Herein, we introduce surface wrinkles as a visualization platform that directly translates dynamic chemical behaviors in polymers into observable macroscopic morphological changes. Using a dual-cross-linked polymer network (DCN) containing quadruple hydrogen bonds and mechanical bonds as a model system, we fabricate stable wrinkles via modulus mismatch in a bilayer architecture. In situ microscopy reveals that acid-triggered dissociation of quadruple hydrogen bonds causes rapid wrinkle erasure due to network disruption, whereas base-induced rotaxane sliding leads to gradual wrinkle erasure owing to network relaxation, reflecting their distinct dynamic mechanisms and time scales. Rheological analyses on single-cross-linked model networks corroborate these macroscopic observations at the molecular level. Moreover, by programming wrinkle patterns with “write–hide–read” functionality, we achieve macroscopic visualization and differentiation of microscopic dynamic processes. This work establishes surface wrinkling as a powerful and intuitive platform for real-time monitoring of dynamic chemistry and provides valuable insights for designing functional polymer materials with tunable macroscopic properties.</jats:p>

title:
General
Synthesis of Inverse Opal Covalent Organic
Framework Photonic Crystals
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Constructing highly crystalline inverse opal covalent organic framework photonic crystals (IO COF PhCs) remains challenging due to the incompatibility between the spatial confinement required for inverse opal replication and the synthesis process of COFs. Inspired by the semi-solid chitin infiltration and confined solidification process in beetle photonic architectures, a solvent-free template-assisted melt pressing (STAMP) strategy is developed for the general synthesis of crystalline IO COF PhCs. The quasi-solid precursor state facilitates efficient template infiltration while remaining reactive for COF crystallization, affording ordered macroporous photonic architectures within 3 min. This strategy is broadly applicable to a library of 16 COFs spanning β-ketoenamine, hydrazone, imine, and imide linkages, yielding decimeter-scale monoliths with designable structural colors across the visible spectrum. By integrating periodic macroporosity, permanent framework porosity, and photonic functionality into one material platform, the resulting IO COF PhCs enable cross-scale programmable optical encoding and visually self-reporting adsorption. The application potential of IO COF PhCs is demonstrated for biomimetic anti-counterfeiting patterns and structural-color-indicated Au capture. This work establishes a general route toward crystalline IO COF PhCs and provides a versatile platform for coupling molecular functionality with photonic regulation in advanced smart materials.</jats:p>

title:
Mechanistic
Insights of Electroreductive Cobalt-Catalyzed
Asymmetric Radical Addition
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Transition-metal-catalyzed asymmetric electroreduction has emerged as a compelling platform for enantioselective C–C bond formation, with notable advances in electroreductive cross-coupling. Translating this success to stereocontrolled radical additions across unsaturated bonds remains a formidable challenge, particularly for the construction of fully substituted stereogenic carbon centers. Herein, we report an electroreductive, cobalt-catalyzed asymmetric radical addition of diverse organohalides to α-imino esters. This protocol delivers enantioenriched α-quaternary amino acid derivatives in up to 95% ee, completely circumventing the need for stoichiometric metal reductants. Beyond its synthetic utility, the electrochemical platform uniquely enables the direct interrogation of the operative electron-transfer events. A comprehensive mechanistic study─encompassing cyclic voltammetry, in situ electrochemical EPR spectroscopy, DFT calculations, stoichiometric experiments, and radical-trapping experiments─elucidates a highly orchestrated catalytic manifold. Crucially, we demonstrate that the α-imino ester serves a dual role, acting as both a radical acceptor and a redox-active ligand for the chiral cobalt catalyst. Subsequent cathodic reduction of the resulting cobalt–imine complex generates a key low-valent species that engages the alkyl halide via a turnover-limiting single-electron transfer (SET) to produce the requisite alkyl radical. Overall, this work establishes a robust electrochemical framework that synergizes reaction innovation with fundamental mechanistic elucidation in asymmetric radical catalysis.</jats:p>

title:
Amorphous Halide Cathodes
Enable 75C All-Solid-State
Lithium Batteries
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Power delivery in all-solid-state lithium batteries (ASSLBs) is often pursued by maximizing the bulk ionic conductivity of cathode active materials (CAMs), while grain-boundary (GB) ion-transport barriers caused by lattice mismatch remain a major kinetic bottleneck. Here, we reveal that minimizing GB transport barriers, rather than simply enhancing intrinsic conductivity, unlocks ultrafast ion-transport in halide CAMs. Amorphization converts crystalline LiVCl4 into a conformal amorphous phase that preserves short-range V–Cl coordination while minimizing long-range ion-transport tortuosity. Despite lower bulk Li+ conductivity, amorphous LiVCl4 dramatically reduces GB-associated interfacial resistance and enables a catholyte-free cathode (CAM content: 90 wt %) to deliver a capacity of 74.3 mAh g–1 at 5 mA cm–2, compared with 10.2 mAh g–1 for the crystalline counterpart. Meanwhile, the ASSLB further operates across a wide temperature range from −30 to 60 °C and achieves 84.2% capacity utilization at an ultrahigh A-LiVCl4 areal loading of 53.4 mg cm–2. Coupled with amorphous LiTaOCl4, the ASSLB achieves 102.1 mAh g–1 at 20 mA cm–2 (∼75C) and retains 82.3% capacity after 16,000 cycles. These results establish amorphization-enabled conformal interfaces as a new paradigm for ultrahigh-power ASSLBs.</jats:p>

title:
Comparing Nuclear Reaction
Coordinates Driving Photoinduced
Proton-Coupled Electron and Energy Transfer
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Proton transfer is coupled to electron transfer or electronic excitation energy transfer in proton-coupled electron transfer (PCET) and proton-coupled energy transfer (PCEnT) reactions, respectively. Although photoinduced PCET and PCEnT have been studied extensively in anthracene–phenol–pyridine molecular triads, the nuclear reaction coordinates for these two pathways are still unknown. Herein, we identify the nuclear reaction coordinates for PCET and PCEnT in the triads by sampling the seam space between the relevant intersecting diabatic states. The reaction coordinate has contributions mainly from anthracene and phenol for PCET but involves the entire triad, including pyridine, for PCEnT. Both reaction coordinates involve motions related to contraction of the phenol C–O bond as well as motions within the anthracene rings that differ for PCET and PCEnT due to different charge distributions. The proton acceptor motion contributes more to the PCEnT than the PCET reaction coordinate. Both PCET and PCEnT reactions are concerted in that there is no stable intermediate, but they are both most likely asynchronous. Our analysis also suggests that PCET proceeds through a conical intersection in its minimum energy pathway, whereas PCEnT moves through an avoided crossing. The quantum mechanical treatment of the transferring proton within a vibronically nonadiabatic framework suggests that the kinetic isotope effect may be greater for PCEnT than for PCET, although more extensive calculations are required for confirmation. Understanding the fundamental similarities and differences between PCET and PCEnT mechanisms will help guide the design of proton-coupled systems that favor either charge transfer or energy transfer.</jats:p>

title:
Cisplatin Conjugated
with Vinylsulfonamide Cross-Links
Pyruvate Kinase M2 to Trigger Ferroptosis
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Cisplatin serves as a first-line chemotherapeutic agent due to its DNA binding property. However, this intrinsic electrophilicity drives off-target interactions with proteins, which compromises anticancer efficacy, and also suggests the presence of unexplored targets. To identify platinum-binding proteins, a class of platinum(II) complexes containing a covalent vinylsulfonamide group were designed to provide stronger affinity for target engagement. By using competitive chemical proteomics technology, pyruvate kinase M2 (PKM2) was identified as the direct target of Pt1. The intracellular binding involved the recognition of the Cys49 pocket via cis-platinum moiety, which was strengthened by the synergistic event of platinum-centered ligand exchange and vinylsulfonamide-mediated covalent anchoring. This effective multimodal interaction disrupted PKM2 oligomerization and promoted its nuclear translocation. Subsequently, Pt1 induced ferroptosis via the PKM2-HMOX1 axis, further enhanced by mitochondrial oxidative stress. In xenograft models, Pt1 exhibited antitumor efficacy comparable to that of cisplatin, along with lower hepatotoxicity. This study presents a cisplatin conjugate that induces ferroptosis through intramolecular protein cross-linking, providing a synergistic coordination-covalent strategy for nonclassical platinum-based therapeutics.</jats:p>

title:
Aligned
Self-Assembled Nanostructure by Chemical Force
Trigger, Biased Migration, and Oscillatory Hydrogel Growth
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Cells generate pico-to-nanonewton forces through metabolic circuits and diffusion for downstream processes, including stress fiber assembly and cellular growth. The inherent complexities of the system’s processing, reactivity, and adaptability make it difficult to recapitulate in a synthetic setting. Herein, we compartmentalized the urease-urea feedback-controlled reaction network (FCRN), demonstrating global vs local function adaptability by coupling with peptide self-assembly. Compartmentalized FCRN (c-FCRN) facilitates chemical energy-to-mechanical energy conversion, creating forces on the piconewton scale, allowing nanofiber alignment, akin to what a cell does. The trade-off between multiple microscale interactions in the chemo-material network implies molecular-biased migration resembling chemotactic-like directed motion in synthetic settings, which promotes spatial self-assembly remodelling. Consequently, regulating the reaction-diffusion chemistry, we demonstrate oscillatory hydrogel growth by encasing the c-FCRN with a physical membrane barrier. Furthermore, c-FCRN provides a rudimentary structure-building system to create various complex hydrogel structures, bypassing the 3D printing tools. Thus, the chemo-material network provides proof-of-concept for biomimetic material development by emulating biologically inspired technologies.</jats:p>

title:
Quantum Ghost Spectroscopy
Reveals Hidden Coherence
in Molecular Aggregates
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Ultrafast spectroscopy of complex molecules has been achieved under light–matter coupling by the use of laser pulses and single photons. Yet, the excited-state dynamics essential to photochemistry is suffering from the convolution of multiple relaxation pathways and limited resolution in nonlinear signal, which still remain challenging. To address these, we develop time-resolved quantum ghost spectroscopy (tr-QGS) with entangled light, which enables a background-free detection of excited-state emission while offering precise control over temporal resolution. We apply this approach to perylene bisimide (PBI-1) trimers by combining a quantum description of light-molecule interaction with time-dependent density matrix renormalization group (TD-DMRG) simulations. This explicitly includes five vibrational modes and nonadiabatic coupling between electronic states. Our simulations reveal that tr-QGS captures electronic coherence oscillating at 0.6 eV for ∼50 fs, a signature of nonadiabatic coupling that was obscured in time-resolved measurements. Moreover, we observe a direct transfer from electronic to vibrational coherence at 200 fs, providing real-time visualization of vibronic relaxation pathways. Photon entanglement eliminates background noise and ground-state bleaching artifacts, which plague time-resolved measurements. These results establish tr-QGS as a transformative tool for interrogating nonadiabatic dynamics in molecular aggregates, light-harvesting complexes, and photocatalysts, offering a route to reveal quantum coherence effects in chemistry with unprecedented precision.</jats:p>

title:
Pressure-Induced Single-Crystal-to-Single-Crystal
Dimerization and Irreversible Optical Reconstruction in a 2D Hybrid
Lead Halide
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>External pressure is a powerful tool for tuning hybrid metal halides (HMHs), yet the resulting structural and optical changes are usually reversible upon decompression. Locking pressure-accessed states through covalent bond formation, particularly while preserving single-crystallinity and optical functionality, remains challenging. Here, we report a pressure-induced single-crystal-to-single-crystal (SC-SC) [2 + 2] dimerization in a two-dimensional lead halide, (S-MAMBA)2PbBr4, which contains acrylate-functionalized S-MAMBA+ cations. This process yields a stable dimerized single-crystal phase upon decompression. The topochemically preorganized arrangement of S-MAMBA+ enables irreversible cyclobutane formation while preserving the crystallinity. High-pressure vibrational and diffraction measurements, together with recovered single-crystal structure determination, establish the pressure-induced bond-forming transformation. During compression, the emission evolves from self-trapped exciton (STE)-dominated to free-exciton (FE)-dominated recombination near the dimerization threshold, indicating a reconstructed excitonic pathway. After decompression, the dimerized phase shows irreversible optical reconstruction, characterized by opposite absorption and emission shifts. Density functional theory (DFT) reveals that this chemical transformation perturbs the inorganic-framework band-edge electronic structure through changes in organic–inorganic interactions and interlayer coupling. This work demonstrates that pressure can be used as a novel and powerful trigger for permanent bond and electronic structure reconstruction in hybrid materials.</jats:p>

title:
Assisted Tandem Catalysis
with M–M Bonded Heterobimetallic
Pd–Pt Complexes: Accessing Both Pd and Pt Catalytic Cycles
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We report the synthesis of M–M bonded Pd–Pt complexes at the Pd(I)/Pt(I) and Pd(I)/Pt(III) oxidation states. These bimetallic complexes act as a reservoir for catalytically active Pd and Pt centers, and catalysis is observed in a variety of Pd- and Pt-catalyzed reactions. We demonstrate that tandem catalytic reactions with our Pd(I)/Pt(I) complex can capitalize on both Pd and Pt catalytic cycles to enable multistep processes. These include tandem hydrosilylation/Hiyama coupling, Suzuki coupling/amide reduction, Buchwald–Hartwig amination/amide reduction, and Heck coupling/amide reduction. Tandem cycloisomerization/Heck coupling is also observed with our Pd(I)/Pt(III) complex. Control studies demonstrate that homobimetallic Pd–Pd and Pt–Pt complexes do not perform the tandem catalytic reactions and that the Pd–Pt complex is stable under air and moisture for at least 9 months. The M–M bond in these complexes enables access to unique Pd and Pt oxidation states and facilitates M–M communication, both of which can have an impact during catalysis.</jats:p>

title:
Regioselective Growth
of Mesoporous Metal–Organic
Frameworks for the Construction of Anisotropic Nanohybrids
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Mesoporous anisotropic nanohybrids (m-ANHs) have attracted growing interest because their structural asymmetry enables unique advantages in applications such as multidrug co-delivery and cascade catalysis. However, anisotropic growth in mesoporous systems has thus far been largely confined to an amorphous framework. Achieving regioselective growth of crystalline functional units integrated with mesoporous frameworks remains highly challenging, primarily because of the intrinsic competition at the heterointerface between crystal nucleation/deposition and micelle-directed mesostructural coassembly. Herein, we report an acidity-gated interfacial crystallization-coassembly switching strategy to construct single-crystalline mesoporous MOF (meso-MOF)-based ANHs. This strategy enables the site-selective growth of a new single-crystalline meso-MOF compartment at predefined heterointerfaces, yielding a diverse family of well-defined frame-like, dumbbell-like, and ternary spiny nanohybrids. Mechanistically, precise regulation of the HCl/CH3COOH ratio modulates the nucleation kinetics of MOF precursors, generating localized supersaturation that is sufficient to trigger site-selective heterogeneous nucleation. Concurrently, synchronization of MOF nucleation/growth with interfacial micelle-directed coassembly allows crystallization and mesopore organization to proceed cooperatively. The applicability of this interfacial regulation is demonstrated in several lattice-compatible and chemically stable MOF systems with different compositions and hybrid configurations. As a proof of concept, the hierarchical spiny topology significantly enhances physical bacteria–material interactions, endowing the ternary ANHs with superior antibacterial performance. Remarkably, even in the absence of any drug loading, the ANHs achieve an approximately 90% inhibition efficiency against drug-resistant bacteria. This work establishes a versatile route to regioselectively integrate single-crystalline mesoporous domains into complex anisotropic nanohybrids and highlights the functional potential of structurally programmed crystalline mesoporous interfaces.</jats:p>

title:
Living
Spatially Organized Hybrid Condensates for
Efficient Light-Driven CO2-to-Chemical Conversion
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Light-driven CO2-to-chemical conversion presents a sustainable route for biomanufacturing, yet the performance of photosynthetic biohybrid systems remains fundamentally constrained by disorganized biotic–abiotic interfaces, which result in inefficient photoelectron transfer, low carbon production, and substantial cellular toxicity. Here, we report a spatially organized intracellular biohybrid system that enables the light-powered conversion of CO2 to 2,3-butanediol inEscherichia coli. Inspired by the algal pyrenoid, we constructed a TiO2/RuBisCO hybrid condensate (TRHC) by integrating protein liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS) with in situ biomimetic mineralization. This spatially defined condensate physically clusters light-harvesting and carbon-fixing modules, thereby facilitating direct photoelectron transfer and contributing to improved long-term cellular robustness under continuous illumination. The TRHC achieved an apparent quantum yield of 12.4% and reduced the light-induced cellular mortality by 64%. By providing a robust photoelectron supply for CO2 assimilation, the integrated system attains a 2,3-butanediol yield of 1.38 mol/mol from the consumed glucose. Moreover, under illuminated fed-batch fermentation, the platform maintains sustained biosynthetic activity over 5 days, producing 62.11 g/L of 2,3-butanediol. This LLPS-guided strategy offers a generalizable framework for engineering efficient biotic-abiotic interfaces in solar-driven biomanufacturing.</jats:p>

title: Catalytic Asymmetric Diels–Alder Reaction of β,β-Disubstituted Enals with Cyclopentadiene: Syntheses of (−)-Camphene, (−)-β-Santalene, and (−)-( Z )-β-Santalol
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Despite the long and rich history of the Diels–Alder reaction, certain aspects of its scope still remain remarkably underexplored. Most prominently, reactions with β,β-disubstituted enals as dienophiles are scarcely represented in the literature. The first general and highly enantioselective method, enabled by a strongly acidic and confined imidodiphosphorimidate organocatalyst, is reported here. The reaction tolerates a broad range of enals, including substrates with functional groups and complex alkenyl substituents, delivering the corresponding cycloadducts in good yields and excellent enantioselectivity. The synthetic utility of the method is further highlighted by concise asymmetric total syntheses of (−)-camphene, (−)-β-santalene, and (−)-(Z)-β-santalol from inexpensive starting materials.</jats:p>

title:
Stable
N-Heterocyclic Carbene-Derived α-Diimine
Radical Cations with Anionic Nitrogen Character
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Nitrogen-centered radicals possessing substantial anionic character have remained highly challenging to isolate because of their intrinsic electronic instability in the absence of metal coordination. Herein, we report a family of stable N-heterocyclic carbene (NHC)-derived α-diimine radical cations that constitute a rare class of persistent organic radicals featuring pronounced anionic nitrogen-centered radical character. Combined crystallographic, EPR, electrochemical, spectroscopic, and computational studies reveal an unusual electronic structure in which the molecular framework is formally cationic whereas both the unpaired electron and substantial negative charge are predominantly localized on the α-diimine nitrogen atoms. These radicals exhibit remarkable stability, undergo selective proton- and hydrogen-atom-transfer reactions, and participate in fully reversible, stepwise interconversion among dicationic, radical cationic, and neutral redox states without degradation of the molecular framework. Two-electron reduction induces reversible C–N bond formation to generate either an azetidinimine or a zwitterionic structure, with their relative stability governed by remote electronic substituents. Variable-temperature spectroscopy, UV–Vis analysis, and DFT calculations reveal dynamic solution-state equilibria that can be thermodynamically tuned through peripheral electronic modulation. These findings establish a new design principle for persistent nitrogen-centered radicals and reveal how redox state, charge distribution, spin localization, and reversible covalent bond reorganization can be coupled within a metal-free molecular framework.</jats:p>

title:
Molecular Diversity
Generation via Selective Enzymatic
C–CN Bond Scission
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Selective removal of functional groups offers a powerful route to streamline molecular design and generate structural diversity. The use of such deletion strategies has surged in organic synthesis, yet achieving these transformations with high selectivity remains a formidable challenge. Here, we present a photoenzymatic platform for stereocontrolled C–CN bond cleavage of malononitriles, enabling access to diverse chiral nitriles. Directed evolution of the flavin-dependent enzyme OYE1 yielded a variant that efficiently converted a wide range of geminal dinitriles, affording products in high yields (up to &gt;99%) and enantioselectivities (up to 3:97 e.r.). The platform was further extended to a one-pot cascade combining Michael addition with enzymatic decyanation. Mechanistic studies revealed a pathway involving a benzyl radical intermediate (Int1), followed by a carbanion species (Int2). This work establishes the first photobiocatalytic cyano group deletion strategy and provides a modular approach for sustainable synthesis of valuable chiral nitrile scaffolds.</jats:p>

title:
Electroenzymatic Cascade
Enables Amino Acid Synthesis
through Simultaneous Nitrite Reduction and NADH Regeneration
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Amino acids are central to life and the chemical industry, yet their sustainable synthesis remains a challenge. An electroenzymatic cascade offers a promising alternative by combining the electron/proton transfer capability of electrocatalysis with the exceptional specificity of biocatalysis. Here we present a conceptually distinct electroenzymatic cascade platform that integrates electrocatalytic nitrogen oxide reduction, NADH regeneration, and enzymatic reductive amination. Using l-glutamate (l-Glu) as a model, we demonstrate that with Cu nanowires as the bifunctional electrocatalyst, the system generates NH4+ and biologically active NADH in situ, driving the production of l-Glu under mild conditions. The coupled cascade not only shifts the reaction equilibrium forward but also provides a favorable orientation and a proton-rich environment for the bioactive cofactor, boosting overall selectivity of bioactive NADH. The modular design allows straightforward adaptation to diverse substrates and electrodes, demonstrating the broad generality of this platform. This work establishes a sustainable and versatile strategy for amino acid synthesis and opens new directions for electroenzymatic production of nitrogen-containing chemicals.</jats:p>

title:
A Photosensitizer Bearing
an Asymmetric “Push-Pull”
Bipyridine Ligand Enhances Excited State Electron Transfer
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Herein we report RuII photosensitizers that bear a single “push-pull” ligand designed to polarize charge on a single pyridine ring of 2,2′-bipyridine (bpy) in the metal-to-ligand charge-transfer (MLCT) excited state for enhanced excited state electron transfer. The photosensitizers have the general structure [Ru(dtb)2(4-CO2H,4′-R-bpy)]2+, where R is –H (RuHcb), −CF3 (RuFcb), and −CH3 (RuMcb) and dtb is 4,4′-(tert-butyl)2-bpy. These photosensitizers were synthesized, characterized spectroscopically and electrochemically, and contrasted with [Ru(dtb)2(dcb)]2+ (RuDcb) that bears the more common dicarboxylic acid ligand, Dcb = 4,4′-(CO2H)2-bipyridine. When anchored to mesoporous TiO2 thin films in a 0.1 M LiClO4/CH3CN electrolyte, RuMcb|TiO2 displayed the largest excited state electron injection yield ϕinj = 0.90 and, generally, ϕinj decreased as R became more electron withdrawing. RuDcb|TiO2 displayed a significantly lower ϕinj = 0.80. Transient absorption spectra recorded on ps and ns time scales and spectroelectrochemical data revealed that ∼70% of the total ϕinj for RuMcb occurred on a sub ps time scale that could not be kinetically resolved, only 20% occurred on this same time scale for RuDcb. Quantum chemical simulations were utilized to characterize the charge transfer excited states, the surface binding, and the interfacial electron transfer kinetics. Apart from RuFcb, the data reveal that the push–pull ligand had little impact on the ground state and a significant one on the MLCT excited state, polarizing charge on a sub-ps time scale for more efficient interfacial electron transfer. More broadly, the data reveals that push–pull ligands can be optimized for excited state electron transfer reactivity.</jats:p>

Chemical Society

title:
Beyond
Linker Length: Three-Dimensional Linker Geometry
Governs Flexibility in Zn–Triazolate MOFs
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Flexible metal–organic frameworks undergo cooperative structural transformations that underpin applications in molecular separations, sensing, and gas storage; however, the molecular origins of framework flexibility remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate the role of linker geometry in directing the structural response of a family of isoreticular Zn–triazolate pillared-layer MOFs incorporating cubane (cdc), bicyclo[1.1.1]pentane (pdc), and bicyclo[2.2.2]octane (boct) dicarboxylate linkers. Variable-temperature and in situ CO2 powder X-ray diffraction, variable-temperature single-crystal X-ray diffraction, gas adsorption measurements, and machine-learning-enabled atomistic simulations reveal fundamentally different mechanical responses despite the frameworks possessing closely related architectures. The cdc framework exhibits reversible cooperative breathing, the pdc analogue undergoes pathway-dependent structural reorganization consistent with kinetic trapping following cooling of the activated framework to 77 K, whereas the boct framework accommodates deformation through continuous elastic distortion without discrete phase transitions. Computational analysis demonstrates that these contrasting behaviors arise primarily from the manner in which linker geometry governs strain accommodation within the flexible Zn–triazolate sheets, rather than from the deformation of the linker itself. These results establish structure–mechanics relationships across this family of flexible MOFs and demonstrate that subtle changes in molecular geometry provide a powerful strategy for programming cooperative structural behavior.</jats:p>

Chemical Society

title:
Catalytic Uncaging
of Anticancer Drugs via a Buchner
Ring Expansion
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Selective drug activation in living systems remains a central challenge in targeted cancer therapy. Bioorthogonal catalysis addresses this by using abiotic transition-metal catalysts to unmask prodrugs at the tumor site, but the repertoire of suitable reactions remains limited. Here, we exploit the Buchner ring-expansion as a new uncaging strategy, in which a metal-carbene catalyzes a regioselective intramolecular ring-expansion followed by spontaneous 1,6-elimination to release a caged payload─a cascade with no biological equivalent. The iridium porphyrin complex [Ir(mPIX)Me] catalyzes this reaction at nanomolar concentrations, and the platform can accommodate structurally diverse payloads. As a proof of concept, functionalization with a bivalent human carbonic anhydrase IX (hCA IX) inhibitor enabled tumor-selective release of epirubicin (Epi) in a cancer cell model. This work thus delineates a new reaction class to the growing toolkit of transition-metal-mediated bioorthogonal chemistry.</jats:p>

Chemical Society

title:
Extended Active Learning-Guided
Design of Multi-Component
Electrolytes with Opposing Cosolvent Properties for Aqueous Zinc-Ion
Batteries
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Multi-component electrolytes offer expanded tunability over electrochemical properties, yet their rational design is constrained by a lack of generalizable principles. Intricate intercomponent interactions obscure the relationship between the molecular properties and battery performance, rendering material selection and compositional optimization intractable. Here, we present an extended active learning-guided framework to efficiently navigate the vast materials space and refine formulations for tri-solvent-based electrolytes in aqueous zinc-ion batteries with minimal experimental workload. Specifically, co-solvent candidates are clustered by molecular properties; co-solvents are then selected, and their pairwise combinations undergo rigorous formulation optimization. Our data-driven approach discovered a nonintuitive electrolyte composition: combining co-solvents with fundamentally opposing properties. This unique formulation, which disrupts the hydrogen-bonded network while reconstructing the solvation structure, enables Zn||NH4V4O10 full-cells to retain 90.2% capacity after 1,000 cycles. This study unveils the possibility of using active learning to discover unconventional electrolyte formulations that would otherwise be infeasible to identify through human insights.</jats:p>

Chemical Society

title:
Cryogenically Flexible
Organic Single-Crystal Heterostructures
via Molecular Alloying for Advanced Optical Tuning
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Organic single-crystal heterostructures (OSCHs) constitute a promising platform for advanced flexible optoelectronics, yet imparting mechanical flexibility to these multiblock systems, especially given the susceptibility to failure at the interfaces between individual crystal segments, remains challenging. This obstacle is particularly aggravated at cryogenic temperatures, where the freezing of vibrational motion may cause brittleness and lead to mechanical failure. Herein, we describe an epitaxial growth strategy using molecular alloys for the fabrication of crystals of cryogenically flexible two-color (blue–cyan–blue) triblock heterostructures, prepared by growing triphenylene (TP) segments onto perylene (PER)-doped alloy seed crystals via crystallization under controlled cooling. The compatibility between the host and guest molecules provides interfaces with low defect densities. Analysis of the crystal structure reveals an abundance of weak intermolecular interactions that are thought to enable the reversible elastic deformation observed at both 298 and 77 K, thereby preventing cracking. Simultaneously, efficient Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) between TP and PER enables continuous emission tuning and doping-ratio-controlled programmability of the optoelectronic properties. The resulting heterostructures not only support low-loss active optical waveguiding and programmable multichannel optical logic and information encoding but also remain fully operational for optical transduction during bending under cryogenic conditions. This work establishes a general molecular alloying approach to structures that integrate low-temperature mechanical compliance with sophisticated photonic functionalities, providing a pathway to deformable, multiemissive optoelectronics elements that remain operational in extreme environments.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Continuous-Flow Irradiation
Facilitates Catalyst-Free
Methane-to-Methanol Conversion
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Converting methane to methanol (MTM) holds far-reaching practical implications, yet achieving both high productivity and high selectivity remains a longstanding challenge owing to the inertness of methane and the susceptibility of methanol to overoxidation. Here, we propose a continuous-flow irradiation system (CIS) by coupling radiation technology and flow chemistry for efficient MTM under ambient conditions. High-energy radiation promises direct methane activation in an oxidant-independent and catalyst-free manner with high efficiency, which enables its integration with continuous-flow synthesis that decouples CH4 activation from methanol formation in time and space, thereby preventing overoxidation and undesirable cascade side reactions. The CIS–MTM achieves a superior methanol production rate (68.3 μmol·h–1, at a dose rate of 7.2 kGy·min–1, 83.2 RH%, CH4 flow rate 60 mL·min–1) than most existing indirect activation routes, with economic scalability comparable to industrial methods. This work introduces radiation technology as a potential direct activation method for methane conversion.</jats:p>
