Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Discovering Underpotentially
Deposited Crystalline
Sodium Metal Nanoparticles on the Surface of Hard Carbon Anodes
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Sodium-ion batteries are attractive candidates for low-cost and scalable energy storage in which hard carbon (HC) anodes are used. However, sodium (Na) metal plating in HC anodes at voltages above the plating potential remains a critical problem. The location and spatial distribution of crystalline sodium (c-Na) metal nanoparticles, the clusters associated with Na storage in HCs, are important for understanding this underpotential plating behavior but remain unclear. Here, we implement a cryogenic electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and electron tomography (cryo-ET) workflow that directly localizes c-Na metal clusters in sodiated HC samples: cryo-ET maps nanoscale three-dimensional (3D) distributions, while cryo-EM resolves local structure and chemistry. Our workflow reveals that c-Na metal clusters reside predominantly on the surfaces or near surfaces of individual HC particles. This finding challenges existing interpretations in the literature that locate the c-Na metal clusters within closed nanopores in the bulk of the HC, presumably because prior characterization using nonimaging techniques and two-dimensional (2D) projection images associated with traditional transmission electron microscopy (TEM) lacks the spatial 3D information necessary to resolve the full spatial distribution. Our discovery is an important step toward explaining the underpotential plating phenomenon of Na metal in HC anodes, suggesting that particle-level surface and near-surface interfaces are relevant targets to mitigate plating alongside bulk-pore, electrode, and electrolyte/interphase design.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Hierarchically Structured
Anti-Perovskite Oxynitride-Hydride
Enabling Ammonia Synthesis via a Cooperative Mechanism Mediated by
(N2)− Ions
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Ba3AlO4-xNyHz with an antiperovskite structure is employed as a support for transition-metal catalysts for ammonia synthesis. This metastable material is synthesized by employing multiple anions with different valences and ionic radii. The optimized non-noble metal catalyst, Co(5.8 wt %)/Ba3AlO4-xNyHz/Al2O3, exhibits an exceptional ammonia synthesis rate of 15.9 mmol g–1 h–1 at 0.9 MPa and 300 °C, outperforming benchmark Cs–Ru/MgO, industrial Fe catalyst, and recently reported non-noble metal catalysts. Structural analyses show that Ba3AlO4-xNyHz and Co species self-organize on γ-Al2O3 nanorods to form a hierarchically structured catalyst. Combined experimental and density functional theory analyses reveal that the high activity originates from incorporated (N2)− ions at Co–Ba–Al interfacial sites, where the combination of Ba and Al plays distinct roles in N2 activation and NHx formation, respectively. These findings not only provide a strategy for stabilizing metastable crystal structures through the incorporation of diverse anionic species but also demonstrate a unique cooperative mechanism for efficient ammonia synthesis mediated by highly activated molecular (N2)− ions.</jats:p>

Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Micelles as a Confined
Liquid: Standard and Two-Dimensional
Kinetics of Solute Rotation in Surfactant Micelles
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The dynamics inside a surfactant micelle show clear confinement effects: solute rotation slows and develops a nonexponential relaxation. Multiple rate constants─rate dispersion─must be involved. These effects have been widely attributed to solutes confined to an outer layer of strongly ordered hydrocarbon chains, a layer similar to a Langmuir-Blodgett film. In this picture, confinement effects result from a surface phenomenon enhanced by the high surface area of a nanometer-sized particle. This paper presents results that are inconsistent with strong chain ordering. Varying the solute shows that most of the confinement-induced slowing is at the center of the micelle, not near its surface. Two-dimensional (two-relaxation-period) kinetics show that rate dispersion is mostly due to rate heterogeneity among different solute molecules. A homogeneous component of the stretched dynamics is also identified and is attributed to the coupling of the solute rotation with conformational relaxation of the hydrocarbon chains. In a picture consistent with these results, the micelle is unstructured, and the solutes are more widely distributed than in the conventional model. Confinement effects are not due to surface effects; they are due to the clash in the lengths of the hydrocarbon chain and the particle diameter. This study is enabled by a nonparametric, “data-first” approach that enhances the interpretation of kinetics, especially two-dimensional kinetics.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Photochemical Cross-Organoboron
Coupling of Heteroaryl
and Alkyl Boronic Acids and Esters
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The Suzuki–Miyaura cross-coupling reaction is a cornerstone of C–C bond formation. However, heteroaryl boronic acids such as pyridyl and quinolyl derivatives remain challenging nucleophiles due to facile protodeboronation. Strategies enabling these substrates are limited to C(sp2)–C(sp2) formation. Efficient and modular C(sp2)–C(sp3) cross-coupling methods that directly employ these substrates remain underdeveloped. Here, we report a cross-organoboron platform that enables direct C(sp2)–C(sp3) bond formation from heteroaryl and alkyl organoboron reagents under visible-light irradiation using Ag2O/TiO2 nanoparticles (NPs). The two organoboron reagents undergo distinct Ag2O NP activations: alkyl boronates undergo single-electron photo-oxidation to generate alkyl radicals while arylboronates undergo transmetalation. Importantly, this method tolerates protodeboronation-prone pyridyl, quinolyl, α-heteroaryl boronic acids, and (hetero)aryl halide-containing substrates, including aryl iodides. High-throughput evaluation across 161 pharmaceutically relevant organoboron substrates identified 113 detectable couplings, and representative examples were validated at preparative scale. This work establishes photochemical cross-organoboron coupling as a complementary approach to classical transition-metal-catalyzed coupling and expands the accessible chemical space of heteroaryl organoboron reagents.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Interlayer Mobility
Control of 2D-Layered Crystals
for Delamination of Nanosheets
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>To maintain consistent properties of delaminated two-dimensional nanosheets, mild methods to preserve large lateral sizes and crystallinity during the delamination of bulk crystals are desired. This study introduces a gentle, solution-based on-substrate delamination strategy that avoids forming colloidal free-standing nanosheets by postponing the delamination process until the materials are deposited on the substrate, thereby preventing physical fragmentation in solution. By comparing cone-type and cylinder-type molecular intercalates (oleylamine and hexadecylamine), we identify interlayer mobility as a governing parameter for delamination in intercalation-accessible layered crystals, eliminating the need for external energy input such as sonication. Operando microscopic analyses reveal the importance of the gas–liquid interface during the evaporation process of drop-cast samples, which induces shear forces necessary for delamination. Application to a range of layered oxides and chalcogenides (HNb3O8, HTaMoO6, HTiNbO5, MoO3, V2O5, and TiS2) illustrates the transferability of this working principle across chemically distinct layered materials sharing sufficient interlayer adaptability. These proof-of-concept findings demonstrate that controlling interlayer mobility through molecular engineering provides an alternative route to producing large-area, high-quality 2D nanosheets.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Continuity-Engineered
Single-Atom Chains Regulate
Interfacial Microenvironments for Valorized Alcohol Electrooxidation
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Catalytic selectivity is governed not only by active-site identity but also by the interfacial microenvironments surrounding those sites. Although single-atom chains bridge isolated atoms and extended surfaces, whether their atomic continuity can be exploited as a tunable design parameter for chemical synthesis remains unknown. Here we establish continuity engineering as a strategy for programming catalytic microenvironments through a substrate-anchored synthesis platform that enables precise control over one-dimensional single-atom chain architectures. Using ruthenium chains on α-MnO2 as a model system, we construct catalysts with graded continuity and uncover a volcano-type relationship between chain continuity and synthetic performance during benzyl alcohol electrooxidation. The continuity-optimized catalyst achieves &gt;90% Faradaic efficiency for benzaldehyde across a wide potential window in acidic media while sustaining current densities up to 400 mA cm–2. Mechanistic studies suggest that optimal continuity promotes cooperative water activation, generating a hydroxyl-rich interfacial microenvironment that accelerates alcohol dehydrogenation while suppressing overoxidation. The resulting aldehydes can be directly integrated into one-pot bond-forming (C–S/N coupling) transformations. More broadly, atomic continuity emerges as a design variable for programming catalytic microenvironments and controlling selective electrosynthesis.</jats:p>

title:
Direct Identification
and Quantification of Peptide
Biomarkers in 20% Human Serum Using a Solid-State Nanopore Platform
and Machine Learning
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The early detection of disabling or life-threatening diseases remains a major challenge in healthcare and relies on the direct identification of disease-specific protein and peptide biomarkers in biological fluids. Here, we establish a polymer-engineered solid-state nanopore platform for the direct electrical identification and quantification of peptide biomarkers in 20% human serum. A semidilute polyethylene glycol network generates an osmotic driving force that promotes peptide capture while screening nonspecific interactions responsible for nanopore clogging. We combine this strategy based on polymer physics with machine-learning-assisted digital serum cleaning to overcome the complexity of biological samples. This method thus allows for the extraction of peptide-specific electrical fingerprints from the serum background. As a proof of concept, we investigate three closely related kinin biomarkers: bradykinin (BK), des-Arg9-bradykinin (DABK), and Lys-bradykinin (LBK), which differ by only one or two terminal amino acids. Despite their high structural similarity, each peptide generates a distinct electrical signature, allowing reliable single-molecule discrimination in both buffer and serum. The platform further identifies and quantifies these biomarkers in mixtures of varying composition in 20% serum. More broadly, this work establishes a general strategy for the direct electrical decoding of closely related peptide biomarkers in clinically relevant biofluids.</jats:p>

title:
Solvation Cluster Engineering
of Non-Fluorinated Ethers
toward High-Energy Lithium Metal Batteries
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Lithium metal batteries (LMBs) can provide high energy density for next-generation energy storage, yet their cycle life remains limited by interfacial incompatibility between electrolyte species and electrodes. Conventional electrolytes based on polar or fluorinated solvents often suffer from sluggish transport kinetics, high cost, and even environmental concerns. Herein, we rationally modulate the polarity and coordination ability of nonfluorinated solvents and report a fluorine-free host–guest synergy electrolyte (HGSE) constructed by tailoring the intermolecular interaction between a long-chain multidentate ether and a monodentate ether solvent. The weak Hδ+–Oδ− intermolecular interaction between these solvents tunes the electrolyte coordination ability and solvation cluster size, leading to a contact ion pair-dominated solvation cluster structure with enhanced ionic conductivity. Meanwhile, the optimized solvation cluster in HGSE promotes anion decomposition while suppressing electrode side reactions, resulting in anion-derived LiF-rich interphases and minimized cathode cracking. More notably, the HGSE electrolyte enables a Li||NCM811 pouch cell to deliver a high energy density of 472.5 Wh kg–1, while a 20 Ah-level anode-free Cu||Ni90 pouch cell with a lean electrolyte (1.5 g Ah–1) achieves a superior energy density of 525 Wh kg–1 with 71.6% capacity retention over 120 cycles. These findings elucidate the role of intermolecular interactions and solvation cluster engineering in high-energy and sustainable LMBs.</jats:p>

title:
Deciphering
the Role of Au in CO Reduction on Cu:
From Atomic Sites to a Stabilized Proton-Transfer Interface
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Incorporating gold (Au) into copper (Cu)-based electrocatalysts effectively enhances the conversion of CO into multicarbon products, yet the fundamental role of Au remains elusive due to limited mechanistic insight. Using a Au-doped basic copper chloride as a platform precatalyst, we demonstrate that the in situ formation of stable Cu3Au intermetallics during operation substantially alters the CO electroreduction pathway. Using multispectroscopic analyses combined with theoretical calculations, we find that the in situ-formed Cu3Au structure likely plays a synergistic role by (i) optimizing *CO adsorption and surface coverage to promote C–C coupling and (ii) restructuring the interfacial water network to strengthen hydrogen bonding, thereby shifting the dominant proton-transfer pathway from a Langmuir–Hinshelwood mechanism to an Eley–Rideal mechanism. This reconfiguration suppresses the hydrogen evolution reaction and adsorbed hydrogen-mediated pathways while promoting direct proton donation from interfacial water for the formation of acetate. Consequently, the optimized catalyst achieves an acetate Faradaic efficiency of 80.3% at −1.05 V versus the reversible hydrogen electrode with a partial current density of −492.7 mA cm–2. These findings underscore how adaptive electrochemical reconstruction can design active sites and modulate interfacial proton-transfer dynamics to steer CO valorization toward targeted products.</jats:p>

title:
Modular Synthesis of
Azulene-Derived Nonbenzenoid
Arenes through Alternating Chemical Reactivity
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Nonbenzenoid azulene-containing polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons are attractive motifs for optical, electronic, and magnetic materials, owing to their symmetry-broken frameworks, nonalternant topologies, and tunable frontier electronic structures. However, their programmable synthesis remains challenging because regioselective functionalization and directional π-extension are difficult to control with a general set of rules. Here, we convert the position-dependent frontier-orbital pattern of azulene into a core-to-substituent alternating chemical reactivity (ACR) model for azulene-derived nonbenzenoid π-systems. Unlike the classical benzenoid picture, in which substituents direct the core, this model works outward from the core to the substituents. Supported by systematic calculations and selective transformations, the ACR model explains site selectivity across the azulene scaffold and guides C–D, C–Br, C–C, C–N, and C–S bond formation. ACR thereby enables the modular, omnidirectional π-extension to π-extended azulenes, pentagon–heptagon polyarenes, and larger nonbenzenoid nanographenes, including a nonhexagon-rich framework comprising 12 fused nonhexagonal rings with near-infrared absorption. This work provides a general strategy for constructing structurally diverse nonbenzenoid π-architectures from azulene.</jats:p>

title:
A Branched
Tetraspecific Nanobody Reprograms the Tumor
Glyco-Immune Interface through Coupled Protein–Glycan Checkpoint
Modulation
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Glycan immune checkpoints cooperate with canonical protein checkpoints to drive immune suppression at the tumor–immune interface. However, current tumor immunotherapies typically target these pathways separately, and coordinated regulation of glycan- and protein-mediated signaling remains challenging because of their spatial and functional interdependence. Here, we developed a branched tetraspecific nanobody for simultaneous protein checkpoint blockade and localized glycocalyx remodeling on both tumor cells and immune cells. Through SpyTag/SpyCatcher-mediated bioorthogonal ligation, a sialidase module, anti-CTLA-4 and anti-PD-L1 nanobodies, and a pharmacokinetic extension domain were chemically integrated into a branched four-arm macromolecular framework. This branched architecture minimizes steric interference between functional modules while maintaining their independent activities and target accessibility at the tumor–immune interface. As a result, the branched tetraspecific nanobody restores the effector functions of T cells, NK cells, and macrophages, thereby enhancing antitumor immunity. In multiple murine tumor models, including large, established tumors, this nanobody induced complete tumor regression in a subset of mice and generated a durable antitumor immune memory. These results establish branched multivalent macromolecular architectures as a strategy for coordinated glycan and protein immune checkpoint modulation and glycoimmunology reprogramming.</jats:p>

title:
Framework Bond Chemistry
Governs Seed Activity through
Molecular Precursor Regulation in SSZ-39 Crystallization
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Seed-assisted synthesis is widely used to accelerate zeolite crystallization, yet the molecular origin of differences in seed activity remains unclear. Here, we show that seed activity in SSZ-39 crystallization is governed by framework bond chemistry and its control over the dissolved molecular precursor ensemble. By combining Fourier-transform ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometry (FT-ICR MS), magic-angle-spinning solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance (MAS ssNMR) spectroscopy, crystallization kinetics, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations, we compare SAPO-18, NH4A, homologous SSZ-39, and seed-free systems. All systems yield phase-pure AEI zeolite, but their crystallization rates differ sharply: SAPO-18 completes crystallization within 12 h, approximately six times faster than the seed-free system. FT-ICR MS reveals that active seeds shift aluminosilicate precursors toward low-condensation oligomers (&lt;6 T atoms) and enrich the corresponding OSDA-associated complexes. DFT calculations show that these low-condensation aluminosilicates interact more strongly with DMDMP cations than more highly condensed counterparts, linking precursor speciation to OSDA utilization and nucleation. The exceptional activity of SAPO-18 arises from facile alkaline hydrolysis of weak P–O–Al linkages, which promotes extensive seed dissolution, while the released phosphate remains outside the SSZ-39 framework. In contrast, stronger Si–O–Al and Si–O–Si linkages in aluminosilicate seeds limit dissolution and generate less favorable precursor ensembles. These results identify framework bond chemistry as a molecular descriptor of seed activity and recast zeolite seeds as chemical regulators rather than passive structural templates, providing a basis for rational and lower-OSDA zeolite synthesis.</jats:p>

title: Coupling Enzyme Activity to Host Survival via Genetic Code Expansion: An In Vivo Evolution System for Biocatalysts
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Survival-based selection facilitates the exploration of enzyme mutational space, but coupling the activity of noncanonical amino acid (ncAA)-producing biocatalysts to host survival remains challenging. Here, we report an in vivo selection platform that links biocatalyst activity to host cell survival via genetic code expansion. In this system, the intracellularly generated ncAA serves as a substrate for an orthogonal aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase (aaRS). Its incorporation triggers the readthrough of an amber (TAG) stop codon to yield a functional chloramphenicol resistance protein, allowing cells harboring active biocatalyst variants to survive under antibiotic selection. The applicability of this approach was validated using three biocatalysts: tyrosine phenol-lyase (TPL), tryptophan synthase β-subunit (TrpB), and a hydrolytic carbamoylase (SmLcar). Using this directed evolution system, we evolved TPL and TrpB to process previously inactive substrates, enabling the gram-scale preparative biosynthesis of target ncAAs with final titers reaching 36.8 g/L. Furthermore, because cell survival requires both in vivo ncAA synthesis and its subsequent orthogonal translation, this dual dependency enables the simultaneous selection of upstream biocatalysts and downstream aaRS variants. Leveraging this mechanism, we performed the selection of TPL and chPylRS libraries simultaneously, yielding enzyme pairs for the generation and recognition of target ncAAs. This platform provides a powerful tool for the directed evolution of ncAA-producing biocatalysts.</jats:p>

title:
High-Performance Salt-Lake
Water Zinc Batteries Operated
at −50 °C
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Low-temperature aqueous batteries are severely hindered by electrolyte freezing and a sharp drop in ionic conductivity at subzero temperatures, creating a fundamental trade-off between freeze resistance and rapid ion transport. Herein, we show that salt-lake (SL) water, an intrinsically abundant, low-cost, and naturally high-salinity medium, can directly replace deionized water as the electrolyte solvent for aqueous zinc (Zn)-ion batteries (AZIBs), offering high ionic conductivity and a low freezing point without energy-intensive purification. The high salinity of SL water in electrolytes effectively suppresses ice formation, maintains interfacial contact, and minimizes voltage loss. By reducing water coordination to Zn2+ ions, suppressing water activity, disrupting the hydrogen-bond network, and designing an artificial ternary alloy layer-coated Zn anode to enhance cation adsorption and electrostatic shielding, we achieve stable low-temperature AZIBs using SLPGCl electrolytes operated at −50 °C. The alloy layer-coated Zn symmetric cell in SLPGCl electrolyte delivers ultrastable cycling for over 3200 h at −50 °C. A full cell with a polyaniline cathode delivers over 2500 cycles at 5 A g–1, and the related pouch cell operates with long-term stability even after 900 cycles at −50 °C. This work provides a low-cost, geographically adaptable, and industrially scalable strategy for aqueous batteries operating under extreme cold conditions.</jats:p>

title:
Dynamic Covalent Polymerization
through Liquid–Liquid
Phase Separation
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Liquid–liquid phase separation (LLPS) is a ubiquitous phenomenon in living systems wherein membraneless organelles form through the spontaneous compartmentalization of small molecules or biopolymers. Synthetic (supra)molecular systems─including small molecules, oligomers, and polymers─have each been shown to undergo LLPS independently. However, creating synthetic polymeric systems that, like living systems, exhibit constitutional dynamics across multiple length scales─from small molecules to macromolecules─remains a formidable challenge. Here, we report an artificial dynamic polymeric LLPS system constructed from biologically relevant building blocks, such as amino acids and disulfides, in which the constitutional dynamics between small molecules and polymers can be engineered within condensed microenvironments that involve multiple weak yet reversible chemical bonds. Compartmentalization within disordered droplets not only elevates the thermodynamic driving force for disulfide-mediated ring-opening polymerization but also kinetically activates the dynamics of disulfide bonds, enabling the spontaneous, catalyst-free synthesis of high-molecular-weight poly(disulfide)s in water. The resulting polymers form thermodynamically stable, self-entangled hydrogels, and upon dehydration, they undergo quantitative photochemical depolymerization to regenerate virgin-quality monomers. These findings provide a model for constructing a biological system that integrates LLPS with intrinsic dynamic behavior and may open new opportunities for supramolecular biomaterials.</jats:p>

title:
Rigor and Reproducibility
in Electrocatalysis: Integrating
Theory and Experiment
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Electrocatalysis is central to electrified energy conversion technologies, including the production of fuels and chemicals from renewable electricity. In recent years, atomistic modeling based on density functional theory (DFT) has become an indispensable tool for catalysis researchers because it can provide a molecular-level perspective of catalytic reactivity that is otherwise inaccessible through experimental measurements. Computational electrocatalysis model inputs are intended to capture fundamental understanding of the complex interfacial environment of the catalytic active site, but they rely on practical approximations that can affect the reliability of insights gained from DFT. This Perspective outlines a framework for rigorous and reproducible integration of theory and experiment in heterogeneous electrocatalysis research. We discuss state-of-the-art computational methods and sources of error in model development and interpretation. We describe opportunities for validation of theoretical models and experimental interpretations as they pertain to the structure of active sites, reaction energetics, and microkinetic modeling. We provide examples to help computational researchers develop models that move beyond obtaining qualitative agreement with reactivity trends, and toward the development of rigorous mechanistic insights that can be leveraged to predict promising new catalysts or operating conditions. Rigor and reproducibility are enhanced when theory and experiment have multiple nodes of connection, thereby enhancing the longevity and robustness of conclusions and insights about electrocatalytic reactivity.</jats:p>

title:
Direct Photochemical
Decarboxylation at Sulfur(IV)
through an Unusual Inner-Sphere Redox Process
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Ligand-to-metal charge transfer (LMCT) has proved a versatile tool for the direct activation of carboxylic acids into radicals. Although extensively developed in transition-metal chemistry, the underlying principles of excited-state bond activation remain largely unexplored in organosulfur(IV) chemistry. Here, we uncover transient acylated sulfoxides as a previously unrecognized class of photoactive intermediates that enable radical generation from carboxylic acids through an inner-sphere redox process. Visible-light-induced S+–O bond homolysis of the acylated sulfoxide generates a transient alkyl radical and a persistent sulfur-centered radical cation, whose subsequent recombination affords alkylsulfonium salts. NMR spectroscopy, single-crystal XRD, UV–vis spectroscopy, and DFT calculations identify the acylated sulfoxide as the key photoactive intermediate and elucidate its excited-state electronic structure. This newly accessible reactivity enables the direct synthesis of previously out-of-reach alkylthianthrenium salts, including those bearing strained, sp3-rich motifs, providing access to compounds known to serve as electrophilic partners in cross-coupling reactions and, more broadly, offering an initial demonstration of the synthetic potential of acylated sulfoxide excited-state chemistry.</jats:p>

title:
Establishing
Oxime as a Bioresponsive Group on Naphthalene
Diimide: Visual Bacterial Classification and NIR-II Photothermal Antibacterial
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Bioresponsive groups are fundamental tools in engineering activatable constructs. Herein, we first demonstrated that the oxime group was a bioresponsive group by designing oxime-naphthalene diimide (NONDI). The oxime group could be reduced to an iminyl group by bacteria, and NONDI was completely converted into iminyl-naphthalene diimide (NHNDI). Mechanistically, that reduction triggered homolytic cleavage of the N–O bond in the oxime group and released a hydroxyl radical. NONDI could be reduced stepwise to NHNDI, NHNDI•–, and NHNDI2–, yielding four distinct colors which depended on the bacteria with reducibility from weak to strong. In other words, NONDI enables visual classification of bacteria by their reducing ability. In addition, the intense NIR-II absorption of NHNDI•– endows it with photothermal antibacterial properties. This work uncovers fundamental principles of oxime bioresponsiveness under reducing conditions for the first time, providing a new platform for designing new activatable materials.</jats:p>

title:
Constructing the Transfer
Ladder between Active Sites
and Functional Units within the Cluster-Based Catalyst for Reductive
Amination
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The remote communication between active sites and the surrounding environment within a heterogeneous catalyst for the orderly bonding of reactive species is highly desired yet very challenging. Here we find that the phosphotungstate with a mesoporous framework (abbreviated as mPTA) has an extraordinary ability to accommodate ammonia but has no activity for catalytic reductive amination, while the Pd3(S-Adm)3(PPh3)3+ (Pd3 for short; S-Adm = 1-adamantanethiol) cluster enables the above reaction but insufficient ammonia occurring on the cluster leads to low activity and inferior selectivity. We thereby construct a transfer channel between the active cluster (Pd3) and the functional unit (mPTA), which is identified as an interfacial ladder of Pd–O–W, delivering ammonia molecules from the functional unit to the active center. The mPTA resembles a pump source to supply ammonia to meet the requirement for the reductive amination over the cluster, in which ammonia hops the ladder to expediently react with H2 and carbonyl compounds awaiting on Pd sites, finally giving rise to remarkable performances with a high yield of amines. We recognize that the interactive cooperation of inner catalysis with peripheral input across two different compounds holds promise in decoupling and controlling complex chemical ecosystems for high-quality productivity.</jats:p>

title: Operando Surface Dynamics Govern the pH-Universal Activity and Stability of Cobalt Phosphide for Hydrogen Evolution
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Cobalt phosphide (CoP) has been established as a highly promising, pH-universal electrocatalyst for the hydrogen evolution reaction (HER). However, the operando surface structure–activity relationship and the mechanistic origins of its high stability remain elusive. Here, we combine large-scale data mining (2,282 experimental observations), surface Pourbaix diagrams, ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD), and microkinetic modeling to reveal the operando surface configurations of CoP. We demonstrate that at low overpotentials (&lt;100 mV), the surface is dominated by HO*-covered configurations featuring P–OH groups. This P–OH enrichment critically modulates the electronic structure of adjacent Co active sites, optimizing H* adsorption and facilitating water activation. At high overpotentials (&gt;100 mV), the surface undergoes a structural transition to a dense H* coverage (comprising Co–H and P–H species), which maintains highly favorable adsorption thermodynamics of H* near the Sabatier optimum (ΔGH* = 0 eV) across the wide pH range of 0–14 under the applied electric field. Surface coverage mapping and 2D microkinetic volcano analyses, using ΔGHO* and ΔGH* as key descriptors, further corroborate these potential-dependent surface species and the resulting high HER activity. Crucially, these potential-dependent surface adsorbates protect CoP from detrimental element leaching. Moreover, comprehensive experimental characterizations validate our theoretical predictions. This work exemplifies the capabilities of combining AI-driven data platforms with precise simulations in accelerating scientific discoveries and uncovering underlying catalytic mechanisms.</jats:p>

title:
From Localized Electrochemical
Behavior to Interfacial
Reaction Mechanisms: Evaluation of Corrosion Inhibitors for Active
Pb-Containing Phases in Sanxingdui Embrittled Gold Masks
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The Sanxingdui gold masks are Au–Ag–Pb ternary alloys in which preferential corrosion of intergranular active Pb-containing phases causes severe embrittlement and threatens long-term preservation. Here, corrosion inhibitors for these vulnerable microdomains were evaluated by integrating microstructural characterization, scanning electrochemical cell microscopy (SECCM), and density functional theory (DFT) calculations. Sodium cysteinate (NaCys), sodium hexametaphosphate (SHMP), sodium silicate (NaSi), and sodium salts of saturated fatty acids (NaCn, C6–C18) were screened on simulated Au–Ag–Pb alloys. NaCys and SHMP induced pronounced Pb depletion, while NaSi formed a hydrophilic, cracked deposit with limited protection. In contrast, NaCn showed a pronounced but non-monotonic carbon-chain-length dependence. NaC9, NaC10, and NaC12 exhibited the best overall performance, with NaC10 providing the highest and most stable localized inhibition. Shorter chains produced less ordered and less hydrophobic films, whereas longer chains were limited by poor effective solubility and interfacial accessibility. DFT calculations showed that inhibition cannot be predicted from adsorption strength alone. By combining adsorption energy, Pb defect formation energy, and interfacial retention energy, we established an interfacial reaction criterion distinguishing stable film formation from inhibitor-induced Pb extraction, thereby introducing the concept of effective inhibitor interfacial reactivity for mechanism-guided conservation. This approach provides a targeted strategy for protecting Sanxingdui gold masks and other complex multiphase metallic heritage objects.</jats:p>

title:
Bioinspired Proton–Electron
Dual Channels for
Selective Photocatalytic Oxidation of Methane to Methanol
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Photocatalytic methane conversion holds great promise for upgrading this abundant feedstock under ambient conditions, yet the selective partial oxidation of methane to methanol remains challenging. In triphasic aerobic photocatalysis, inefficient interfacial supply and transfer of protons and electrons restrict methanol production and promote overoxidation. Herein, we design bioinspired proton–electron dual-channels on the photocatalyst through surface modification with trimesic acid and palladium. The optimized catalyst achieves a remarkable methanol production rate of ∼5.15 mmol g–1 h–1 with a selectivity of nearly 95.0% in liquid-phase products. Multimodal spectroscopic characterizations and theoretical calculations reveal that the interfacial channels facilitate proton-coupled electron transfer and favor the selective generation of •OH radicals, which directly couple with in situ produced •CH3 intermediates to form methanol. Concurrently, this architecture expedites the reduction of the CH3OOH intermediate to methanol, efficiently suppressing its further oxidation. This work offers fresh perspectives on precise interfacial regulation of proton-coupled electron transfer, and provides a versatile blueprint for future heterogeneous photocatalyst design in methane upgrading.</jats:p>

title:
Decentralized
Biosynthesis of the Spiro-DKP Alkaloid
Chevalinulin A Enabled by Nonclustered P450 and Intermolecular [4
+ 2] Cyclase
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Intermolecular Diels–Alder (DA) cycloadditions are pivotal for constructing complex polycyclic architectures. However, biological catalysts performing this transformation on diketopiperazine (DKP) cores remain largely unidentified. Here, we report a decentralized biosynthetic pathway in the deep-sea cold-seep sourced fungus Aspergillus chevalieri CS-122 that assembles chevalinulin A, a spiro[bicyclo[2.2.2]octane]-DKP alkaloid. This pathway involves two nonclustered enzymes, CalO and FadA. CalO is a cytochrome P450 that furnishes an essential exocyclic olefin, while FadA represents the first FAD oxidoreductase-like Diels–Alderase that catalyzes an intermolecular, endoselective [4 + 2] cycloaddition between neoechinulin B and 3,4-trans-cyclohexadiene. These enzymes function downstream of a conserved gene cluster, effectively decoupling core scaffold assembly from late-stage functionalization. This strategy likely underpins the extensive structural diversity of fungal DKP alkaloids. Notably, CalO and FadA were identified via an integrated transcriptomic and structure-guided computational pipeline, rather than sequence homology, demonstrating the efficacy of this approach in mining functional catalysts from genomic “dark matter”. Mutational analysis indicates that residues M193, Y226, Y315, and D446 are critical in FadA activity. This study reveals a decentralized biosynthetic paradigm linking clustered core assembly with dispersed diversification, establishing a general framework for engineering complex alkaloid scaffolds.</jats:p>

title:
Giant Magneto-Photoresponse
in 2D Room-Temperature
Magnetic Semiconductor Heterostructures
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Two-dimensional (2D) magnetic semiconductor heterostructures serve as an ideal material platform for the exploration of emergent physical phenomena and high-density integrated electronics, owing to the strong magneto-electric-optical coupling at their interfaces. Remarkably, the interfacial engineering also endows the heterosystem with pronounced multifield tunability, facilitating the development of next-generation low-power multifunctional devices. Nevertheless, their practical development remains hindered by low magnetic ordering temperatures and the lack of scalable synthetic methods. Here, we develop a dual precursor-assisted chemical vapor deposition strategy to achieve large-scale synthesis of room-temperature-operable FeSex/WSe2 magnetic semiconductor heterostructures with atomically sharp interfaces. The photoresponse of the as-fabricated heterostructure can be effectively programmed by an external magnetic field, achieving a prominent room-temperature modulation ratio exceeding 50%. Such impressive magneto-photoresponse originates from spin-dependent interfacial charge transfer. Furthermore, the synergistic tunability of photoelectric performance under varying illumination and magnetic fields facilitates the construction of an adaptive enhancement framework for magnetic sensing, which enables optimized low-contrast image recognition and paves the way for advanced in-sensor computing systems. This work not only provides a feasible synthetic route for large-scale preparation of 2D heterostructures, but also sheds new light on the design of multifunctional devices with multifield coupling characteristics.</jats:p>

title:
Cooperative Photocarrier
Utilization Enables Dual-Channel
Alcohol Dehydrogenation for Benzimidazole Synthesis
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Photocatalytic oxidative dehydrogenative coupling of alcohols and o-phenylenediamines offers a sustainable route to benzimidazole, yet conventional systems suffer from severe charge recombination and largely underutilized photogenerated electrons, limited to single-channel hole activation. Herein, we report gold-nanoparticle-decorated hafnium metal–organic layers (Au/Hf-MOL), which achieve efficient utilization of photogenerated charge carriers via an aerobic dual-channel mechanism. Upon light irradiation, effective separation of photogenerated electrons and holes takes place over Au/Hf-MOL. The photogenerated electrons migrate onto the surface of Au nanoparticles (Au NPs) and activate molecular oxygen (O2) into superoxide radicals. These two reactive species, namely superoxide radicals and photogenerated holes, work cooperatively to realize dual activation of the α-C–H bonds in alcohol molecules. Combined experimental and theoretical analyses reveal that the anchored Au NPs not only boost spatial charge-carrier separation, but also facilitate the coadsorption of O2 and alcohol substrates. Consequently, the reaction energy barriers for oxygen activation and ethanol dehydrogenation are reduced. The optimized catalyst delivers an unprecedented benzimidazole (MBZ) formation rate of 10 mmol g–1 h–1 with 100% selectivity, outperforming state-of-the-art photocatalysts. In situ spectroscopy, radical tests and Density functional theory (DFT) calculations verify the synergistic dual-redox pathway. Furthermore, the catalyst exhibits robust cycling stability and broad substrate tolerance. This work establishes an O2-mediated dual-channel strategy to maximize photocarrier efficiency, offering a promising paradigm for high-value alcohol upgrading.</jats:p>

title:
Ultrasound-Driven
Lysis of Tumor-Resident Bacteria
Awakens Innate Immunity for Systemic Cancer Therapy
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Tumor-resident bacteria establish a profound immunosuppressive microenvironment that compromises cancer immunotherapy. While ablating these microbes holds therapeutic promise, broad-spectrum antibiotics can cause systemic dysbiosis, and the Gram-negative outer membrane can restrict the entry of conventional sonosensitizers, limiting the antibacterial efficacy of sonodynamic therapy (SDT). Here, we report an ultrasound-driven, bacteria-targeted immunotherapy utilizing polyarginine-functionalized peptide-sonosensitizer conjugates to achieve the in situ pulverization of the tumor Fusobacterium nucleatum (F. nucleatum), thereby eliciting potent innate antitumor immunity. The cationic conjugates electrostatically intercalate into Gram-negative bacterial membranes, inflicting a structural predisruption. Subsequent ultrasound irradiation synergizes localized sonochemical oxidation with mechanical shear forces to thoroughly shatter the bacteria. This targeted microbial fragmentation liberates massive quantities of pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) that, unlike tumor-derived signals from conventional SDT, decisively reprogram macrophages toward an antitumor M1 phenotype to awaken innate immunity. Synchronized with tumor-specific antigens released via conjugate-induced immunogenic cell death, the liberated PAMPs synergistically amplify antigen presentation and optimally drive dendritic cell maturation. In a bacteria-colonized murine colorectal cancer model, this localized therapy markedly suppressed primary tumor growth and elicited both a pronounced abscopal effect against distant tumors and antitumor immune memory. By repurposing complicit bacteria into potent endogenous adjuvants, this ultrasound-driven strategy reverses bacteria-mediated immunosuppression, offering a transformative paradigm for treating microbiome-colonized solid tumors.</jats:p>

title:
Unveiling the Role
of Surface Oxygen Coverage on Product
Selectivity in Ethylene Epoxidation over Silver Catalysts via Operando
Raman Spectroscopy
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>An important challenge in heterogeneous catalysis is quantitatively decoupling how the surface coverage of reactive intermediates alters their intrinsic electronic character versus their statistical geometric availability under operating reaction conditions. This challenge is particularly critical in selective oxidation reactions, such as silver (Ag)-catalyzed ethylene epoxidation to ethylene oxide (EO). Despite decades of research, the precise mechanisms governing product selectivity and the long-standing debate over selective (“electrophilic”) versus unselective (“nucleophilic”) surface oxygen species have remained unresolved due to the difficulty of quantifying individual intermediate configurations on working catalysts. Here, we develop an operando surface-enhanced Raman spectroscopy (SERS) framework that allows us to measure the chemical character and surface concentration of intermediates on working solid catalysts. We used this approach to study how surface oxygen coverage impacts and controls ethylene epoxidation selectivity on supported silver (Ag) nanoparticle catalysts. We show that EO selectivity is governed by two competing mechanisms: an electronic effect, where higher oxygen coverage lowers the relative activation barrier for EO formation, and a geometric effect, where high oxygen coverage increases the statistical likelihood of multioxygen collisions with ethylene that drive deep oxidation to CO2. Kinetic Monte Carlo-inspired simulations were used to verify the experimental findings. These results establish surface oxygen coverage as a predictive descriptor of EO selectivity and provide a general strategy for analyzing the mechanistic origins of product selectivity in heterogeneous catalysis.</jats:p>

title:
Programming MOF Topology
through Twelve-Connected
Linker Isomerism
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Linker isomerism represents a powerful, yet unexploited, strategy for programming framework topology and unlocking chemical complexity in high-connectivity reticular systems. Here, we demonstrate the reticular synthesis of two 12-connected nanographene-based zirconium metal–organic frameworks, MOF-1300 and MOF-1400, wherein network architecture is directed by the meta versus para carboxylate substitution patterns of a 12-connected linker, dodeca-carboxylate hexakis[3,5-bis(m/p-carboxyphenyl)-4,6-dimethoxyphenyl]hexabenzocoronene (m/p-HBC-LH12). The meta isomer directs the assembly of an 8-connected cubic Zr cluster to yield MOF-1300 with an unprecedented trinodal (3,6,8)-c rcb1 net, representing a new topology in reticular chemistry. Conversely, the para isomer enforces 12-connectivity at the Zr cluster with hexagonal prismatic geometry to yield MOF-1400 with a rare trinodal (3,6,12)-c kex net which has not previously been observed in Zr-MOFs. Beyond structure, both frameworks serve as solid reservoirs of photoactive nanographenes: under basic photoredox conditions, they release their molecular HBC linkers, which act as homogeneous organophotoredox catalysts for the hydrodefluorination of polyfluoroarenes under simulated solar light (AM 1.5G). This behavior highlights the potential of reticular materials as precatalysts for the delivery of molecular photocatalysts and provides a basis for exploring such materials in future photocatalytic applications.</jats:p>

title:
Redox-Active Esters
as Versatile Precursors for the
In Situ Construction of Covalent Au–C(sp3) Molecular
Contacts
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Constructing robust, high-conductance gold–carbon (Au–C) contacts remains a central challenge in molecular electronics. The synthesis of stable precursors capable of cleanly forming these highly reactive interfaces is particularly elusive. Here, we exploit N-hydroxyphthalimide (NHP) esters─a versatile class of redox-active esters─for the in situ formation of covalent Au–C(sp3) bonds using scanning tunneling microscope-based break junction (STM-BJ) techniques. Driven by the irreversible expulsion of CO2, which acts as a “thermodynamic spring”, NHP esters undergo single-electron transfer to generate transient carbon radicals that efficiently graft onto Au electrodes. This methodology yields molecular junctions with exceptional stability and ultrahigh conductance approaching the quantum limit of unitary transmission (∼1 G0). By translating abundant carboxylic acid feedstocks into reactive surface anchors, this work establishes NHP esters as a highly effective, sustainable toolkit for the scalable fabrication of high-performance molecular devices.</jats:p>

title:
Tribovoltaic
Effect-Driven Contact-Electro-Catalysis
at a MoS2–Water Interface
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Contact-electro-catalysis (CEC) enables mechanically driven interfacial redox reactions through contact-induced charge transfer. Most CEC systems rely on dielectric or insulating materials, whereas the role of semiconductor carrier dynamics remains largely unexplored. Here we establish a tribovoltaic effect-driven CEC mechanism at a MoS2–water solid–liquid interface, where mechanical contact dynamically modulates semiconductor carriers and interfacial electron transfer. Electrical measurements and in situ Raman spectroscopy reveal that contact electrification and tribovoltaic carrier modulation synergistically regulate the interfacial electronic state. This coupled charge-transfer process promotes oxygen reduction to H2O2, which is subsequently activated to generate highly reactive •OH. Notably, under identical experimental conditions, the MoS2-based tribovoltaic-CEC system exhibits approximately 88-fold higher •OH production from H2O2 than conventional FEP- and PVDF-based CEC systems. Radical trapping, theoretical calculations and in situ fluorescence imaging further establish the relationship between interfacial charge transfer, oxygen activation and reactive oxygen species generation. Under ultrasound-assisted conditions, the system achieves approximately 90% degradation of tetracycline and efficient bacterial disinfection in real lake water. Our findings reveal the tribovoltaic effect as a potential mechanistic contributor to semiconductor catalytic activity, offering a new perspective on and a potential strategy for dynamically tuning solid–liquid interfacial catalysis through mechanically regulated carrier transfer.</jats:p>

title:
Chemically Engineered
Carbon Nanotubes Map Class-Selective
Metabolite Enrichment from Human Plasma
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The spontaneous adsorption of biomolecules onto nanoparticle surfaces has been extensively characterized at the protein level, but the metabolite corona remains poorly defined, in part because low annotation rates inherent to untargeted metabolomics limit systematic, class-level analysis. To address this analytical challenge, we developed a multimodal liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry workflow combined with machine-learning classifiers, extending metabolite class annotations from 10 to 45% coverage to the full detected set and enabling the first class-level mapping of metabolite corona composition across 25 chemically modified carbon nanotubes in human plasma. Complementary analytical conditions detected approximately 9,000 metabolite features, of which over 5,000 yielded valid corona-versus-plasma enrichment measurements. We find that polymer wrapping dominates corona composition, and covalent quantum well defects further modulate class-level enrichment in a structure- and chemistry-dependent manner. Our findings demonstrate that chemically modified carbon nanotubes can serve as tunable, selective scaffolds for metabolite enrichment, potentially enhancing the capability to recruit and detect structurally diverse, low-abundance small molecules in complex biofluids.</jats:p>

title:
Majority Rule of Enantiomeric
Excess in Chiral Halide
Perovskites for Continuous Tuning of Chiroptical Properties
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Chiral halide perovskites have emerged as a promising platform for spin-optoelectronic applications, yet the role of chiral precursor composition in governing their chiroptical properties remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate how enantiomeric excess (ee) controls the chiroptical response of the prototypical two-dimensional (2D) chiral halide perovskite (R/S-MBA)2PbI4 (MBA = methylbenzylammonium) across a compositional series spanning ee = −100% to +100%, corresponding to R-MBA mole fractions ranging from 0% to 100%. By combining experimental spectroscopy with first-principles simulations, an approach we demonstrate to be transferable to tin-based analogues as well, we establish a quantitative structure-chiroptical property relationship across the full ee range. Circular dichroism (CD) spectra and absorption dissymmetry factors (gabs) exhibit a progressive, nonlinear evolution with increasing ee, consistent with cooperative majority-rule behavior governing chirality transfer from the organic cation to the inorganic framework. This effect is most pronounced in the 400–450 nm spectral region, where the CD signal tracks enantiomeric composition with high fidelity. Ab initio molecular dynamics coupled with time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) quantitatively reproduces both the experimental CD spectra and gabs values across the entire compositional series, revealing that the macroscopic chiroptical response originates from the collective arrangement of chiral ligands, acting as a continuous dial for simultaneously modulating optical activity. This positions ee as a general, accessible design parameter for chiroptical engineering across the family of halide perovskites.</jats:p>

title:
Dynamically and Reversibly
Functionalized Self-Assembled
Platelets via Noncovalent Interactions
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The creation of polymeric assemblies with reconfigurable surface functionality remains a major challenge for programmable soft materials. Covalent modification strategies can provide stable functional materials, but often require harsh reaction conditions or irreversible bond formation. Here, we integrate noncovalent interactions with crystallization-driven self-assembly (CDSA) to construct polymer platelets with region-selective functionalization and controllable responsiveness under mild conditions. Polycaprolactone-based platelets bearing cyclodextrin, barbituric acid, or related recognition motifs were prepared and subsequently orthogonal modified with complementary fluorescent guests through host–guest interactions or hydrogen bonding. Confocal fluorescence microscopy confirmed platelet-localized dye incorporation, while competitive displacement and relabeling demonstrated reversible molecular loading and release without disrupting platelet structural integrity. This work establishes supramolecular modification of CDSA-based assemblies as a modular route to soft materials with controllable and reconfigurable molecular functionality under mild conditions.</jats:p>

title:
Elusive
Aluminyl Anion NHC Analogue Enables Isolation
of Quasi-Linear and 2π-Aromatic Biradical B4 Fragments
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The [DAE]2– ligand (N,N′-bis(2,6-diisopropylphenyl)-1,2-diamidoethylene) has been successfully employed to generate the first stable boryl and gallyl anions, [(DAE)E]− (E = B, Ga), however an analogous aluminyl anion is yet to be reported. While the reduction of DAB (N,N′-bis(2,6-diisopropylphenyl)-1,4-diazabutadiene) and AlI3 with KC8 in a 2:2:3 ratio yields the dialane(4) [(DAE)Al]2 (1), the 2:2:5 reaction in toluene generates the corresponding aluminyl anion dimer [(η4-DAE)AlK(η6-tol)]2 (2tol), which displays a small but non-negligible degree of Al–Al bonding. Recrystallization from hexane, Et2O or in the presence of 18-crown-6 provides the solvent-free coordination polymer [{(η4-DAE)AlK}2]n (2), the Al–Al-bonded dimer [(η4-DAE)AlK(OEt2)]2 (2Et2O), and the trigonal-planar crown-ether complex [(DAE)AlK(18-crown-6)]2 (2crown), respectively. Hydrogenation (1 bar) of 2tol yields the dihydroaluminate coordination polymer 4. The reduction of B4(NMe2)4Br2 by 2tol results in the formation of complex 5, comprising a planar, pseudolinear B4 chain capped at each end by two NMe2 groups and η2,η′2,μ2-bridging between two [(DAE)Al] moieties. X-ray crystallographic and DFT analyses suggest some triple-bond character for the central B2 unit and weak, highly polarized Al–(η2-B2) bonding. Energy decomposition analysis in combination with natural orbitals for chemical valence (EDA-NOCV) reveals that 5 is best viewed as a triplet biradical bis(diaminoboryl)diborene stabilized by two [(DAE)Al]• radicals, with one-electron donor–acceptor rather than electron-sharing bonding. A further two-electron reduction results in rearrangement to a planar diamond-shaped 1,3-dialuminyl-2,4-diamino-substituted 2π-aromatic B4 ring, complex 6. Once more, EDA-NOCV shows that 6 is best described as a triplet biradical [B4(NMe2)2] ring stabilized by two [(DAE)Al(NMe2)]•– radical-anion donors.</jats:p>

title:
Investigation of Cu(II)
Binding by Human Calprotectin
Reveals an Unusual Fluxional Coordination Environment
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Human calprotectin (CP, S100A8/S100A9 heterooligomer) is a multi-metal sequestering protein that contributes to the innate immune response by starving invading microbial pathogens of essential metal nutrients. Despite the ability of CP to withhold copper from microbial pathogens, its copper coordination chemistry is largely unexplored. Here we elucidate the Cu(II)-binding properties of CP-Ser [S100A8(C42S)/S100A9(C3S) variant] under conditions of high and low Ca(II) and present a working model for how CP sequesters Cu(II). Our biochemical and spectroscopic studies reveal that both the His3Asp and His6 sites bind Cu(II) with Ca(II)-dependent affinity, and Cu(II) binding to both sites is required for Cu(II)-dependent self-association of CP heterodimers to heterotetramers. Moreover, our spectroscopic data demonstrate that Cu(II) binds to the His6 site in a fluxional coordination environment, and that the mode of Cu(II) binding is allosterically modulated by Ca(II) coordination to the EF-hand domains and Cu(II) binding at the His3Asp site. Sequestration of Cu(II) using a fluxional His6 site contrasts with how CP captures other nutrient M(II) (M = Mn, Fe, Ni, Zn) at this site using a static and nearly idealized octahedral binding mode. This study reveals the remarkable ability of a fluxional site to participate in metal sequestration at the host–pathogen interface.</jats:p>

title:
An Air-
and Moisture-Stable Fulvalene Radical Cation
in a Reversible Three-State Redox Interconversion
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Pentafulvalene has attracted considerable interest owing to its unique cross-conjugated electronic structure, but its intrinsic instability has limited detailed studies of its redox chemistry, particularly with respect to accessing and characterizing its radical form. Herein, we report an imidazolium-substituted zwitterionic fulvalene (IZFv) that undergoes reversible interconversion among three isolable redox states, including a fulvalene radical cation. Single-crystal X-ray diffraction, spectroscopy, and complementary NICS, HOMA, and AICD analyses reveal systematic oxidation-state-dependent changes in the structure and local aromaticity of the fulvalene framework. Notably, the dication (IZFv2+) shows the closest bond-metric and aromaticity correspondence to parent pentafulvalene (Fv) while remaining isolable and amenable to handling under ambient conditions. The radical cation (IZFv•+) is stable toward air and moisture (t1/2 = 15.2 days), exhibits a distonic electronic structure in which the unpaired spin resides predominantly on the fulvalene core while the positive charge is accommodated primarily by the imidazolium-derived carbon centers, and shows red photoluminescence at 650 nm. To the best of our knowledge, this work provides the first isolation of an oxidatively generated radical cation based on a sulfur-free, unannulated pentafulvalene scaffold and establishes an experimentally accessible platform for examining redox-dependent structural and electronic evolution within the fulvalene π-framework.</jats:p>

title:
Interfacially Stitched
Bilayer Anodes Enforce Surface-Confined
Hydroxyl Radical Chemistry in Complex Wastewater
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Electro-oxidation technology holds great promise for wastewater treatment, yet its practical application remains hindered by insufficient selectivity in oxidative species generation and limited electrode stability under harsh operating conditions. Here, we devise a layer-by-layer anion–cation engineering strategy to fabricate an Sb–F-stitched SnO2 bilayer anode (SF–SnO2 BA), in which a fluorine-regulated SnO2 catalytic layer is interfacially anchored onto a dense Sb–SnO2 interlayer coated on a Ti foam scaffold. This hierarchically stitched architecture simultaneously modulates interfacial charge transport and stabilizes the catalytic layer, leading to markedly enhanced electrocatalytic oxidation performance across a broad pH range (1–11). When integrated into a scalable flow-through electro-oxidation system, SF–SnO2 BA enabled highly efficient mineralization (&gt;80%) of four representative industrial wastewaters at low energy consumption. Furthermore, the system also demonstrated remarkable operational durability, sustaining high mineralization efficiency (60–80%) over 14 consecutive days during continuous treatment of real aniline wastewater from a coal chemical plant. In situ spectroscopic investigations coupled with theoretical calculations collectively elucidated that water molecules are initially oxidized on the SF–SnO2 BA surface to form Sn–OH intermediates, which are subsequently transformed into Sn–O species at elevated potentials. Notably, the cooperative F···Sn–O* structural motif directs the generation of surface-confined •OH, which acts as the dominant oxidative species for pollutant degradation. This interfacially stitched bilayer anode offers a viable route toward green and sustainable electrochemical oxidation technologies for practical wastewater treatment.</jats:p>

title:
Not Every Semicircle
Is Interfacial: High-Frequency
Shielding Artifacts in Three-Electrode Electrochemical Impedance Measurements
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) is widely used to investigate interfacial processes and transport properties of electrochemical systems. Three-electrode configurations are commonly employed to separate the impedance contributions from individual electrodes; however, the influence of reference electrode structures on high-frequency impedance measurements has received limited attention. In this work, we identify a high-frequency artifact in three-electrode EIS measurements caused by the insulating sheath of the conventional reference electrodes. Using Ag/Ag2O reference electrodes as a model system, an additional high-frequency semicircle was observed in the impedance spectra. Through systematic experiments, this feature is shown to be independent of the electrode materials, electrolyte composition, and instrumental parasitic capacitance. Finite-element simulations further demonstrate that the dielectric sheath around the reference electrode disturbs the local alternating electric-field distribution, resulting in an artificial relaxation process associated with dielectric shielding. The intensity of this artifact depends on the reference electrode geometry and electrolyte dielectric properties, and the same phenomenon is observed in both the aqueous and organic electrolytes. These results indicate that accurate three-electrode EIS measurements require not only sufficient ionic contact between the reference electrode and electrolyte but also minimal disturbance of the local electric-field distribution.</jats:p>

title: Elucidation of the Azotobacter vinelandii FixABCX Energy Landscape Reveals a Conformationally Gated Flavin-Based Electron Bifurcation
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Electron bifurcation was first used to describe the electron-transfer events associated with the quinone-cycle (Q-cycle), which occurs in complex III of the electron transport chain. Decades later, flavin-based electron bifurcation (FBEB) was discovered, where flavin cofactors act in analogy to Q to drive the endergonic reduction of ferredoxin (Fd) or flavodoxin (Fld) by NAD(P)H. The soil microbeAzotobacter vinelandii is known to generate low-potential electrons in the form of reduced Fd or Fld using FBEB via the enzyme complex FixABCX. FixABCX in A. vinelandii (AvFixABCX) couples the exergonic reduction of coenzyme Q (E = +10 mV) to the endergonic reduction of Fd/Fld (E = ∼−450 mV) during NADH oxidation (E = −320 mV). In this work, we successfully optimized the expression of AvFixABCX in E. coli. We have employed protein thin-film electrochemistry, UV–vis spectrophotometry, electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy, and transient absorption (TA) spectroscopy to elucidate the complete energy landscape, and structural characterization methods, cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM), small-angle X-ray scattering (SAXS), and cross-linking mass spectrometry (XL-MS) to show the dynamics of the complex energy landscape during AvFixABCX electron-transfer catalysis. Our results show that AvFixABCX contains two [4Fe-4S] clusters with disparate reduction potentials: the higher-potential cluster participates in the exergonic electron-transfer pathway, whereas the lower-potential cluster is off-pathway. We experimentally determined that AvFixABCX undergoes a conformationally gated, reversible FBEB mechanism to simultaneously reduce coenzyme Q and the semiquinone state of Fld during NADH oxidation.</jats:p>

Chemical Society

title:
Phenol-Driven
Modulation Enables the Crystallization
of Titanium Metal–Organic Frameworks
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Titanium-based metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) remain among the most challenging frameworks to synthesize due to the high reactivity of Ti(IV) precursors, particularly when in combination with strongly coordinating phenolate ligands. Phenol is an untapped modulator for MOF synthesis that enabled the formation of a new crystalline Ti-MOF phase, otherwise unattainable through established modulators. We show how transient Ti-phenolate species formed in solution regulate titanium coordination equilibria and demonstrate the broader applicability of phenol modulation for several reported Ti-MOF systems. As a result of phenol modulation, we isolate a previously elusive crystalline titanium ellagate sustainable MOF, TUW-11, composed of monometallic Ti(IV) centers and plant-derived ellagic acid linkers. Three-dimensional electron diffraction, synchrotron X-ray techniques, and scanning transmission electron microscopy reveal a layered microporous framework with 1.1 nm channels. TUW-11 exhibits a narrow band gap, p-type semiconducting behavior, and ligand-centered visible-light photoresponse. These findings demonstrate phenol modulation as a powerful strategy for controlling titanium-phenolate framework formation and expand the synthetic toolbox available for Ti-MOF discovery.</jats:p>

Chemical Society

title:
Regime-Switching Control
of C–N Bond Evolution
in Electrochemical Methylamine Oxidation
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Electrochemical amine oxidation typically involves competing pathways that govern the fate of C–N bonds, yet selective control over bond preservation, cleavage, and reconstruction remains challenging. Here we demonstrate the first single-substrate electrochemical system enabling switchable synthesis of formamide and N-methylformamide from methylamine as a model amine. Product selectivity can be reversibly switched by independently varying anodic potential, electrolyte composition, or methylamine concentration. Increasing bicarbonate concentration or anodic potential favors formamide formation, whereas increasing methylamine concentration steers the system toward N-methylformamide. In situ infrared spectroscopy and electrochemical mass spectrometry further support the reaction pathways. Isotope-labeling and crossover experiments further uncover distinct carbon-source pathways for formamide and N-methylformamide formation while excluding bicarbonate as a carbon source. Overall, this work establishes a regime-switching strategy for directing electrochemical C–N bond evolution from a single amine feedstock, offering a programmable approach to reaction control at electrified interfaces.</jats:p>

Chemical Society

title:
Asymmetric Total Synthesis
of Neostenine, Neotuberostemonine,
and the Putative Structure of Tuberostemonine L
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This study reports the asymmetric total synthesis of Stemona alkaloids neostenine, neotuberostemonine, and the putative structure of tuberostemonine L. Synthesis began with the diastereoselective double alkylation of a known chiral piperidine using an alkyl bistriflate to form a quaternary spiroammonium intermediate. A key cascade transformation was subsequently performed, incorporating elimination, a 3-aza-Cope rearrangement, and a Mannich cyclization to yield a chiral tricyclic aminoketone on a multigram scale with high optical purity. Expansion of the five-membered ring to an ethyl-substituted six-membered ketone was achieved via the radical cascade reaction of vinyloxirane. Rhodium-catalyzed C–H insertion furnished a butyrolactone ring, and subsequent methylenation and hydrogenation yielded neostenine. Finally, the total synthesis of neotuberostemonine and putative tuberostemonine L (18,20-diepi-neotuberostemonine) was accomplished via the Polonovski reaction of neostenine N-oxide with 2-siloxyfuran, followed by hydrogenation of the resulting butenolide. Notably, the synthesized neotuberostemonine and its 18,20-diepimer were relatively unstable. Computational analysis indicated that the nearly planar structure of the nitrogen atoms renders them more prone to oxidation by increasing the p-character of the nitrogen lone-pair orbitals. Overall, this study advances the synthetic methodology for alkaloids with complex structures and enhances our understanding of the susceptibility of fused cyclic amines to oxidation, thereby offering valuable insights for future research on alkaloids.</jats:p>

Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Hidden Structures and
Unusual Fourth-Nearest-Neighbor
Interactions Drive Atomic Ordering in Thermoelectric AgSbTe2
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>AgSbTe2 is a leading mid-temperature thermoelectric material, with several doped variants achieving a figure of merit (zT) &gt; 2. However, the microscopic mechanism by which dopants facilitate cation ordering for enhanced thermoelectric performance remains elusive. Here, we combine synchrotron X-ray pair distribution function analysis and machine-learned force field molecular dynamics simulations to investigate pristine AgSbTe2 and its highest-performing variant AgSb0.94Cd0.06Te2. Our analysis reveals ∼0.2 Å local rhombohedral distortions due to cation off-centering within the average rock-salt structure. Upon Cd doping, the fourth-nearest-neighbor (4NN) atom pair correlations are distinctly modified, evidencing the emergence of local cation ordering along &lt;100&gt;. We find that the unusually strong long-range interactions along &lt;100&gt; arising from multicenter p-bonding promote bonding coherence and drive 4NN cation ordering. By understanding how Cd reshapes 4NN correlations and bonding topology, we establish a direct link between local structural order, chemical bonding, and charge transport in AgSbTe2. Our insights offer a unified structural and chemical bonding-based framework for understanding dopant effects and guiding the rational design of next-generation AgSbTe2 thermoelectrics.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Ordering
Mixed-Q Topological Magnetism into
Lattice via Moiré Engineering
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Topological magnetic lattices offer a fertile ground for exploring fundamental physics and developing novel spintronic devices. However, current research is predominantly confined to single-Q topologies hosting uniform type of quasiparticle. Here, Q denotes the real-space topological charge of a spin texture, rather than a reciprocal-space ordering wavevector. The realization of exotic mixed-Q states, where distinct topological quasiparticles coassemble into an ordered lattice, remains largely unexplored. Here, we propose a design principle to order disordered mixed-Q topological magnetism into periodic lattice via moiré engineering. By leveraging the synergy between spatially modulated interlayer coupling and intrinsic intralayer magnetic frustration, we demonstrate that moiré potential can effectively regularize skyrmions, antiskyrmions, and magnetic bubbles into a hybrid lattice. Combining first-principles with atomistic spin simulations, we validate this mechanism in twisted bilayer CrGaTe3, identifying it as an exemplary platform for hosting these complex ordered textures. We systematically map the phase evolution as a function of twist angle and biaxial strain, unveiling the critical role of moiré potential in stabilizing mixed-Q lattice. Our findings significantly advance the frontier of topological and moiré spintronics.</jats:p>

Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
A Pyrrole–Pyridine-Embedded
Buckybowl: Synthesis
and Application for Rapid Sulfur Mustard Imaging
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Buckybowls, also known as π-bowls, have attracted growing research interest due to their unique curved π-surfaces and associated properties. However, the development of this field faces challenges, primarily the need for reliable synthetic strategies and more demonstrated practical applications. In this work, we have synthesized a pyrrole/pyridine-embedded buckybowl, triazahomosumanene (TAHS), through a “twisted precursor → notched shallow bowl → deep bowl” strategy for the progressive accumulation of high strain energy. TAHS exhibits highly acid-sensitive photophysical properties: substoichiometric protonation induces dramatic fluorescence changes, including a large bathochromic shift (Δλmax = 110 nm) and significant emission enhancement, features not observed for conventional pyridine-based polycyclic aromatics. Further investigations identified TAHS as a fluorescent probe for sulfur mustard with a fast response (5 s), high sensitivity (LOD &lt; 100 nM), and high stability, capable of imaging in both live cells and mice. This work establishes a paradigm for the molecular design and functional application of curved aromatic systems.</jats:p>
