Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Tuning Superconductivity
and Topological Bands in
Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–C Medium-Entropy Carbides
by Valence Electron Concentration
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The search for unconventional superconductors is a hot topic in materials science and condensed matter physics, yet remains challenging. Here we report a series of medium-entropy carbides (MECs) within the Ta–Nb–Hf–Zr–C system with finely tuned valence electron concentration (VEC). Through VEC engineering, the type-II Dirac points are deliberately shifted from approximately 0.19 eV below the Fermi level in the base composition Ta0.25Nb0.25Hf0.25Zr0.25C to within 6.7–59.1 meV of the Fermi level in the optimal composition Ta0.1875Nb0.1875Hf0.3125Zr0.3125C. All five compositions form single-phase rock-salt structures and exhibit type-II bulk superconductivity with TcMid ranging from 2.2 to 4.9 K. Among these, the equimolar Ta0.25Nb0.25Hf0.25Zr0.25C composition exhibits the highest Tc of 4.9 K, with μ0Hc2GL = 1.16 T, μ0Hc1(0) = 65.9 Oe, and ΔC/γTc = 1.16, alongside excellent stability in acidic/alkaline environments and under pressures up to 52 GPa. Our findings establish VEC engineering as a potentially transferable strategy for bridging topological band physics with superconductivity in medium/high-entropy ceramics, positioning this MEC family as a candidate platform for investigating topological superconductivity in disordered systems.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Cooperative Reactivity
of Mangano–Germylene
and Germylidyne Complexes Featuring a Ge≡Mn Triple Bond
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Multiple bonding between heavier group 14 elements and transition metals has long fascinated chemists, yet manganese–germanium bonds remain virtually unexplored. We now report a germylidyne-manganese complex featuring a structurally authenticated Ge≡Mn triple bond, supported by detailed electronic structure analysis. The Ge≡Mn triple bond further exhibits pronounced π-reactivity toward Au(I), affording a heterotrinuclear Ge–Au–Mn metallacycle and providing chemical support for its multiple-bond character. In parallel, two monomangano–germylene complexes were isolated. These species display distinctive reactivity in regioselective alkyne carbonylation and nitrene insertion, transformations that are inaccessible to conventional single-site systems. Density functional theory calculations elucidate the cooperative roles of manganese and germanium in governing reactivity. Together, these results provide new insights into group 14–transition-metal multiple-bond chemistry and illustrate the ability of mangano–germylene frameworks to mediate unusual bond transformations.</jats:p>
journal:
Journal of the American
Chemical Society

title:
Acidity-Driven Spontaneous
Degradation of Trifluoroacetic
Acid at Droplet Air–Water Interfaces
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Trifluoroacetic acid (TFA), an ultrashort-chain per- and polyfluoroalkyl substance, is increasingly detected in the environment and has raised widespread concern because of its negative effects on health and ecosystems. However, whether TFA can degrade naturally in the environment remains unresolved. Here, we report the spontaneous degradation of TFA at the air–water interface of droplets, yielding F– and fluorine-containing transformation products, including CHF3O, CF3O2H, and CH2F2O2. The extent of degradation is strongly dependent on droplet acidity, with the F– yield at pH 10 being 12-fold higher than at pH 5. Density functional theory calculations reveal a mechanism favored by alkaline conditions and oxygen in which interfacial decarboxylation triggers sequential oxidation and defluorination. These findings identify the air–water interface of pH-regulated droplets as a reactive microenvironment for spontaneous TFA degradation, offering new insights into the environmental transformation of ultrashort-chain PFAS.</jats:p>

title:
Electron–Nuclear
Hyperfine Coupling Enables
Electron Paramagnetic Resonance Detection of Diamagnetic Cu(I) with
Trityl Spin Probes
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Copper homeostasis is tightly regulated in biological systems, and its dysregulation is implicated in various diseases. In the intracellular reducing environment, Cu(I) is the predominant oxidation state of labile copper; however, its detection remains highly challenging because of strong buffering by endogenous ligands and competition from biologically abundant metal ions. Here, we report an electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR)-based strategy that enables detection of otherwise EPR-silent Cu(I) by converting Cu(I) coordination into a characteristic spectroscopic fingerprint through electron–nuclear hyperfine coupling. A series of Cu(I)-hyperfine spin probes (CHYPs) were developed by tethering stable trityl radicals to Cu(I)-selective ligands through various linkers. Among these probes, CHYP7 formed a 1:1 complex with Cu(I) and displayed a well-resolved four-line EPR signal arising from hyperfine splitting by the copper nucleus (I = 3/2). CHYP7 exhibited high Cu(I) affinity, excellent metal-ion selectivity, and a low detection limit of ∼4 nM (0.2 pmol). A hydrophilic analogue, CHYP8, further enabled quantitative Cu(I) measurement under acidic conditions in the presence of endogenous ligands and competing metal ions. CHYP8 was also applied to measure cellular labile copper pools and monitor copper-level changes following copper supplementation or hypoxia-reoxygenation treatment, as well as to quantify labile copper pools in tissues and serum from mice subjected to ischemia/reperfusion injury. Overall, this work establishes hyperfine-coupling-enabled EPR detection as a new strategy for probing Cu(I) in biological systems and provides a platform for investigating copper homeostasis and copper-associated pathophysiology.</jats:p>

title:
Protein Scaffolds Modulate
the Electronic Structure
of a Common Ketyl Radical Intermediate in Thiamine Pyrophosphate-Dependent
Radical Biocatalysis: Insights from EPR and ENDOR Spectroscopy
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>New-to-nature radical biocatalysis has emerged as a powerful strategy for asymmetric C–C bond formation, yet the enzyme-bound radical intermediates that underpin these transformations have remained largely uncharacterized. Here, we combine photobiocatalytic reaction development with multifrequency electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR), electron–nuclear double resonance (ENDOR) spectroscopy, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations to elucidate the ketyl radical intermediates formed during thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP)-dependent radical biocatalysis. We first develop an oxidative photobiocatalytic cross-coupling of aldehydes with alkyltrifluoroborates catalyzed by engineered benzoylformate decarboxylase (BFD) variants, providing enantioenriched α-chiral ketones through a new oxidative radical manifold inaccessible to benzaldehyde lyases (BALs). Freeze-quench multifrequency EPR and ENDOR spectroscopy directly identify the catalytically generated TPP-bound ketyl radical and reveal that this common radical intermediate adopts distinct electronic structures in BFD and BAL despite their identical chemical composition. Analysis of 1H, 19F, 31P, and 14N hyperfine interactions, together with DFT calculations, demonstrates that enzyme-specific active-site conformations redistribute spin density between the TPP cofactor and substrate fragment. Greater substrate-centered spin delocalization in BFD provides a mechanistic basis for its superior radical C–C coupling activity relative to BAL. These results establish a direct relationship between protein-controlled electronic structure and catalytic function in TPP-dependent radical biocatalysis and demonstrate that engineering the electronic properties of a common radical intermediate represents a useful strategy for controlling enzyme reactivity in radical biocatalysis.</jats:p>

title:
Diazo DOC: A Diazomethane
Sulfonyl Fluoride Surrogate
for Diversity-Oriented Clicking and SuFEx-Driven Protein Labeling
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Diversity-oriented clicking (DOC) is a unified click approach for the modular synthesis of lead-like structures through the application of the wider family of click transformations. Here, we present a diazomethane sulfonyl fluoride surrogate, tert-butyl(((diazomethyl)sulfonyl)methoxy)dimethylsilane (tBu-DMSM, a diazo DOC hub), as the latest connective hub in DOC, marking a significant advancement in the field. Through a series of processes that adhere to many of the click chemistry principles, followed by silyl deprotection and electrophilic fluorination, we highlight the potential of this DOC hub in the synthesis of a library of unprecedented clickable heterocycles (tetrazoles, 3,3′-cyclopropyl spirooxindoles, and benzo[d]oxepines). The diversification of these novel cores through sulfur fluoride exchange (SuFEx) click chemistry yields the corresponding sulfonate esters, showcasing the versatility of the DOC strategy. Additionally, simple removal of the silyloxymethane group increases the scope further for the selective synthesis of heterocycles, with tBu-DMSM acting as a diazomethane alternative or a one carbon synthon. Furthermore, the utility of this method is showcased in the synthesis of a novel aggregation-induced emission (AIE) fluorescent tetrazole probe for covalent protein labeling via SuFEx, revealing selective and structure-dependent protein modification.</jats:p>

title:
Redox-Active Spin Trapping
for the Electrochemical
Detection, Quantification, and Kinetic Analysis of Sulfate Radicals
in Aqueous Media
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Sulfate radicals (SO4•–) are important intermediates in synthetic and environmental chemistry, yet robust methods for their selective detection and quantification remain underdeveloped. Spin traps such as 5–5-dimethyl-1-pyrroline-N-oxide (DMPO) are used to extend the lifetime of these radicals, but the resulting adduct (DMPO–SO4•–) is unstable in water, undergoing nucleophilic substitution to DMPO–OH•, causing misidentification and mechanistic confusion in aqueous systems. Here, we report an electrochemical approach for the selective and quantitative detection of sulfate radical spin-trap adducts in aqueous conditions. Using electrochemical electron paramagnetic resonance (EC-EPR) spectroscopy, we measured the half-life of DMPO–SO4•- in water to be ∼98 s. This short half-life makes the quantification of SO4•– by traditional EPR methods challenging. To overcome this, we used an approach to electrochemically detect spin-trap adducts and found that DMPO–SO4•– could be electrochemically oxidized at ∼0.75 V vs Ag/AgCl. Coupling this approach to microband interdigitated electrode arrays (IDAs) in generation-collection mode, automated electrochemistry, and finite-element simulations, we leveraged the short detection time (ms) of IDAs to capture DMPO–SO4•– before it decays. Quantitative understanding allowed us to estimate the DMPO spin trapping rate constant for SO4•– (4 × 105 M–1s–1). Finally, changes in the DMPO–SO4•– collection current were used to extract the kinetics of a competing reaction (oxidation of benzyl alcohol) in a radical clock-type approach. These results demonstrate the broad utility of redox-active spin trapping for quantifying electrogenerated radical intermediates such as SO4•– with sufficient versatility to capture their transient processes.</jats:p>

title:
Dynamic
Site Heterogeneity in Nanoparticle Catalysis
from Hierarchical Machine Learning
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Identifying the activity of all individual surface sites on catalytic nanoparticles is challenging but critical for heterogeneous catalysts, especially for understanding site heterogeneity. Here, we developed a hierarchical machine learning approach that links the atomic local environment to both energy and reaction barrier predictions with similar computational costs, opening the feasibility of extensive catalytic reactivity exploration on nanoparticle catalysts. Applying the methodology to propane dehydrogenation at a reaction temperature of 973 K on Pt nanoparticles up to a size of 5 nm revealed a highly dynamic and heterogeneous activity with a wide distribution of propane C–H cleavage barriers (0.5–1.3 eV) and rare highly active or inactive sites. Conventional global optimization methods underestimate the catalytic activity, even by considering a large set of metastable structures. Instead, accurate activity and size effect trend emerge by using ensemble-averaged molecular dynamics trajectories, emphasizing the dynamic nature of site activity and heterogeneity. Notably, classical polyhedral models, like those obtained from a Wulff construction, can predict correct trends for larger nanoparticles but do so through error cancellation between missing dynamics and overestimating probabilities of metastable sites. Furthermore, our simulations reveal a fast barrier fluctuation at the reaction temperature for a given surface Pt atom within 100 ps trajectories with a barrier shift by up to 0.8 eV, indicating that individual atoms can switch between active and inactive states on a picosecond time scale. This work provides a feasible approach to shift the views of catalysts from a combination of static active sites to highly heterogeneous and fast dynamically evolving sites.</jats:p>

title:
Total Synthesis of
Damasterpenes II, IV, V, and VII
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Damasterpenes are highly oxygenated, multiply acylated dolabellane diterpenoids with anti-herpes simplex virus type 1 activity. These compounds share an 11/5-trans-fused carboskeleton with three methyl groups and one isopropyl group, but differ in their unsaturation, oxidation, and acylation patterns. Here, we present the first total synthesis of damasterpenes II, IV, V, and VII. In the first stage, a common 11/5-fused intermediate was convergently assembled using radical-polar crossover three-component coupling to install the two carbon branches onto the five-membered ring, followed by ring-closing metathesis to form the medium-sized 11-membered ring. In the second stage, this intermediate was transformed into damasterpenes II, IV, V, and two possible structures of damasterpene VII by tuning the oxidation levels and introducing three to four acyl groups. These architecturally complex molecules bearing 8 to 10 stereocenters were synthesized in 26–29 steps, and the previously unknown stereochemistry of damasterpene VII was elucidated. This work demonstrates the value of radical-polar crossover reactions for the rapid construction of densely substituted molecular frameworks and highlights the importance of controlling the three-dimensional conformations of 5- and 11-membered rings to achieve site- and stereoselective functional group manipulations.</jats:p>

title:
Copper-Catalyzed Diastereoselective
and Enantioselective
α-C–H Allenylation of Alkylamines
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Herein, we report a diastereoselective and enantioselective α-allenylation of N-α-cyanoarylidene alkylamines with propargylic carbonates via a sequential copper-catalyzed imine propargylation and aza-Cope rearrangement process. This method features broad substrate scope with respect to both reaction partners, thereby establishing an unprecedented protocol for the efficient asymmetric synthesis of chiral amines containing both central and axial chirality from readily accessible alkylamines and propargylic carbonates. Additionally, we demonstrated that these chiral α-allenyl amines could be readily transformed into a diverse range of chiral amine derivatives. Mechanistic studies revealed that the simultaneous coordination and π–π interaction between the cyano group and dicopper-allenylidene complex played decisive roles for the induction of the chemoselectivity, diastereoselectivity, and enantioselectivity during imine propargylation. The subsequent aza-Cope rearrangement proceeded with an efficient central-to-axial chirality transfer to generate the chiral allene motif.</jats:p>

title:
Fast ON/OFF Emission
Photoswitching of Turn-On Mode
Fluorescent Diarylethenes
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Fluorescent chromophores having reversible photoswitching ability are applicable for various types of analysis and imaging. 1,2-Bis(2-ethyl-6-phenyl-1-benzothiophene-1,1-dioxide-3-yl)perfluorocyclopentene (1) is known to undergo turn-on mode fluorescent photoswitching. One serious drawback of the chromophore is its very low photocycloreversion (switching off) quantum yield (&lt;10–3). To improve the yield, derivatives bearing various alkyl substituents at 2- and 2′-positions were prepared. It was found that introduction of bulky substituents, such as isobutyl or neopentyl groups, is effective in increasing the yield. The yield increases by almost 3 orders of magnitude from 5.9 × 10–4 to 4.6 × 10–1 by replacing ethyl substituents with neopentyl groups. Theoretical analysis revealed that the energy barrier in the photocycloreversion reaction is inferred from the calculated potential energy difference between 2Ao and 2Ac local minima in the excited-state (S1) potential energy surface, and the decrease in the energy difference by introducing bulky primary alkyl substituents at 2- and 2′-position increases the photocycloreversion quantum yield. Although substitution of primary alkyl groups increases the yield, secondary alkyl substituents are ineffective. 1,2-Bis(2-neopentyl-6-phenyl-1-benzothiophene-1,1-dioxide-3-yl)perfluorocyclopentene (6) undergoes very fast ON/OFF emission photoswitching cycles over 2000 times even in the presence of air without any marked fatigue, and the colored closed-ring isomer is stable at 80 °C for 50 h.</jats:p>

title:
Dual Regulation of
Electronic Structure and Hydrogen
Distribution through Co Single-Atom-Functionalized Supports for Efficient
Ru-Catalyzed Ammonia Synthesis
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Under mild reaction conditions, ammonia synthesis over Ru catalysts is severely constrained by hydrogen poisoning because excessive surface hydrogen blocks the Ru B5 sites required for efficient N2 activation. To overcome this challenge, we design an atomically functionalized support by anchoring isolated Co single atoms at framework sites of K-modified KL zeolite, creating a dual-function support. The Co single atoms serve as hydrogen-accepting sites that continuously remove surface H atoms from Ru via hydrogen spillover, i.e., spatial regulation of surface hydrogen. Moreover, they indirectly strengthen the electron donation from framework K to Ru for N2 activation, without any direct Co → Ru charge transfer, thereby enhancing both the availability and the intrinsic activity of Ru B5 sites for efficient N2 dissociation. This cooperative mechanism is collectively revealed by comprehensive kinetic analyses, operando spectroscopy, isotope-exchange measurements, chemisorption studies, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations. Consequently, Ru/Co1–KL achieves a near-equilibrium ammonia synthesis rate of 65.3 mmol g–1 h–1 at 400 °C and 1 MPa and maintains stable performance for over 1500 h. This work demonstrates that atomic support functionalization can spatially decouple competing adsorption processes at catalytic interfaces, offering an effective strategy for overcoming site-blocking limitations in heterogeneous catalysis.</jats:p>

title:
Machine Learning-Guided
Precise Electrolyte Engineering
Enables Stable Lithium Metal Pouch Cells Exceeding 350 Wh/kg at −40
°C
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>High-energy-density lithium metal batteries (LMBs) with wide-temperature adaptability are urgently needed for aerospace and military fields, yet extreme temperature conditions disrupt Li+ transport kinetics and cause failure in solid–electrolyte interphase (SEI) chemistry regulation. To guide molecular selection for wide-temperature electrolyte design, we constructed Electrolyte-65K, a rule-defined library of electrolyte-relevant molecules, and trained D-P Compass using batch-computable molecular descriptors to efficiently predict and rank dipole moment (D) and polarizability (P). Applying the trained models to a literature-derived set of electrolyte molecule candidates, D-P Pareto analysis identified N,N-dimethyltrifluoromethanesulfonamide (DMTMSA) as the candidate at the Pareto knee. The thermally sensitive dipole–dipole interactions between DMTMSA and weakly solvating solvent 1,2-diethoxyethane (DEE) enable a temperature-autoresponsive electrolyte that maintains an anion-dominated solvation structure across a wide temperature range, enabling SEI chemistry engineering regulation from −40 to 60 °C. A 5.8 Ah pouch cell achieves a high energy density of 503.7 Wh kg–1 at 25 °C with a lifespan of 275 cycles and retains 365.5 Wh kg–1 at −40 °C with 99.8% capacity retention over 50 cycles. This work establishes a data-driven molecular screening framework for wide-temperature electrolyte engineering design.</jats:p>

title:
Mechanistic Insights
into Sodium Storage in N-Doped
Graphene/MoS2 Heterostructures Revealed by Operando Raman
Spectroscopy
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Two-dimensional (2D) heterostructures offer tunable interlayer spacing and accessible surfaces that can overcome key limitations of conventional sodium-ion battery (SIBs) anodes. Here, we investigate Na+ storage mechanisms in three-layer 2D heterostructures composed of horizontally stacked graphene (G), nitrogen-doped graphene (NG), and MoS2 (M) by combining cyclic voltammetry with operando spectroelectrochemical Raman spectroscopy. Restricting the active thickness to three atomic layers enables direct spectroscopic access to interfacial charge transfer and strain during cycling. Electrochemical analysis reveals that Na+ storage is governed by two coupled factors: the permeability of the electrolyte-facing outer layer, and the electronic–mechanical interactions within the interlayer space. NG outer layers facilitate ion access and deliver up to 40-fold higher capacities than pristine graphene stacks, whereas MoS2 top layers suppress ion infiltration. Operando Raman correlates faradaic features with reversible structural changes, allowing separation of charge-doping and strain effects during cycling. The results demonstrate that Na+ storage proceeds predominantly via reversible accumulation in confined interlayer and blister-like reservoirs formed during solvent cointercalation. Incorporating MoS2 as a middle layer redistributes charge and buffers mechanical strain, enhancing cycling stability. These findings provide insights into charge storage mechanisms in 2D materials.</jats:p>

title:
Acoustic
Cavitation-Enhanced Remodeling of Lymph Node
Microenvironment Enables Deep Infiltration for Potent Cancer Vaccination
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The efficacy of peptide-based tumor vaccines is often constrained by the size-exclusion barrier of the subcapsular sinus (SCS), which restricts infiltration of macromolecules into the lymph node (LN) parenchyma essential for T-cell priming. Here, inspired by the clinical contrast agent Sonazoid, we developed an ultrasound-assisted vaccine platform with tunable phase-transition behavior for the active modulation of the LN microenvironment. The system integrates phosphoserine-decorated lipid chemistry to promote cell-mediated LN trafficking, a covalently conjugated adjuvant–antigen construct for synchronized immunostimulation, and liquid-state perfluorocarbon nanodomains programmed for ultrasound-triggered liquid–gas transition. Upon localized ultrasound irradiation, the chemically programmed phase transition triggers cargo release, while the resultant acoustic cavitation generates transient openings in the SCS endothelium. This process enables deep parenchymal infiltration of vaccine components that would otherwise be excluded. Beyond the physical barrier disruption, RNA sequencing reveals that acoustic stimulation drives both structural and immunological reprogramming of LN into an immune-permissive niche. By synergizing mechanical stimulation with biological modulation, this strategy induces benign and persistent LN expansion, amplifies antitumor T-cell responses, and establishes durable immunological memory, resulting in both prophylactic and therapeutic outcomes. This approach is versatile across both model antigens and neoantigens, offering a bioinspired, two-stage LN-targeted delivery strategy that serves as a framework for designing more effective therapeutic vaccines.</jats:p>

content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Dynamic DNA nanomachines are programmable devices capable of executing certain controlled movements, structural reconfigurations, and functional tasks. Over the past few decades, extensive advancements have been made in designing DNA-based molecular systems driven by strand displacement, catalytic reactions, enzymatic processes, chemical or physical stimuli. The development of DNA nanotechnology has further enabled the construction of highly precise and complex DNA nanomachines. Herein, we review dynamic DNA nanomachines from a motion-to-function perspective, emphasizing how programmable movement, structural reconfiguration, or autonomous operation can be converted into biomedical output. Structural platforms, driving mechanisms, biomedical functions, and translational barriers are discussed. Particularly, we focus on the systems in which DNA dynamics directly contribute to biosensing, bioimaging, therapeutic activation, cell regulation, and molecular decision-making. This framework distinguishes dynamic DNA nanomachines from static DNA nanostructures, which also highlights the design requirements needed to move these systems toward practical biomedical applications.</jats:p>

title:
In-Situ Visualization
of Thermal Transformation Pathways
in Leaf-Shaped Zeolitic Imidazolate Framework Derived Nanocarbon
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) are versatile precursors for nanostructured, heteroatom-doped carbons. However, understanding the spatiotemporally resolved mechanisms that govern crystalline-to-amorphous framework collapse, diffusion-mediated reorganization of transient intermediates, and the subsequent formation of graphitic carbon remains challenging. Here, we elucidate the transformation of the 2D leaf-shaped zeolitic imidazolate framework ZIF-L into Zn-dispersed N-doped carbon using a combination of in situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD). These measurements directly capture the sequential collapse of the layered MOF framework and the associated morphological evolution under controlled heating, decoupled from beam-induced effects during electron microscopy. Complementary ex-situ pyrolysis (700–1100 °C), together with high-resolution TEM, synchrotron X-ray pair distribution function (X-PDF) analysis, and electron energy-loss spectroscopy (EELS), reveals the diffusion of Zn-containing species, ligand decomposition, and progressive graphitization within the amorphous matrix. We identify temperature-dependent stages involving ligand breakdown, migration of Zn–Nx species, followed by Zn loss, and ultimately forming porous N-doped carbon at 1000 °C that exhibits the strongest electrochemical response within this series. These findings establish temperature-dependent structure–property relationships that enable the thermal engineering of MOF-derived ORR catalysts.</jats:p>

title:
Size-Dependent Surface
Evolution Controls Luminescence
in Ln3+-Doped Nanocrystals
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Lanthanide-doped luminescent nanocrystals (NCs) hold significant promise for bioimaging, theranostics, catalysis, sensing, lighting, and displays, motivating an in-depth understanding of their optical properties. This work reveals the profound, yet widely disregarded, impact of surface structure changes on the luminescence of growing NCs through a model study of Eu3+ surface-exchanged Sr2YF7 NCs. Contrary to expectation, a stark drop in luminescence intensity exceeding several orders of magnitude was observed as the particle size increased. Atomic-resolution electron microscopy imaging shows that the NCs evolve from spheroidal to cuboidal morphologies during growth, with a shift in preferentially exposed crystal facets from {111} to {200} that renders lattice distortion less favorable. High-resolution optical spectroscopy probing surface Eu3+, together with energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy and reaction kinetics study, reveals a high extent of Eu3+ exchange in the small spheroidal NCs with lattice distortion extending far from the surface into the interior. This starkly contrasts the situation in the large cuboidal NCs, where the extent of Eu3+ residing in the surface region is severely limited, thereby causing the dramatic drop in luminescence. These findings demonstrate surface structure control as a powerful strategy for tailoring the luminescence properties of Ln3+-doped NCs and other nanomaterials for advanced applications.</jats:p>

title: Three-in-One Injectable Hydrogel Orchestrating Host-Bacteria Targeting, Retention, and Autophagy for Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus aureus -Infected Mastitis Therapy
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>MRSA mastitis is clinically refractory and characterized by progressive inflammation driven by intracellular bacteria that form persistent niches in mammary epithelial cells and macrophages to evade antimicrobial clearance. Conventional antibiotics, particularly β-lactams, are widely used but suffer from poor intracellular accumulation, failing to reach these reservoirs. Even nanocarrier-based strategies struggle to achieve efficient endosomal escape and precise intracellular targeting. Herein, we report a fibronectin-functionalized, fluorinated PLGA nanoparticle encapsulating amoxicillin and sulbactam (Fn-F-PLGA@A/S) engineered with a 2.5% (w/w) fluorinated core for efficient endosomal escape. The fibronectin decoration enables sequential targeting of both host integrins and bacterial fibronectin-binding proteins (FnBPs). Fn-F-PLGA@A/S achieved efficient intracellular delivery, clearing 90% of intracellular MRSA in macrophages and epithelial cells within 4 h in vitro. To prolong mammary retention, Fn-F-PLGA@A/S was loaded into a thermosensitive hydrogel. In a murine MRSA mastitis model, a single intramammary dose of the gel formulation achieved &gt;90% bacterial reduction, attenuated TNF-α and IL-6, and preserved alveolar architecture and tight junctions. Proteomic analysis revealed upregulation of AMPK-mediated autophagy, suggesting that beyond direct antibiotic action, the potent intracellular clearance achieved by Fn-F-PLGA may involve the engagement of host autophagic machinery, potentially facilitating the sequestration of MRSA within degradative compartments. Collectively, by integrating sequential targeting, sustained local retention, and autophagic engagement, this platform provides a robust strategy to address the key limitations of conventional antibiotics against intracellular pathogens in refractory infections.</jats:p>

title:
Inhalable Multifunctional
Liposomes Disrupt the Inflammation-Oxidative
Stress Cycle for Acute Lung Injury Therapy
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Acute lung injury (ALI) is characterized by an uncontrolled cycle of inflammation and oxidative stress. However, conventional therapeutics are limited by physiological pulmonary barriers and poor targeted bioavailability. In this study, an inhalable multifunctional liposomal system (designated as R&I/Lip@PEG-M) was elaborately engineered to codeliver Resveratrol and IMD-0354 to disrupt the inflammation-oxidative stress cycle for ALI therapy. Upon nebulized inhalation, the negatively charged R&I/Lip@PEG-M liposomes would efficiently penetrate the mucus barrier, extensively accumulate in the pulmonary alveoli, and be specifically taken up by alveolar macrophages via mannose-mediated targeting recognition. Particularly, the internalized liposomes could exert combined therapeutic effects by scavenging intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) and blocking the NF-κB signaling pathway to inhibit inflammation. In the LPS-induced ALI mouse model, the designed R&I/Lip@PEG-M significantly reduced the population of inflammatory macrophages, reprogrammed the redox microenvironment, and successfully mitigated lung damage and pulmonary edema.</jats:p>

title:
The Temperature
Dependence of the Pathogenic Bacterial
Adhesin Complex SdrG:Fgβ under Sustained Loads: A High-Force
Slip Bond
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Staphylococcus epidermidis is the leading cause of medical-implant-related infections. This pathogen attaches to medical implants coated in host fibrinogen via adhesin proteins. To resist high shear forces, adhesin-ligand rupture forces can exceed 2000 pN, a force that is much higher than streptavidin–biotin (150–300 pN). Yet, these adhesin-ligand complexes have a quite moderate KD (∼380 nM). This nanomechanics is explained, in part, by catch-bond behavior where adhesin-ligand lifetimes increase with force. Notably, prior reports of adhesin catch-bond mechanics at both low (3–30 pN) and high (1100–1400 pN) forces have lifetimes that are difficult to reconcile. Here, we combined constant-velocity and constant-force assays and thereby showed slip-bond behavior over six decades of lifetimes first for SdrG:Fgβ (1000–2400 pN) and then for SdrE:CFH (800–2200 pN) from Staphylococcus aureus. Individual lifetimes for SdrE:CFH exceeded 15 min at 800 pN. To investigate the thermodynamics of SdrG:Fgβ stability, we measured its lifetime using the constant-force assay as a function of both force (1000–1800 pN) and temperature (10–37 °C). Analysis yielded the enthalpic-dissociation barrier (ΔH‡ = 40 ± 4 kBT) and, assuming an enthalpy-dominated barrier, the dissociation attempt frequency (∼6 × 1010 s–1). Our results unambiguously demonstrate high-force slip-bond behavior for two different adhesin-ligand pairs and provide biophysical parameters governing the stability of key virulence factors.</jats:p>

title:
Fast-Gelling, Adhesive,
and Conductive Epidermal Electrode
for Accurate Physiological Signal Monitoring and Real-Time Brain-Controlled
Drone Flight
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Conductive hydrogel electrodes are vital components for achieving human-machine interfaces. However, the inherent trade-off between high conductivity and favorable mechanical/adhesive properties remains a significant challenge for hydrogel-based epidermal electrodes. Here, we developed a multifunctional MXene/WPU/PAA (MWA) hydrogel electrode that combines robust mechanical properties, strong adhesion, and excellent conductivity. The introduced MXene nanosheets can induce free-radical polymerization, resulting in fast gelation (&lt;5 min) at room temperature. Theoretical analyses reveal that MXene nanosheets form abundant hydrogen bonds with polymer chains, thus enhancing the cross-linking density and mechanical strength of the hydrogel electrode. The MWA hydrogel can form a stable skin-electrode interface, enabling high-fidelity multimodal physiological signal monitoring. Specifically, the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) for sEMG reached 36.0 dB, while the SNR for ECG was 30.1 dB, outperforming the Ag/AgCl electrodes. The MWA hydrogel exhibits outstanding adhesion under repeated cycles and simulated sweat conditions, reaching 94.2 and 55.5 kPa, respectively. Furthermore, the MWA hydrogel electrode demonstrates precise scalp EEG monitoring, enabling wireless drone flight control via real-time brainwave decoding. This work provides insight into MXene-polymer interactions and demonstrates the applicability of the developed electrode to brain-computer interface applications.</jats:p>

title:
Spectroscopic Identification
of Dimensionality-Driven
Anticorrelation between Charge-Density-Wave Order and Superconductivity
in Ultrathin NbSe2
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Intertwined electronic orders in low-dimensional quantum materials often evolve in a strongly thickness-dependent manner, yet direct spectroscopic access to their mutual evolution remains a key challenge. NbSe2 is a prototypical layered superconductor in which charge-density-wave order coexists with superconductivity, but spectroscopic signatures of the charge-density-wave state are frequently obscured, limiting direct comparison with superconducting order. Here, we demonstrate all-van der Waals planar tunnel junctions as a spectroscopic platform for simultaneously probing charge-density-wave and superconducting states in NbSe2 from the bulk to the bilayer limit. Temperature-dependent tunneling spectra reveal distinct anomalies associated with charge-density-wave formation and superconducting gap opening, allowing both quantum phase transitions to be tracked within the same device architecture. We find that the charge-density-wave transition temperature increases from ∼34 to ∼56 K as the NbSe2 thickness is reduced from 11L to the bilayer, while the superconducting transition temperature decreases from ∼7.2 to ∼5.4 K. These results reveal a clear anticorrelation between the two ordered states as dimensionality is reduced. Moreover, our spectroscopic studies reveal that the emergence of charge-density-wave order modifies the electronic states of NbSe2 over a broad energy window extending up to ±300 meV, a widely anticipated but previously experimentally inaccessible characteristic. Our results provide comprehensive spectroscopic evidence for the thickness-dependent competition between charge-density-wave order and superconductivity in ultrathin NbSe2 and position planar van der Waals tunnel junctions as a powerful platform for investigating emergent quantum phases in layered materials.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Coupled
Design of Silicon Anodes and Solid-State Electrolytes
for High-Performance All-Solid-State Batteries
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Silicon-based solid-state batteries (Si-SSBs) offer enhanced safety and higher energy density over conventional liquid-electrolyte systems, yet their practical realization is critically hindered by severe volume expansion of silicon anodes and poor interfacial compatibility with solid-state electrolytes. This review provides a comprehensive evaluation of recent advances from a coupled design perspective, integrating silicon anode engineering, electrolyte compatibility optimization, and interfacial stabilization. We systematically examine emerging strategies for silicon anodes alongside compatibility approaches tailored to each electrolyte type, with a particular focus on the coupled chemo-mechanical degradation at the silicon/electrolyte interface. A systematic compatibility mapping linking different Si architectures with specific electrolyte families reveals the most promising material combinations and their underlying design principles. Beyond materials design, we address critical manufacturing challenges including stack pressure management, scalable processing, and prelithiation techniques essential for industrial translation. Finally, we propose a forward-looking roadmap integrating multiscale characterization, AI-assisted design, and scalable fabrication, providing both theoretical guidance and practical strategies for developing high-performance, commercially viable Si-SSBs.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Highly Confined
Magnetophononic Polaritons and Electron–Phonon
Interactions in Atomically Thin MnBi2Te4
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Atomically thin materials can strongly confine light into quanta of lattice vibrations, leading to strong light–matter interactions. Some of these materials can exhibit topology, which protects the edge states embedded inside the bulk from backscattering, while some host magnetism, providing another degree of freedom to control topological properties. The simultaneous observation of all of these phenomena in a single material can lead to various applications by enabling light-controlled topological electronic and nanophotonic devices. Here we demonstrate via first-principles density functional perturbation theory calculations that atomically thin MnBi2Te4 is a promising platform for hosting three highly confined, tunable, and long-propagating magnetophononic polaritons. These polaritons strongly modulate exchange interactions, especially the second polariton in 2 SL MnBi2Te4, inducing strong light–matter coupling in the presence of light. Intriguingly, this coupling not only induces an antiferromagnetic-to-ferromagnetic phase transition but also drives an electronic phase transition from trivial to topologically nontrivial states in 2 SL MnBi2Te4. We also show that these polaritonic modes have relatively weak electron–phonon scattering rates and that these scattering rates change with layer thickness and magnetic ordering due to spin–phonon coupling. Overall, our results suggest that MnBi2Te4 is a promising material for topological electronics, nanophotonics, and nanophonics capable of providing greater control of data signals via light.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Controllable Refraction
of Highly Confined Hyperbolic
Phonon Polaritons Using van der Waals Dielectric Superstrates
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In stark contrast with traditional refraction phenomenon in isotropic media, refraction of hyperbolic polaritons enables extreme confinement and nanofocusing of mid-infrared light. However, the tuning of hyperbolic refraction typically relies on plasmonic systems (e.g., gating graphene and phase-change materials), and therefore, the electron–electron scattering introduces inevitable propagation losses of polaritons. Herein, we demonstrate that refraction of highly confined hyperbolic polaritons in α-phase molybdenum trioxide (α-MoO3) crystal strongly depends on the dielectric superstrate. We theoretically and experimentally indicate that both the wavevector (its direction and magnitude) and the propagation direction of refracted hyperbolic polaritons can be controlled by varying the twist angle between the vdW dielectric layers of tungsten diselenide (WSe2) and α-MoO3 crystals. Moreover, we observe the total internal reflection and zero-phase propagation of nanoscale-confined polaritons in hyperbolic media. Our study of the propagation of hyperbolic polaritons not only deepens the understanding of polariton refraction at the nanoscale and in strongly anisotropic media but also promises the development of functional nanophotonic elements and devices.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Near-Infrared Neuromodulation:
Principles, Nanotechnology-Enabled
Platforms, and Emerging Biomedical Frontiers
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Optogenetics enables highly specific regulation of neuronal activity with exceptional spatiotemporal precision, providing powerful tools for neural circuit interrogation and the treatment of neurological disorders. However, the limited tissue penetration of visible light restricts its application to deep neural tissues. Near-infrared (NIR) neuromodulation has emerged as a promising alternative by leveraging the superior tissue penetration and minimal invasiveness of NIR light. Recent advances in NIR-responsive nanomaterials, optical engineering, and neurotechnology have rapidly transformed the field from nonspecific photobiomodulation to cell-specific nanotransducer-mediated neuromodulation and integrated neuromodulation systems. In this review, we summarize the optical principles governing NIR propagation in biological tissues and the mechanisms underlying NIR-mediated neural stimulation. We then discuss recent advances in representative NIR nanotransducers, including photothermal, optoelectric, photoacoustic, and NIR-to-visible upconversion platforms together with integrated neuromodulation systems that combine NIR stimulation with multimodal neural recording and closed-loop feedback. We further highlight emerging applications in the central nervous system, optic nerve, and peripheral nerve disorders. Finally, we discuss the key challenges toward clinical translation, including improving tissue penetration, cell specificity, biosafety, and translation, developing intelligent multidisciplinary neuromodulation platforms, and integrating artificial intelligence with closed-loop neural interfaces to achieve adaptive, precise, and personalized neuromodulation.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Kinetic Access to
Focal Conic Domains in Photonic
Cellulose Nanocrystal Films
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Cellulose nanocrystals (CNCs) self-assemble into cholesteric structures that enable sustainable photonic films, but controlling their pitch, domain morphology, and angular color response remains challenging. Here, we investigate how salt concentration and sonication dose jointly regulate the evaporation-induced self-assembly of CNC suspensions. Across 24 dish-cast films, polarized optical microscopy, time-lapse imaging, rheology, electron microscopy, and angle-resolved spectroscopy reveal that these processing parameters affect not only the cholesteric pitch but also tactoid nucleation, transport, coalescence, and the onset of kinetic arrest. Increasing NaCl concentration generally blue-shifts the photonic response, whereas sonication red-shifts it by fragmenting CNC bundles, with the magnitude of this effect decreasing as ionic content increases. At intermediate ionic content, low sonication doses produce extended cholesteric domains with comparatively narrow spectral responses, while the abundance of focal conic domains (FCDs) increases with sonication dose, culminating in FCD-rich films at moderate sonication. Refined parameter scans show that FCDs form within a finite processing window. Time-lapse imaging shows that FCDs appear abruptly after tactoid growth and coalescence, as macroscopic motion becomes strongly restricted during late-stage evaporation. Concentration- and residence-time-dependent rheology further demonstrates that the material response evolves throughout the assembly pathway. The FCD-rich film retains a narrow local reflection band while exhibiting the smallest angular displacement of the reflection maximum among the films examined. These findings show that salt and sonication regulate the kinetic accessibility of elastically driven focal conic structures, providing a route to tune domain morphology, spectral bandwidth, and iridescence in CNC photonic films.</jats:p>

title:
Selective
Electronic Pre-Activation of OH Bonds in
Extremely Confined Water
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Water under molecular-scale confinement is not simply a geometrically restricted form of bulk water, but can acquire distinct electronic, structural, and collective properties. However, how such an extremely confined state reshapes water’s intrinsic chemistry remains poorly understood. Here, using ab initio calculations and enhanced-sampling machine-learning potential molecular dynamics, we show that extreme two-dimensional confinement activates water for proton generation. Monolayer-confined water exhibits a substantially lower free-energy barrier for forming separated H3O+ and OH– ions than bulk water, and this tendency is further enhanced by lateral compression and nuclear quantum fluctuations. This enhanced reactivity does not arise from a uniform weakening of all water molecules. Instead, confinement makes OH bonds breaking selectively. The water molecule contains electronically distinct OH bonds, with weak in-plane bonds preferentially activated for proton release, while stronger dangling bonds remain relatively inactive. The surrounding hydrogen-bond network then provides disordered pathways for proton relocation, and the enhanced in-plane polarization stabilizes the charged products. Our results suggest that two-dimensional confined water can act as an active and superdielectric medium as indicated by recent experiments. Our findings reveal extreme confinement as a route to tune water-mediated chemistry, with implications for nanofluidics, geochemical pores, biological environments, and catalytic interfaces.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Nanoscale Immune
Activator for Enhancing CD8+ T Cell Infiltration in Hepatocellular
Carcinoma
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The infiltration of CD8+ T cells into the hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) microenvironment is a well-established determinant of immunotherapy efficacy and patient prognosis. However, the regulatory mechanisms governing this process and the therapeutic strategies capable of modulating it remain largely unexplored. Here, we identify HCC-IN-247 as a candidate compound that enhances IFNβ-driven CD8+ T cell infiltration both in vitro and in vivo. Mechanistic investigations reveal that the long noncoding RNA LINC02084 directly interacts with the transcription factor GLIS1 and facilitates its recruitment to the IFNβ promoter. HCC-IN-247 was identified through screening to target the LINC02084-GLIS1 binding interface, thereby stabilizing this RNA–protein complex. Stabilization of the complex significantly enhances IFNβ transcription, which in turn upregulates CXCL10 and CXCL11 expression and promotes CD8+ T cell infiltration. Furthermore, this study engineered a nanoparticle-based delivery system, designated Lip@RA@BSA-PD-L1/IN-247, for the codelivery of HCC-IN-247 and the anti-PD-L1 antibody atezolizumab in HCC treatment. These nanoparticles exhibited robust tumor-specific accumulation and elicited potent synergistic antitumor activity against HCC in mice. Collectively, our findings establish HCC-IN-247 as an activator of the tumor immune microenvironment and provide a preclinical basis for a combined immunotherapeutic approach to HCC.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
All-in-One
Mitochondria-Targeted Iron-Based MOF “Nanomissiles”
for Synergistically Potentiated Tumor Ferroptosis, Dual Phototherapy,
and Chemotherapy
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Pronounced heterogeneity and adaptability of tumors inherently curtail monotherapeutic efficacy, necessitating rationally integrated multimodal regimens that enable precise intervention, overcome resistance, and eradicate heterogeneous cell populations within the complex tumor microenvironment (TME). All-in-one mitochondria-targeted “nanomissiles” were created by emodin (Em)-Fe3+-gated, doxorubicin (DOX)-loaded PCN-600(FeIII) (denoted as DOX@ME) nanoparticles for synergistic multimodal tumor therapy integrating ferroptosis, photodynamic therapy (PDT), mild photothermal therapy (MPTT), and chemotherapy. DOX@ME achieved on-demand release of DOX in response to the TME [such as low pH, glutathione (GSH), hydrogen peroxide (H2O2), and adenosine-5′-triphosphate (ATP)] and near-infrared laser, via the disassembly of the Em-Fe3+ gating films and/or the degradation of the PCN-600(FeIII) nanocarriers. Under both 660 and 808 nm laser irradiation, DOX@ME effectively triggered apoptosis via chemotherapy, PDT, and MPTT while robustly accelerating reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, GSH depletion, glutathione peroxidase 4 (GPX4) downregulation, and lipid peroxide (LPO) accumulation to enhance ferroptosis. Moreover, DOX@ME could alleviate thermotolerance by depleting intracellular ATP and downregulating protective heat shock protein 70 to boost the curative efficacy of MPTT. DOX@ME exhibited excellent antitumor efficacy and good biocompatibility and biosafety in A549 tumor-bearing nude mice. Collectively, DOX@ME demonstrates robust clinical translational potential for precision cancer therapy.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Disulfidptosis-Driven
Immune-Activated Multimodal
Therapy for Glioblastoma with Systemic Safety Control
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Effective glioblastoma therapy requires simultaneous solutions to poor blood–brain barrier (BBB) penetration, insufficient tumor-selective killing, and treatment-related systemic toxicity. We hypothesized that a BBB-penetrating nanoplatform capable of generating distinct H2S exposures in tumor and normal tissues could enhance antitumor efficacy while mitigating doxorubicin (DOX)-induced cardiotoxicity. Here, DOX-loaded metastable molybdenum disulfide nanoflowers functionalized with an I6P8 peptide (DOX@MSI) were developed. After BBB transport and tumor accumulation, the acidic, H2O2-rich, and GSH-rich microenvironment accelerates nanoplatform degradation, promoting GSH depletion and enhanced H2S/DOX release. High local H2S upregulates xCT, while H2S/DOX-mediated mitochondrial inhibition suppresses NADPH regeneration, synergistically triggering disulfidptosis. Meanwhile, H2S suppresses the JAK2/STAT3/IDO axis, alleviating DOX-induced immunosuppression and enhancing immunogenic cell death and T-cell-mediated antitumor immunity. In contrast, slower degradation under physiological conditions enables sustained low-level H2S release, reducing the level of oxidative stress and ERK-associated apoptosis in cardiomyocytes. Together with NIR-enhanced photothermal therapy, DOX@MSI suppresses orthotopic glioblastoma while reducing cardiac injury, thereby integrating tumor-selective multimodal therapy with active organ protection.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Watching Electrochemical
Interfaces in Motion with
High-Speed Atomic Force Microscopy
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Electrochemical processes involve transient phenomena, including nucleation and growth, phase transformations, dissolution, ion transport, and interfacial restructuring, which are difficult to capture simultaneously at nanoscale and in real time under electrochemical controls. High-speed atomic force microscopy (HS-AFM), originally developed for dynamic biological imaging, combines nanometer-scale spatial resolution with frame times of approximately 0.1–5 s/frame, extending into the subsecond regime, enabling direct visualization of electrochemical interfaces under operando conditions. This perspective highlights emerging applications of HS-AFM in electrochemistry, including electrodeposition, nanoparticle dissolution, corrosion, lithiation-induced morphological evolution, protein adsorption, and nanobubble dynamics. HS-AFM reveals that mechanistic insight often resides in transient, nonequilibrium pathways rather than equilibrium structures alone. Advances will enable real-time nanoscale correlation of interfacial structure, kinetics, and electrochemical function.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Subshell-Confined
Symmetry Lowering and Prolonged
Excited-State Dynamics in Large Silver Nanoclusters
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Symmetry breaking has the potential to counteract the shortening of excited-state lifetimes with increasing nuclearity and metallicity but is difficult to accomplish in large nanoclusters, whose multishell frameworks are strongly coupled. Here, we report a four-shell silver nanocluster, Ag104, in which the principal reconstruction is concentrated in an Ag52S22 subsurface shell, and whose inner core and outer ligand-protected motifs retain closely similar topologies relative to its highly symmetric Ag100 analogue – a structurally related pair that enables the correlations accompanying localized symmetry distortion to be examined. The two clusters also differ in composition and thiolate substitution pattern, so the comparison probes coupled structural and electronic changes. Electronic-structure calculations and real-space charge analyses showed that subshell-confined symmetry breaking lifts electronic degeneracies, redistributes oscillator strength, and induces pronounced spatial charge separation, thereby reducing electron–hole overlap. Ultrafast transient absorption spectroscopy further revealed an unexpected order-of-magnitude increase in carrier lifetime from ∼500 ps in Ag100 to ∼5 ns in Ag104 and distinctly activated phonon-assisted relaxation in Ag100 compared to Ag104. This establishes a strategy for engineering large atomically precise nanoclusters with long-lived excited states.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Mechanics-Guided
Conformal Probes Enable Crystallographically
Resolved Anisotropic Interlayer Friction Measurements in Low-Symmetry
2D Materials
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Interlayer sliding in two-dimensional (2D) materials is generally assumed to be weakly anisotropic, even as low-symmetry layered crystals with strongly direction-dependent properties continue to emerge. Here we adopt a mechanics-guided conformal probe design that enables quantitative measurement of crystallographically resolved interlayer friction between anisotropic 2D materials. Using Ta2NiSe5 as a model system, we demonstrate pronounced interlayer friction anisotropy approaching 2 orders of magnitude, substantially larger than its moderate in-plane friction anisotropy and the values reported for high-symmetry layered materials. Atomic-resolution lateral force mapping reveals a hierarchical friction landscape composed of atomic lattice corrugation and twist-induced moiré modulation, with the moiré wavelength evolving systematically with relative misorientation. These results show that interlayer friction in low-symmetry 2D materials is governed by a multiscale, orientation-dependent potential energy landscape and constitutes an independent mechanical degree of freedom. The conformal probe platform provides a general route to probe and engineer direction-selective interlayer mechanics in van der Waals systems.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Phase Homogenization
via Decoupled Nucleation and
Growth for High-Efficiency Quasi-Two-Dimensional Perovskite Light-Emitting
Diodes
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Quasi-two-dimensional (quasi-2D) perovskites with multiquantum-well structures hold great potential for light-emitting diodes (LEDs) due to their cascaded energy funnels, yet their performance is hampered by defect-rich low-n phases and disordered crystallization. Here, we present a phase-homogenization strategy that combines a self-adaptive solvent by doping ethyl acetate (EA) with dimethyl phosphonate (DPP), which simultaneously modulates the polarity and evaporation kinetics of EA, guiding the crystal growth and phase distribution of quasi-2D perovskites. The strong coordination of DPP with Pb2+ also passivates deep-level traps, thereby drastically reducing nonradiative low-n-phase recombination. We further use the bridging molecules to enhance perovskite/transport layer interfaces by incorporating sodium 4-amino-1-naphthalenesulfonate tetrahydrate (SANT) into the PEDOT/PSS hole transport layer, which weakens PEDOT–PSS electrostatic attraction, enhancing conductivity while reducing acid-induced corrosion of the ITO electrode and perovskite film. SANT also templates perovskite nucleation via its functional groups, promoting ordered crystallite growth. Overall, the resulting green-emitting quasi-2D perovskite LEDs achieve a peak external quantum efficiency (EQE) of 32.81% (average 30.74%) and a luminance of 44338 cd m–2, with a lower surface temperature during operation. Moreover, the devices exhibit a 10-fold enhancement in operational stability compared to the control counterparts. Our findings provide a strategy for combining crystallization control and interface passivation in quasi-2D PeLEDs.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Synergistic Tuning
of Diffusion Enables Surface-Passivation-Directed
Electrodeposition of Shaped Bimetallic Nanoparticles
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Many applications for shape-controlled metal nanoparticles require their immobilization on a surface, creating a need for development of direct substrate-based synthesis routes for increasingly complex materials. Colloidal chemical syntheses for shape-controlled nanoparticles are common, but transferring insight from synthesis in solution to growth on a substrate requires accounting for significant differences in reagent diffusion between these two growth environments─a nontrivial challenge. In the present work, we establish fundamental principles for rationally adapting reaction parameters from colloidal syntheses to electrodeposition such that the growth of nanoparticles on the electrode proceeds under comparable reagent diffusion conditions to those that drive shape direction during colloidal growth. To demonstrate these principles, we successfully translate reaction conditions from colloidal synthesis to electrodeposition for a series of dilute bimetallic (silver) gold nanoparticles whose shapes are controlled by surface deposition of silver: concave cubes, octahedra, rhombic dodecahedra, truncated ditetragonal prisms, and tetrahexahedra. By comparing open-circuit potential measurements of the colloidal syntheses with chronopotentiometry measurements from galvanostatic electrodeposition, we determine the adjustments required to establish ideal growth kinetics for each electrodeposition. We identify specific synthetic handles─mode of mass transport, surfactant concentration, applied current density, and secondary metal concentration─required to modulate reagent transport to the electrode surface, as well as the direction they must be modified so that the relative rates of silver and gold ion reduction mimic colloidal growth. These generalizable synthetic parameters for controlling reagent diffusion and concentrations near the electrode surface open possibilities for the electrodeposition of complex multimetallic and shaped nanomaterials.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Emergent
Higher-Order Optical Nonlinearity in Self-Assembled
Polar Supertextures
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Giant optical nonlinearities enable advanced materials control and bridge exotic light-matter phenomena to next-generation photonics. However, materials exhibiting strong higher-order optical nonlinearity beyond the second order are typically rare. Here, we report the discovery of a giant and ultrafast second-harmonic generation (SHG) in self-assembled polar skyrmions under mid-infrared excitations. The transient SHG intensity exhibits a distinctive power dependence originating from higher-order nonlinearity. More generally, we show that large higher-order nonlinearity emerges across diverse domain structures in polar superlattices. Phase-field simulations demonstrate a strong and periodic local permittivity variation within each polar texture at equilibrium, and further confirm the fast polarization oscillation in polar skyrmions with mid-infrared excitations. This intense local permittivity modulation can satisfy epsilon-near-zero conditions, unlocking dramatically enhanced nonlinear optical responses without photonic engineering. Consequently, the self-assembled polar topologies with strong inherent optical nonlinearity could establish a platform for quantum information processing and high-speed optical communications.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title: Au Nanoparticle-Functionalized Antheraea pernyi Silk Nanofibrils: A Spatially Adaptive Anti-Inflammatory and Pro-Regenerative Paradigm for Disparate Chronic Epithelial Diseases
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Management of disparate chronic epithelial diseases relies on fragmented site-specific protocols yet remains hindered by common pathological barriers and sustained inflammation. Herein, we developed a top-down strategy to exfoliate short nanofibrils from Antheraea pernyi silk fibers featuring inherent Arg-Gly-Asp (RGD) motifs, followed by in situ growth of Au nanoparticles. The resulting platform (Au@ASFs) achieved superior spatial adaptability via catalytic oxygen propulsion, navigating across barriers to reach deep-seated lesions. Once localized, Au@ASFs provided phase-spanning multifunctional therapy through near-infrared (NIR)-triggered photothermal sterilization. Through RGD–integrin interactions, they also promoted hemostasis and M2 macrophage polarization to resolve persistent inflammation while enhancing fibroblast migration, angiogenesis, and neuronal differentiation. In vivo, Au@ASFs (+NIR) significantly improved closure of infected diabetic oral ulcers from 43.1 to 95.5% by day 7 and restored colon length in ulcerative colitis from 66.3 to 97.7% of healthy controls. In infected diabetic wounds, Au@ASFs (+NIR) increased closure from 63.8 to 89.1% by day 14. Transcriptomic analysis of wound tissues revealed reprogramming through suppressed NF-κB inflammatory signaling, activated Wnt5a/GSK-3β signaling for neuronal differentiation, and modulated PI3K-Akt signaling for tissue regeneration. Collectively, Au@ASF (+NIR) consistently resolves chronic epithelial diseases across disparate anatomical sites, establishing a unified drug-free paradigm that transcends site-specific constraints.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Strain-Engineered
Deterministic Quantum Dots for Telecom
O-Band Emission Using Buried Stressors
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The deterministic realization of quantum light sources operating at telecom wavelengths is essential for long-distance fiber-based quantum communication and distributed quantum computing. In this work, we demonstrate that telecom O-band emission can be achieved from site-controlled InGaAs/GaAs quantum dots (QDs). Our concept utilizes a buried AlAs/AlOx stressor layer with the unique feature of inducing a well-defined and controllable tensile strain field at the growth surface, enabling both site-selective nucleation at the mesa’s centers and a redshift of QD emission to the ∼1.3 μm wavelength range. This concept not only eliminates the need for strain-reducing layers (SRLs), which are known to degrade optical coherence, but also provides spatial control and spectral tunability. The grown telecom QDs show single-photon emission with g(2)(0) = (5.0 ± 1.0) × 10–2 at 4 K and (2.8 ± 0.3) × 10–1 at 77 K, demonstrating the quantum nature and thermal stability of the emitters. The emission characteristics of complex excitonic states are analyzed using 8-band k·p and configuration-interaction modeling, which quantitatively reproduces the experimental observations. Finally, we present a theory-supported strategy to further redshift the emission toward the center of the O-band and beyond by employing a multiburied stressor approach. This combined framework of experiment and theory establishes the buried stressor concept as a scalable route toward highly coherent, position-controlled O-band quantum emitters compatible with scalable photonic integration.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Ultrasensitive
Enantioselective Chiroptical Sensing
with Large-Area Twisted Aligned Carbon Nanotube Films
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Enantioselective chiroptical sensing is gaining traction across various applications. However, intrinsic molecular chiroptical responses are weak, and existing amplification approaches add synthesis, manufacturing, or operational complexity that limits sensitivity and scalability. Here, we present an enantioselective sensing paradigm merging adsorption-driven chirality induction with large-scale optical transduction in twisted stacks of aligned carbon nanotube (CNT) films. Chiral molecules adsorb onto CNTs to form chiroptically active composites that are macroscopically assembled by alignment and rotational stacking, yielding large ultraviolet circular dichroism (CD). We resolve enantiomer handedness and quantify concentration in single-enantiomer aqueous solutions using a single sensor without lithography, hotspot delivery, or a paired opposite-handed reference. We achieve high sensitivity with estimated sub-μM minimum detectable concentrations for glucose and provide a proof-of-concept demonstration with alanine. Neither analyte-only solution shows detectable CD under the present measurement conditions. We demonstrate Langmuir-type adsorption behavior using molecular dynamics simulations and reproduce experimental results using optical simulations. This platform provides a foundation for future development toward cost-effective in situ enantiomer monitoring in aqueous environments.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Chirality-Functionalized
Covalent Organic Frameworks
for Enantioselective Neuroprotection with Restored Neuroactive Signaling
in Alzheimer’s Disease
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is driven by amyloid-β (Aβ) accumulation and a cascade of interconnected neurotoxic events, including oxidative stress, glutamate excitotoxicity, calcium dysregulation, and impaired neuroactive ligand–receptor signaling. To address the multifactorial nature of AD pathology, chiral d- or l-cysteine-functionalized covalent organic framework (COF) nanoparticles are developed as a multitarget nanotherapeutic platform. Both enantiomers effectively inhibit Aβ aggregation, scavenge reactive oxygen species, reduce extracellular glutamate levels, and attenuate calcium dysregulation. In parallel, d/l-Cys-COFs rescue compromised neuroactive ligand–receptor signaling, as evidenced by normalized expression of neuropeptide Y and brain-derived neurotrophic factor. In transgenic AD mice, d/l-Cys-COF treatment significantly improves memory and cognitive performance. Notably, the d-enantiomer affords superior neuroprotection through enhanced suppression of pathological intracellular calcium overload, whereas restoration of neuroactive ligand–receptor signaling remains chirality-independent. These findings identify chirality as a key design element for multitarget nanotherapeutics against AD, with enantioselective efficacy arising primarily from differential regulation of calcium dysregulation and shared restoration of neuroactive signaling contributing to the overall therapeutic benefit.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Ion
Transport Enhancement
in Charge-Regulating Hydrogels
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Weak polyelectrolyte hydrogels are emerging as a versatile platform for ion transport and separation, desalination, and energy applications. However, a predictive understanding of how dynamic charge regulation at the nanoscopic scale influences ionic mobility in these polymer networks remains elusive. Here, using large-scale molecular simulations, we dissect the coupled mechanisms governing small-ion transport in weak polyelectrolyte hydrogels, and reveal how charge density, competitive binding, and dynamic charge regulation jointly control ion mobility. By systematically isolating these effects, we uncover a pronounced nonmonotonic dependence of ion self-diffusion on hydrogel pKa and salt concentration for multivalent ions. Strikingly, allowing the hydrogel backbone to dynamically regulate its charge eliminates this nonmonotonicity and leads to dramatic enhancements in ion mobility, with diffusion coefficients increasing by more than a factor of 2 for trivalent ions. We attribute this effect to a protonation-assisted hopping mechanism that continuously remodels the local electrostatic landscape, providing an additional molecular-scale pathway for ion unbinding beyond translational escape and accelerating ion-pair kinetics without affecting the fraction of free ions. Our results demonstrate that dynamic nanoscale charge regulation can decouple ion mobility from equilibrium binding strength, offering a powerful design lever unavailable in fixed-charge materials. Building upon these insights, we propose simple molecular design principles for next-generation ion-conducting hydrogels and suggest alternative strategies for nanostructured membranes, energy materials, and biologically inspired charge-adaptive soft matter.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
Centrosymmetry Breaking
of Cobalt–Vanadium-Layered
Double Hydroxide Nanosheets via Nitrogen Doping for Enhanced Piezocatalytic
Tumor Therapy
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Piezocatalysis has emerged as a promising tumor therapeutic strategy because it enables oxygen-independent generation of multiple reactive oxygen species (ROS) with deep tissue penetration. However, the piezocatalytic efficiency of piezoelectric nanomaterials remains constrained by limited lattice distortion, low carrier separation efficiency, and insufficient catalytic active sites. Herein, we report the centrosymmetry breaking of cobalt–vanadium-layered double hydroxide (CoV-LDH) nanosheets via nitrogen doping for efficient ultrasound (US)-mediated piezocatalytic tumor therapy. Owing to the nitrogen doping-induced disruption of the centrosymmetric structure and lattice distortion in CoV-LDH, nitrogen-doped CoV-LDH (N-CoV-LDH) achieves an ultrahigh piezoelectric coefficient of 89.4 pm·V–1, which is superior to that of previously reported piezocatalytic nanomaterials. Moreover, nitrogen doping introduces an unsaturated coordination environment, significantly promoting the adsorption and activation of O2 (Eads = −2.63 eV) and H2O (Eads = −2.37 eV), thereby enhancing piezocatalytic redox reaction kinetics (k &gt; 1.1 × 103 min–1·g–1). Consequently, under low-power US stimulation (0.15 W·cm–2), N-CoV-LDH nanosheets exhibit markedly enhanced ROS generation efficiency, including that of hydroxyl radicals (·OH), superoxide anions (·O2–), and singlet oxygen (1O2). This robust piezocatalytic ROS generation induces tumor cell apoptosis and immunogenic cell death, thereby activating an antitumor immune response characterized by dendritic cell maturation, M1 macrophage polarization, and T cell activation. Ultimately, N-CoV-LDH-mediated piezocatalytic therapy achieves suppression rates of 97.78% for primary tumors and 87.67% for metastatic tumors, establishing an efficient therapeutic paradigm for suppressing tumor metastasis and recurrence.</jats:p>
journal: ACS Nano

title:
When Transition
Metal Dichalcogenides Twist: Opportunities
for Spintronics and Quantum Technologies
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Moiré superlattices form quantum-active interfaces in which geometric reconstruction of stacked two-dimensional (2D) materials generates emergent quantum phases that are not present in the parent materials. These engineered interfaces give rise to a wide range of quantum phenomena, including strongly correlated electronic states, flat-band formation, topological phases of matter, and spin–valley locking, all of which can be tuned in situ through the twist angle. Twisted hetero/homostructures of 2D transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) exhibit an unprecedented degree of control over electronic and spin degrees of freedom, driving rapid advances in the emerging field of twistronics and opening pathways toward next-generation spintronic device applications. In this Review, we examine the fundamental concepts, applications, and prospects of twisted 2D TMDs. We outline the evolution from three-dimensional (3D) to 2D materials and the concept of twistronics, then highlight the emergent structural and magnetic properties of twisted 2D TMDs and their heterostructures. Finally, we discuss the remaining challenges and future directions toward applications in spintronic and quantum technologies.</jats:p>

title:
Oxygen-Promoted
Dehydrogenation on Size-Selected Cu–Pd
Pentamer Clusters for Low-Temperature Hydrogen Release from Cyclic
Hydrocarbons
content:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Despite extensive studies on cycloalkane and cycloalkene dehydrogenation for liquid organic hydrogen carrier applications, the mechanisms governing selective H2 release under mild conditions remain poorly understood. Here, subnanometer CuxPdy pentamer clusters supported on ZrO2 represent a highly active and selective class of low-temperature dehydrogenation catalysts. Pd5 exhibits the highest benzene and molecular H2 formation rates from dehydrogenation of cyclohexene, followed by Cu2Pd3 and Cu3Pd2, whereas Cu5 is inactive. All active catalysts favored H2 over H2O as the hydrogen-containing product and completely suppressed combustion pathways, with no detectable CO2 formation. Oxygen-lean conditions further favored H2 formation across all active catalysts, with H2 selectivity exceeding 99% for Pd5. Kinetic analysis of Cu3Pd2 reveals positive fractional apparent orders in both C6H10 and O2 and an effective apparent activation energy of approximately 66 kJ·mol–1, while reactant composition and temperature systematically control H2/H2O branching. In situ XPS and in situ GIWAXS reveal that catalytic activity and cluster stability arise from the interplay of atomic composition, electronic structure, metal–oxygen interactions, and the chemical environment, with Cu exhibiting a composition-sensitive redox response and Pd-containing clusters accommodating oxygen while retaining electronically active Pd-derived states near the Fermi level. DFT/MLIP free-energy calculations identify kinetically accessible O-assisted first C–H activation pathways involving H transfer to cluster-bound O, with barriers strongly dependent on cluster composition and O configuration. These findings establish an ensemble-based structure–activity framework for controlling dehydrogenation pathways and provide design principles for catalysts that efficiently promote selective hydrogen release suitable for hydrogen carrier applications.</jats:p>
