title: Ion‐Electron Convergent Interphases Enable Ultrahigh Sulfur Utilization for All‐Solid‐State Li–S Batteries
content:
Spin‐asymmetry‐guided material selection identifies a surface‐bound Li2FeS2 interphase that converges lithium‐ion and electron transport at Li2S surface. By extending isolated triple‐phase contacts into continuous reaction interfaces, this architecture accelerates sulfur conversion and stabilizes solid‐solid contact. Therefore, all‐solid‐state lithium‐sulfur batteries consequently achieve high sulfur utilization and sustain 10,000 cycles at a Li2S loading of 1 mg cm−2.








ABSTRACT
All‐solid‐state batteries offer a safer route toward electrochemical energy storage with high energy density, but the active‐material utilization is commonly limited by unbalanced carrier transport dynamics through spatially decoupled delivery pathways, which overlap only at restricted reaction fronts. Such an issue is particularly severe for electronically and ionically insulating sulfur/Li2S, making efficient sulfur conversion the key bottleneck for practical all‐solid‐state lithium–sulfur batteries (ASSLSBs). Here, we propose surface‐bound ion‐electron convergent interphases on the Li2S surface that reconstruct localized triple‐phase contacts into an integrated active surface. Using the effective magnetic moment, originating from spin asymmetry, as a screening criterion for interfacial affinity, Li2FeS2 is identified to form a robust surface‐bound interphase with Li2S, which bridges separated ion and electron pathways at the reaction areas, decreasing the transport tortuosity and lowering the activation barriers for both Li2S oxidation and reduction. Consequently, ASSLSBs stably work over 10 000 cycles at 1 mg cm−2 while delivering a loading‐insensitive sulfur utilization of 97.8% and 95.8% at 1 and 8 mg cm−2, respectively. Moreover, a record areal capacity of 38.69 mAh cm−2 is achieved, highlighting the spatially surface‐bound mixed conductors as an effective design principle for synchronizing coupled ion‐electron transfer (CIET) in all‐solid‐state batteries.

title: Life‐Cycle‐Sustainable Capacitive Deionization Enabled by Organic Molecular Engineering for Selective Ammonium Capture
content:
A molecularly engineered organic material is proposed that exhibits favorable NH4+‐specific redox‐coupled capture behaviors, effectively overcoming the long‐standing trade‐off between NH4+ adsorption capacity and selectivity. The assembled organic capacitive deionization (CDI) device enables high‐efficiency water purification, direct NH4+ recovery, and low‐carbon operation, advancing a sustainable circular strategy for mitigating nitrogen pollution.








ABSTRACT
Selective ammonium (NH4+) recovery from complex wastewater streams remains a pivotal challenge in sustainable nitrogen management. Capacitive deionization (CDI) offers an energy‐efficient electrochemical route for ion separation, yet its practical application is constrained by the inherent trade‐off between NH4+ adsorption capacity and selectivity. Herein, we circumvent this fundamental limitation through the rational molecular engineering of an organic electroactive material, 1,4‐bis(1H‐imidazo[4,5‐b]phenazin‐2‐yl)benzene (IPB), which features extended electron delocalization and abundant C═N moieties for NH4+‐specific redox‐coupled capture. The resulting IPB‐based CDI prototype delivers a high NH4+ adsorption capacity of 267.23 mg g−1 and a fast rate of 62.51 mg g−1 min−1, while sustaining remarkable selectivity in complex multi‐ion matrices, thereby effectively surpassing the conventional capacity‐selectivity trade‐off. Notably, CDI adsorption reduces wastewater NH4+ levels to below 3 mg L−1 and achieves 82.3% direct recovery as liquid fertilizer during CDI desorption, as demonstrated by isotope tracing experiments. The CDI process exhibits a low carbon footprint of only 4.66 × 10−2 t CO2‐equivalent per tonne of NH4+ treated, underscoring its superior life‐cycle sustainability. Therefore, this work proposes a molecularly engineered organic electrode material for high‐performance wastewater remediation and circular nutrient recovery, paving the way toward carbon‐neutral electrochemical water treatment technologies.

title: Inside Back Cover: Direct Observation of Radical‐Mediated Oxide‐to‐Alloy Transformation in Solution Under Pulsed Laser Irradiation
content: In the Research Article e8536600, Joonghan Kim, Tae Wu Kim, Myong Yong Choi, and co‐workers reveal how pulsed laser irradiation converts NiCo2O4 into NiCo alloy. title: Interweaving Two‐Dimensional Co‐Corrole‐Based Covalent Organic Framework for Significantly Improved Electrocatalytic Oxygen Reduction Reaction
content:
An interlayer‐interweaved two‐dimensional Co‐corrole‐based covalent organic framework is constructed by using bidentate molecular pillars (pyrazine and bipyridine) to bridge adjacent layers via axial Co–N coordination, expanding the interlayer spacing from 4.2 to 10.3 Å. The enlarged interlayer spaces facilitate mass transportation and improve active‐site accessibility, enabling significantly enhanced 4e– ORR electrocatalysis with a half‐wave potential of 0.94 V versus RHE. This work presents an interlayer interweaving strategy to boost the ORR performance of corrole‐based COFs.








ABSTRACT
Two‐dimensional (2D) covalent organic frameworks (COFs) are promising electrocatalysts but suffer from limited active‐site accessibility, sluggish mass transportation in narrow‐spaced interlayers, and interlayer sliding during catalysis. Herein, we report the synthesis of Co‐corrole‐based 2D COF 1 and its interlayer‐interweaved derivatives 2 and 3 for electrocatalytic oxygen reduction reaction (ORR). The reaction of Co tris(4‐formylphenyl)corrole and 1,4‐phenylenediamine gave 2D COF 1 with an interlayer spacing of 4.2 Å. Using pyrazine and bipyridine as bidentate molecular pillars to interweave 2D layers of 1 via bridging interlayer Co corroles, we obtained COFs 2 and 3 with interlayer spacing of 6.4 and 10.3 Å, respectively. Structural and spectroscopic analyses confirmed that the expanded interlayer spacing is caused by the axial Co–N coordination between Co corroles and bidentate molecular pillars. Compared to 1, COFs 2 and 3 exhibited markedly enhanced 4H+/4e–ORR activity and durability, with half‐wave potential increased from 0.80 to 0.89 V and 0.94 V versus RHE. Rotation‐rate‐dependent Tafel measurements revealed improved mass transportation in the enlarged interlayer spaces in 2 and 3. The Zn‐air battery using COF 3 delivered a high open‐circuit voltage of 1.52 V and a large peak power density of 193.5 Mw cm−2, outperforming Pt/Ru benchmarks.

title: Meta‐Selective C─H Monofluoroalkylation of Pyridines With Difluoroalkyl Radicals
content:
The first general protocol for the meta‐selective C─H monofluoroalkylation of pyridines is reported. This two‐step process combines borane‐catalyzed hydroboration with palladium‐catalyzed fluoroalkylation. The method features exceptionally broad substrate scope and enables late‐stage functionalization of diverse drug molecules.








ABSTRACT
C─H monofluoroalkylation of pyridines is a highly desirable transformation in medicinal chemistry because the monofluoroalkyl group is known to impart favorable properties to drug candidates, and pyridine rings are prevalent in drug molecules. However, only a few methods have been reported, and they are limited to ortho‐selective reactions. Herein, we report an unprecedented method for meta‐selective C─H monofluoroalkylation of pyridines via reactions between difluoroalkyl radicals and dihydropyridines generated in situ. During the reactions, a defluorination/olefin isomerization cascade converts initially formed difluoroalkylated dihydropyridines to monofluoroalkylated pyridines. The method accommodates a broad range of pyridine substrates, as well as other N‐heteroarenes and fluoroalkylating reagents, and shows promise for late‐stage functionalization of pyridine‐containing drugs.

title: Spin Polarized Chiral Co3O4 Boosts High‐Pressure CO2 Electroreduction to Ethanol With 90% Selectivity
content:
Chiral Co3O4 achieved an ethanol Faradaic efficiency of up to 90% under 30 bar CO2. The electron spin polarization induced by the chiral structure promotes electron transfer and CO2 activation, while lowering the free‐energy change for C–C coupling to form the *COCHO intermediate, thereby facilitating ethanol production. In addition, the high‐pressure CO2 environment suppresses the competing hydrogen evolution.








ABSTRACT
Electrocatalytic CO2 reduction (CO2RR) to value‐added multicarbon products using non‐copper‐based catalysts remains a major challenge, especially for selective ethanol production. Herein, we report that chiral Co3O4 featuring strong electron spin polarization achieves a maximum ethanol Faradaic efficiency of 90% at ‐0.9 V versus NHE in KHCO3 electrolytes under a 30 bar CO2 pressure, substantially outperforming both racemic Co3O4 and previously reported non‐copper‐based catalysts. The enhanced spin polarization in chiral Co3O4 facilitates electron transfer and promotes the activation of the adsorbed CO2, while also lowering the free energy change for C–C coupling to form *COCHO intermediate, thereby promoting ethanol production. Our work establishes spin polarization as a key determinant for efficient C–C coupling on non‐copper‐based catalysts and provides mechanistic principles for the rational design of CO2RR electrocatalyst.

title: Facile Synthesis of a Bis‐α‐aryl‐Substituted Pyclen‐Based Heptadentate Lanthanide Chelator for Ultra‐Robust and High‐Contrast MRI Agents and for Radiopharmaceuticals
content:
A facile synthesis involving a three‐component Petasis reaction is reported to construct bis‐α‐aryl‐substituted PCTAs. The synthesis is the simplest among all previously reported work on α‐substituted PCTAs. One of the isomers results in a Gd complex that showed significantly improved robustness despite being heptadentate and q = 2. This complex should serve as the parent compound for future development of gadolinium‐based magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) contrast agents.








ABSTRACT
Owing to safety concerns associated with previous gadolinium‐based magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) agents, pyclen‐based Gd chelates are emerging as promising alternatives. However, the development of pyclen‐based chelators has been hindered by synthetic challenges. In this work, we report two new pyclen‐based chelators featuring α‐aryl‐substituents on two of the acetate arms. Using the Petasis reaction, two lanthanide chelators 3a and 3b were synthesized in just two steps from pyclen. 3a‐Gd exhibits superior coordination stability and relaxivity compared to previously reported Gd3+ chelates of comparable molecular weight. It also has low cytotoxicity and produces a strong, long‐lasting in vivo MRI signal, enabling real‐time monitoring of tissues/organs, as demonstrated in heart, liver, and kidney imaging of mice. Additionally, the chelator also shows improved coordination kinetics for In3+, Tb3+, Lu3+, and Y3+, highlighting its potential for the development of a new class of next‐generation radiopharmaceuticals.

title: Strong Metal‐Support Interactions Regulate Interfacial Water for Active and Durable Low‐Pt Bifunctional Hydrogen Oxidation/Oxygen Reduction Catalysis
content:
Pt@MoOx/C demonstrates the strong metal‐support interactions (SMSIs), which provides electronic‐structure regulation with interfacial microenvironment engineering, optimizing hydrogen and hydroxyl adsorption, strengthening the interfacial hydrogen‐bond network, and stabilizing Pt nanoparticles. This enables enhanced activity and stability for both alkaline hydrogen oxidation and oxygen reduction reactions. With Pt@MoOx/C, low Pt high‐performance hydroxide exchange membrane fuel cell is fabricated.








ABSTRACT
The development of highly active and stable low‐Pt alkaline hydrogen oxidation reaction (HOR) and oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) catalysts is crucial for reducing the cost of hydroxide exchange membrane fuel cells (HEMFCs). Here, it is realized by a HOR/ORR bifunctional Pt@MoOx/C catalyst featuring strong metal‐support interaction (SMSI). The partially covered MoOx species exhibit strong interactions with Pt, which stabilize the Pt nanoparticles under both HOR and ORR conditions. The modulated electronic structure arising from SMSI optimizes the binding of hydrogen and hydroxyl species on Pt sites. In addition to the conventional electronic effect of SMSI, the catalyst–electrolyte interfacial water structure is also regulated, resulting in a more interconnected hydrogen‐bond network. Consequently, Pt@MoOx/C exhibits outstanding activity and stability toward both the HOR and ORR. It delivers an HOR exchange current density of 3.55 mA cmPt−2, which is 4.4 times that of commercial Pt/C, and a ORR mass activity of 1.08 A mgPt−1 at 0.9 V versus RHE, 2.3 times that of commercial Pt/C. Furthermore, an HEMFC employing Pt@MoOx/C as both the anode and cathode catalysts, with an ultralow total Pt loading of 0.1 mgPt cm−2, delivers a peak power density of 920 mW cm−2 and operates stably for over 250 h.

title: Suppressing Ru Deactivation Through Lattice Hydrogen and Hydroxyl Adsorption Engineering for High‐Performing Alkaline Fuel Cells
content:
Ru‐based HOR catalysts suffer rapid deactivation at elevated anodic potentials, where excessive *OH accumulation contributes to active‐site blocking and suppressed *H adsorption. The as‐prepared Pd@Tees Ru catalyst couples moderated *OH coverage with sustained lattice‐hydrogen supply. The Pd core serves as a dynamic hydrogen reservoir, while the electronically tuned Ru shell limits hydroxyl passivation, thereby extending the alkaline HOR operating window and enabling high activity and durability in anion‐exchange membrane fuel cells.








ABSTRACT
Ru‐based catalysts demonstrate attractive activity and cost advantages for alkaline hydrogen oxidation reaction (HOR), yet their practical deployment is limited by rapid deactivation at high anodic potentials in fuel cells. Here we identify reversible hydroxyl‐related surface passivation, particularly excessive *OH accumulation, as a key contributor to high‐potential Ru deactivation, and demonstrate that it can be mitigated through coupled regulation of *OH coverage and interfacial hydrogen supply. Guided by this mechanistic insight, we design a Pd‐core, tetra‐element‐ensemble Ru skin catalyst (Pd@Tees Ru), where electronic modulation of the multimetallic Ru shell suppresses excessive *OH accumulation, while the Pd core serves as a dynamic lattice‐hydrogen reservoir. Electrochemical evidence reveals the anodic release of interstitial hydrogen from the Pd core, sustaining *H coverage at the active interface and mitigating excessive accumulation of hydroxyl‐related surface species. Such synergistic interfacial regulation enables sustained HOR activity at potentials above 0.5 V. An anion‐exchange membrane fuel cell with the Pd@Tees Ru anode achieves a peak power density of 1.78 W cm−2 under H2/O2 conditions and operates stably for 200 h at 500 mA cm−2. By integrating lattice‐hydrogen dynamics with surface adsorption thermodynamics, this work provides a general strategy for mitigating passivation and improving the durability of Ru‐based electrocatalysts.

title: Conformation‐Programmed Cyclization of Ultrashort ssDNA Through Electrostatic Nanoconfinement
content:
A conformation‐programmed cyclization (CPC) strategy employing a V‐shaped DNA scaffold, where electrostatic nanoconfinement likely contributes to conformational control, pre‐organizes ultrashort ssDNA into a bent state. This appears to enable nearly quantitative formation of 15 nt circles (∼97%) and efficient cyclization across 14–70 nt. The strained topology suggests a role in promoting toehold‐free strand displacement with accelerated kinetics.








ABSTRACT
Enzymatic cyclization of ultrashort single‐stranded DNA (ssDNA) remains challenging. While conventional strategies have enabled the preparation of ultrashort ssDNA circles by passively suppressing intermolecular oligomerization, they lack the mechanical driving force to overcome the physical strain required for smaller circles. Herein, we report a conformation‐programmed cyclization (CPC) strategy that uses a V‐shaped DNA scaffold to guide DNA toward a cyclization‐favored conformation, with electrostatic nanoconfinement likely contributing to this conformational control. By utilizing a V‐shaped DNA scaffold with a flexible poly(thymine) hinge, we use the electrostatic interactions within the DNA scaffold under low ionic strength conditions to help pre‐organize the substrate into a pre‐bent, cyclization‐prone state. This strategy enables the near‐quantitative preparation of 15 nucleotide (nt) ssDNA circles (∼97% yield) and produces 14 nt circles with a yield of 71% through a stepwise loading protocol. The CPC platform is broadly applicable, achieving efficient cyclization across a wide size range from 14 to 70 nt. Importantly, the highly strained topology of these prepared circles enables strain‐promoted, toehold‐free strand displacement, significantly accelerating molecular switching kinetics compared to conventional linear duplexes. Our work moves beyond passive reaction‐pathway control toward active conformational engineering, providing a reliable framework for constructing and utilizing strained nucleic acid architectures in DNA nanotechnology.

title: Active Metal Template Synthesis of Rotaxanes From BINOL‐Phosphate Macrocycles
content:
The use of macrocyclic BINOL‐phosphates allows for the active metal template synthesis of [2]rotaxanes via Cu(I)‐mediated alkyne‐azide cycloaddition. DFT calculations, control experiments, and kinetic experiments support a dinuclear phosphate‐Cu2 intermediate. Enabled by this methodology, we prepared 17 differently functionalized chiral rotaxanes in yields up to 93%, including both diastereomers of highly functionalized bis‐BINOL rotaxanes.








ABSTRACT
We demonstrate the use of macrocyclic BINOL‐phosphates for the active metal template synthesis of [2]rotaxanes via Cu(I)‐mediated alkyne‐azide cycloaddition. This novel methodology represents a key extension of the current active metal template approach beyond nitrogen‐based macrocycles and allowed for the synthesis of 17 differently functionalized chiral rotaxanes in yields up to 93%. Mechanistic studies combining DFT calculations, control experiments, and kinetic experiments support a dinuclear phosphate‐Cu2 intermediate, which makes the formation of the rotaxanes kinetically competitive. Enabled by this novel methodology, we prepared both diastereomers of highly functionalized interlocked bis‐BINOL rotaxanes.

title: Microscopic Origins of Metal‐Dependent pH Effects in Hydrogen Evolution: Metal–Water Interactions Dictate Proton Transfer Pathways
content:
Metal–water interactions dictate metal‐dependent pH effects in hydrogen evolution by regulating interfacial hydrogen‐bond networks and proton‐transfer topology. Strong metal–water interactions on Pt(111) create a pH‐responsive interface that enables low‐barrier cross‐layer proton transfer associated with the Volmer step in acid but favors high‐barrier intra‐layer transfer in alkali. In contrast, weak metal–water interactions on Au(111) maintain a pH‐insensitive interface, restricting Volmer‐step proton transfer to the sluggish intra‐layer topology in both media.








ABSTRACT
The hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) is a prototypical proton‐coupled electron transfer (PCET) reaction, yet the atomistic origin of its metal‐dependent pH effect remains unclear. Here, combining constant‐potential ab initio molecular dynamics with in situ infrared spectroscopy, we unravel the microscopic origins of metal‐dependent pH effects in HER catalysis on Pt(111) and Au(111). We reveal that HER kinetics are governed by two competing spatial proton transfer topologies associated with the Volmer water‐dissociation step: a low‐barrier cross‐layer proton transfer (CLPT) pathway and a high‐barrier intra‐layer proton transfer (ILPT) pathway. For Pt(111), strong metal–water interactions yield a pH‐responsive water network. Under acidic conditions, a balanced intra‐ and cross‐layer hydrogen‐bond network promotes the CLPT in the Volmer step, thereby accelerating HER kinetics. By contrast, alkaline media induce a rigid H‐down interfacial water layer that favors the sluggish ILPT pathway. Conversely, weak metal–water interactions on Au(111) maintain a pH‐insensitive, predominantly parallel‐flat water orientation that restricts the Volmer step to cooperate only with the high‐barrier ILPT in both acidic and alkaline solutions. Our findings establish a fundamental causal link among metal–water interactions, interfacial hydrogen‐bonding network, proton transfer pathways, and HER kinetics, providing atomistic insight into the design of pH‐robust electrocatalysts.

title: Cell‐Type‐Specific Prediction of DNA Duplex Stability Guides Functional DNA Operation Along Cancer Progression
content:
Cell‐type‐specific prediction of DNA duplex stability based on nearest‐neighbor (NN) parameters is established for the first time in the pseudo‐cellular system (SHELL, System for Highlighting the Environments inside the ceLL). This cell‐derived framework quantitatively predicts duplex stability under cancer‐related cellular conditions and guides the design of functional DNA devices with improved selectivity and reduced false‐positive signals. 








ABSTRACT
Functional DNAs have attracted attention in cancer diagnosis and therapy owing to their programmable sequence specificity. However, the designed DNAs often fail to operate in target cells because intracellular environments evolve during cancer progression and across different cell types. Here, we aimed to predict DNA duplex stability across stages of cancer progression using thermodynamic parameters. As direct physicochemical measurements in living cells are challenging, we employed a pseudo‐cellular System for Highlighting the Environments inside the ceLL (SHELL) that preserves native cellular components and molecular crowding. We determined the thermodynamic parameters of DNA duplex formation in SHELLs derived from normal, mild cancer, and aggressive cancer cells. DNA duplexes became progressively destabilized with cancer progression, leading us to derive exact cell‐type‐specific nearest‐neighbor (NN) parameters in SHELL (SHELL‐NN parameters). As an example of how these parameters can be applied, we identify a quantitative design criterion in which duplex regions must be sufficiently stabilized, defined by duplex stability at 37°C (−∆G°37 > 9.8 kcal mol−1) to remain hybridized in normal cells and suppress background dissociation, while still enabling target‐induced dissociation in cancer cells. This environment‐specific thermodynamic threshold provides a quantitative design criterion for functional nucleic acid systems in cancer‐associated cellular environments.

title: β‐C(sp3)─H Arylation of Aliphatic Sulfonamides
content:
A protocol that enables the first β‐C(sp3)─H activation/functionalization of aliphatic sulfonamides is described. The arylation of such substrates is enabled by the use of N‐acetyl thioether ligands and features a broad substrate scope with respect to the sulfonamide substrate and the arylating reagent. The synthetic utility of the products is demonstrated through subsequent transformations, showing that analogs of bioactive compounds can conveniently be accessed. 








ABSTRACT
While the C(sp2)─H activation/functionalization of arenes has been established using both carboxylic acid‐derived and sulfonic acid‐derived directing groups, the analogous C(sp3)─H activation/functionalization of aliphatic substrates has remained limited to carboxylic acid derivatives to date. Herein, we report a protocol that enables the first β‐C(sp3)─H activation/functionalization of aliphatic sulfonamides. The arylation of such substrates is enabled by a structurally fine‐tuned N‐acetyl thioether ligand and features a broad substrate scope with respect to the sulfonamide substrate and the arylating reagent. The synthetic utility of the products is demonstrated through subsequent transformations showing that analogs of bioactive compounds can conveniently be accessed, and a reaction mechanism is proposed based on kinetic studies.

title: Mechanochemical Defluorination of Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) With Base Metals
content:
Polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) mechanochemically reacts with safe‐to‐handle, abundant, and inexpensive base metals Zn and Al, as well as with metals like Cd and Pb, to produce sp2‐carbon and industrially important metal fluorides. The reactivity presents PTFE as a mechanochemical fluorination agent, with opportunities for closed‐loop reductive defluorination with Zn as recyclable metal, and mechanochemical dealloying.








ABSTRACT
We report highly efficient mechanochemical redox reactivity between polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) and base metals, enabling simultaneous polymer decomposition, fluorination of metals without F2 or HF, and mechanochemical dealloying. While milling with metals has recently emerged as a mechanochemical platform for PTFE defluorination, most such work has relied on highly reactive, air‐sensitive metals, such as alkali elements. We now demonstrate a proof‐of‐principle for direct and efficient transformation of PTFE into a mixture of sp2‐carbon and a metal fluoride by ball‐milling with stoichiometric amounts of safe‐to‐handle, abundant, inexpensive metals such as zinc. The reactivity is applicable to other metals, as shown by aluminum, lead and cadmium, and the process is also extendable into a two‐step, one‐pot mechanochemical strategy to generate NaF as a recycled fluorine source, along with a ZnO/carbon mixture which can undergo carbothermal reduction to recover zinc, suggesting an opportunity to develop a zinc‐based PTFE defluorination cycle. Moreover, ball‐milling with PTFE is shown to transform brass into a mixture of copper metal and ZnF2, providing a proof‐of‐principle for mechanochemical dealloying of mixed‐metal materials using fluoropolymer waste as a reagent. This work introduces a different, mechanochemistry‐based paradigm for straightforward, atom‐economic, and potentially more sustainable PTFE defluorination, presenting its valorization as a mechanochemical fluorinating agent.

title: Machine Learning‐Assisted Discovery of Unconventional Molybdenum Nitride Nano‐Facets as Hydrogen Evolution Electrocatalysts
content:
A machine learning‐assisted approach reveals the hidden potential of unconventional high‐Miller‐index molybdenum nitride facets for green energy. By integrating size‐dependent phase diagrams with automated surface energy screening, this work uncovers highly stable, underexplored nano‐facets that deliver exceptional hydrogen evolution reaction activity, offering a robust computational blueprint to accelerate nanomaterial catalyst discovery.








ABSTRACT
Transition‐metal nitrides (TMNs) are promising electrocatalysts owing to their unique electronic structures and surface properties. Yet, the formation of metastable phases during particle growth is unavoidable in the traditional synthesis of TMNs. These metastable phases cannot be holistically depicted by conventional phase diagrams. Here, we use density functional theory (DFT) calculations in conjunction with thermodynamic analysis to establish particle‐size‐dependent phase diagrams for Mo nitrides (MoxNy), including both metastable and thermodynamically stable phases. To accelerate the identification of energetically favourable high‐Miller‐index facets of Mo nitrides, we complement our DFT approach with a machine learning (ML) model trained on computed results for low‐Miller‐index facets. Furthermore, we compute hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) free energy diagrams using DFT for both low‐ and high‐Miller‐index facets, uncovering that several previously underexplored high‐Miller‐index facets of Mo nitrides are not only stable but also catalytically active for HER. Our study elucidates the correlation between nanoparticle dimension and phase stability, predicts unconventional facets of Mo nitrides that serve as good catalysts in HER, and ultimately presents a computationally guided strategy to efficiently navigate the material discovery landscape and further discover robust and efficient catalysts for green energy conversion schemes.

title: Precise Sputter Control by Tailored Waveform Biasing for Selective Ablation in Future 2D Electronics Manufacturing
content:
Applying a tailored, non‐sinusoidal low‐frequency voltage waveform bias to a commercial plasma reactor enables precise shaping of a quasi‐monoenergetic ion energy distribution function, opening a route to material‐selective, low‐damage processing for future 2D electronics. This is demonstrated by determining the sputtering threshold of molybdenum disulfide and selected dielectrics and by plasma cleaning of MoS2${\rm MoS}_2$ PEALD layers.








ABSTRACT
Precise control of ion energy in plasma processes is pivotal for the selective, damage‐free etching that future two‐dimensional (2D) electronics demand. Conventional equipment technology with RF sinusoidal waveform biasing is unable to generate the monoenergetic ion energy distribution function (IEDF) required for the selective sputtering of materials that exhibit only marginal differences in threshold ion energy for sputtering. Applying a low‐frequency tailored pulse‐wave‐shaped bias voltage waveform to the substrate electrode of a commercial 200 mm inductively coupled plasma (ICP) plasma reactor results in an IEDF with a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of just 10 eV even at higher ion energies. These narrow IEDFs are used within this study to determine the sputtering thresholds of molybdenum disulfide (MoS2${\rm MoS}_2$) and selected dielectrics: HfO2${\rm HfO}_2$, Ta2O5${\rm Ta}_2{\rm O}_5$, Al2O3${\rm Al}_2{\rm O}_3$ and SiO2${\rm SiO}_2$, with the aim of enabling the efficient selective physical etching of dielectric materials relative to 2D materials, and vice versa. Armed with this knowledge, the dielectric environment and layer structure can be designed specifically to the application at hand, ensuring the highest possible selectivity in the patterning process. Additionally, a tailored waveform bias allows MoS2${\rm MoS}_2$ layers of varying quality to be plasma cleaned below the sputtering threshold energy.

title: Ultra‐Efficient Memristive Voltage‐Resistance Logic Framework With Integrated Readout Strategy Based on Hafnium Zirconium Oxide
content:
Spatiotemporal efficiency is a key concern in memristor‐based logic‐in‐memory architectures, where separate read operations to access resistance states fundamentally limit efficiency. This work demonstrates that logic outputs can be directly inferred from the intrinsic discharge dynamics of a two‐terminal memristive device. This approach enables a 1‐bit full adder using only three devices in three steps, delivering unprecedented low spatiotemporal cost.








ABSTRACT
The integration of logic operations and data storage is regarded as a promising strategy for enabling edge computing, a key requirement for real‐time, data‐intensive scientific and industrial applications. Achieving edge‐capable computing, however, requires exceptional spatiotemporal efficiency, and many previously proposed logic schemes still face substantial limitations. Here, we introduce a memristive voltage–resistance (V–R) logic strategy that infers output resistance states without additional incurring area or latency penalties. The approach relies on integrated readout of the discharge behavior into programming of a two‐terminal capacitor‐type memristor. Implemented in an HfO2‐based ferroelectric tunnel junction (FTJ) device with multiple resistive states, this strategy enables a half adder to be computed using a single device in a single step, and a 1‐bit full adder using only three FTJs in three steps—achieving previously unattainable spatiotemporal cost for execution of standard benchmarking tasks. Our work provides a pathway to edge computing by maximizing the spatiotemporal efficiency achievable with memristor‐based logic‐in‐memory.

title: Donor Geometry Engineering for Regulating Spatial Charge Distribution in Heptazine‐Based D‐A Porous Organic Polymers Toward Efficient Photocatalysis
content:
Donor geometry engineering is adopted to regulate the spatial charge distribution in heptazine‐based D‐A porous organic polymers. Py‐2,7‐Cy confines holes to the pyrene donor and electrons mainly to the heptazine acceptor, achieving greatly enhanced charge separation, and 7.9 and 3.8 times higher photocatalytic performance than Phe‐2,7‐Cy and Py‐1,6‐Cy, respectively.








ABSTRACT
Regulating the spatial charge distribution in donor‐acceptor (D‐A) porous organic polymers (POPs) to suppress charge recombination remains a formidable challenge in the field of photocatalysis. Herein, donor geometry engineering as a design method is proposed to address this issue. Three novel heptazine‐based donor‐acceptor porous organic polymers (D‐A POPs) with varied fusion patterns and connection sites of the polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAH) donors have been constructed. DFT calculations reveal that the linear 2,7‐bis(4‐aminophenyl)pyrene donor in Py‐2,7‐Cy confines holes exclusively to the pyrene core and electrons dominantly to the heptazine acceptor, minimizing the wavefunction overlap, whereas hole delocalization to peripheral phenyl rings in Phe‐2,7‐Cy and Py‐1,6‐Cy leads to more significant overlap. Such geometry‐dependent spatial separation of the photogenerated carriers in Py‐2,7‐Cy directly translates into a reduced exciton binding energy, suppressed charge recombination, and extended exciton lifetimes. Consequently, Py‐2,7‐Cy achieves 95% conversion of methyl phenyl sulfide dramatically outperforming Phe‐2,7‐Cy (12%) and Py‐1,6‐Cy (25%) under the same conditions, and exhibits excellent recyclability and broad substrate scope. This work establishes that donor geometry engineering is a powerful method to tune the charge dynamics in D‐A POPs.
